Uniform Title: Prāṇatoṣiṇī Dharmakāṇḍa Author: Rāmatoṣaṇa Compiler: Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya Description: Compiled by Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya. Originally published in Calcutta in Bengali script as part of the Tantrasārādivividhatantrasaṃgraha.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: December 11, 2007.
Publisher: Kalikātā.
Year of publication: Pre-1900.
Country of Publication: India | Title Page || Śrīḥ ||
The *Prāṇatoṣiṇī* was composed by Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya,
having compiled it from the Tantric scriptures.
And it was published by the learned family patriarch and holder of titles,
Śrī Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara Bhaṭṭācāryya, in the city of Calcutta.
Printed at the Kālikātā Press;
though inconceivable, she is to be meditated upon within the hearts of all, and, beautiful as the darkness [of night], she utterly dispels the dense darkness of the mind.
Though you are an ocean of compassion,
you are Mahākālī, the independent one; you possess every form and are yet invisible to the eyes of those filled with pride— may you, the most wonderful of all, be victorious!
There was a man named Rāmahari, who attained fame whose waves were exceedingly cool, which dispelled the heat of the moon-like Rākā (the full moon),
and which fulfilled the hopes of all; he, the purifier of the lineage of Viśvāsa, a vessel of the Guru’s grace and the illuminator of his family, was begotten by the gods as a virtuous son.
[He] named Śrīprāṇakṛṣṇa.
The son of Kṛṣṇamaṅgalavidyāvāgīśa and the son of Gaṅgādevī has composed this second section, the Dharmakāṇḍa, for the delight of the virtuous.
Now the second section, the Dharma-kāṇḍa, which concerns the refinement of the self, is being described.
First, therein, is the praise of that refinement.

The ten sacraments (*saṃskāra*) of the twice-born (*dvija*) grant eligibility for ritual action (*karma-mātra*). For the Śūdras and those of similar status, it should be understood that there are only nine.
The nature of the mantras as being composed of *māyā* and so forth should be recognized as being in accordance with the Kali age.
Then the rite for the fertile period, followed by the impregnation ceremony (garbhādhāna), then the rite for ensuring a male child (puṃsavana),

the offering of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and likewise the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana). Then the birth-rite (jātakarma), followed by the rite for generating intelligence (medhājanana) which bestows poetic skill.

The gift of illusory wealth (māyādāna) to Brahmins for the nourishment of the child should be understood; after that, the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa) is prescribed, followed by the first outing (niṣkramaṇa),
then the first feeding of solid food (annāśana), and after that, the tonsure (cūḍā) and the piercing of the ears.

For maidens and those of the Śūdra caste, all of this is performed without mantras. Regarding the various Vedic traditions, the initiation (upanayana) is proclaimed to consist merely of the sacred thread (sūtra). [This includes] the preparation of the thread, the consecration rites, and the presiding deity of the thread.

The reception of the Sāvitrī, the rite of Samāvartana, the censure of those who have not taken a wife, the description of a lawful wife, and thereafter the marriage ceremony and the performance of the ten sacraments.
Thus ends the first chapter of the second book.
First, the characteristics of a guru, and then the characteristics of a true guru;
the praise of the Kaula guru, the refutation of those who fabricate the meaning of the secret (kūṭārtha);
and the description of the specific types of gurus—these are the necessary requirements regarding the guru in the scripture.
The sequence for meditating on the oneness of the guru, the mantra, and the deity;

the fruit arising from the satisfaction of the guru and so forth; the fruit born from the utterance of the guru’s name; when the guru is satisfied, the entire world is satisfied—the superiority of the guru in every respect.
When the lotus-feet of the Guru are worshipped, one obtains the fruit of worshipping the entire world.
The classification of Gurus according to the distinctions of initiation (*dīkṣā*), instruction (*śikṣā*), and so forth, is now described. Mahākāla alone is the Guru; he is never merely a human being.
By virtue of that [divine] presiding power, there arises the majesty of the human being,
as well as the boundaries of the lineage of gurus— distinguished by animal-mantras and so forth—
and immediately thereafter, the distinction between the higher and lower [levels] of the gurus.

The characteristics of a woman who is to be considered a Guru must be avoided; likewise, [the characteristics of] one who is to be considered a Guru must be avoided. A Guru should be abandoned by a disciple if he possesses [certain] characteristics, and likewise, [the disciple's] avoidance [of such a person] is required.
Censure directed at the disciple by the Guru is to be avoided, as is the transgression of the Guru’s command.
The fault of stealing the teacher's property and so forth, as well as performing undesirable acts;
the fault arising from the teacher’s curse and from hearing his censure;
and the remedy for hearing that [censure] regarding one who reviles the teacher.
There is fault in perceiving the Guru as a mere human being, as well as in censuring him;

there is fault in acts of hostility toward the Guru and the like, as well as in abandoning the Guru’s household; and likewise, there is a prohibition against showing disrespect or failing to honor the Guru’s lineage.
The sanctity of the time for seeing the guru is the worship of the guru;
likewise, the fault of performing worship other than that which is desired [by the guru], and the fruit born from the worship of the guru;
as well as the imperishability of the merit from duties performed while staying at the guru’s house.
A description of the majesty of the water from the lotus-like feet of the Guru;
the fruit of eating the Guru’s food, as well as the fruit of the Guru’s leavings;
and immediately thereafter, the fault arising from not eating those leavings.
Prostration before the sandals of the Guru and so forth is forbidden in the presence of the Guru;
yet, there is no sin in performing what was forbidden [by him] with the Guru’s permission.
One must abandon pride regarding one's caste, learning, and the like in the presence of the venerable Guru.
The determination of the fruit of constant meditation upon the lotus feet of the venerable Guru;
likewise, the abandonment of sitting on the same seat as the Guru is the fruit of devotion to the Guru;
the fault of abandoning one's father and the Guru’s family; and the glorification preceded by the word "Śrī."
The utterance of the names of the guru and others at the very time of their worship;
the fourfold service consisting of honoring the guru, friends, and so forth;
and immediately after that, the manner of entering the guru’s residence.
Thus ends the second section of the second book.

(143) Furthermore, there is the investigation of the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*), followed by the examination of the ground (*bhūparīkṣā*). Then follows the auspicious floating [of the site] in specific directions, which bestows excellent results; the knowledge of the earth beginning with *brahmaṇī*, and the description of the auspicious ground.
Indeed, the ground and the circle must be abandoned, along with its explanation;
the extraction of the pin is twofold, consisting of the determination of the directions by means of a peg.
Following that is the construction of the pavilion, and after that, the archway.
The planting of the sprout, its examination immediately thereafter,
and the pacification of the inauspicious sprout are treated in the third chapter.
The determination of the meaning of the word *dīkṣā*, the glorification of the majesty of *dīkṣā*,
the censure of one who is uninitiated (*adīkṣita*), and the praise of one who is initiated (*dīkṣita*); furthermore,
seniority by means of *dīkṣā* and *dīkṣā* as the means to liberation.
By the accomplishment of a single mantra, there is the accomplishment of all mantras.
There is censure for the unauthorized reception of mantras and for reading books and so forth.
Without initiation (*dīkṣā*), one has no entitlement to worship and other rites; one who is improperly initiated is censured.

And thus, initiation (dīkṣā) is proclaimed to be threefold, yet also fourfold: the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), the ritual deposit (nidhi), the rites beginning with the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) and the consecrations (adhivāsayaḥ),
and the practical application (prayoga), which is the conclusion of the fourth chapter.
First, there is the invitation of the Guru for the ritual procedures beginning with the ceremonial bath;
then the mention of the solar month, the worship of the Mātṛkās and others,
the Vṛddhi-śrāddha, and the worship of the five deities in every rite.

Then follows the worship of Lakṣmī and others, and thereafter the mantra of the planets (grahas). Next is the procedure for the worship and offerings to the planets, followed by the armor (kavaca) of the planets.
Immediately after that is the meditation, mantra, worship, and armor of the lunar days (tithis).
Next follows the purification of the colors, meditations, and postures;
thereafter, the rites of worship and fire-oblations are described in brief.
Thus is declared the conclusion of the fifth section.

The various types of initiation (*dīkṣā*) have been proclaimed in the sixth [chapter], while other matters have been treated according to their respective places. I have provided this mere enumeration by means of a glossary (*nirghaṇṭa*);
because of the perceived bulk of the text, I have not yet provided a detailed commentary.
Only the means of valid cognition have been set forth, and the critical inquiry (mīmāṃsā) has been provided here and there.
Now, as the occasion has arisen, the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) are described.

Since the performance of these rites is mandatory, their practical application will be set forth hereafter; therefore, no detailed commentary is provided now, but only the essential authority (pramāṇa) is recorded.
In the ninth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra.
Sadāśiva said:

O Goddess! Without *saṃskāra*, purification of the body does not arise; one who has not undergone *saṃskāra* is not entitled to perform rites for the gods (*daiva*) or the ancestors (*paitrya*). Therefore, by the castes beginning with the Brahmins, the respective *saṃskāras* prescribed for their own caste [must be performed].
Those who desire welfare in this world and the next should by all means and with great effort perform the following rites:
the sprinkling of the seed (*bījaseka*), the rite for the production of a male (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*),
as well as the naming (*jātanāman*), the first outing (*niṣkramaṇa*), and thereafter the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*).
The ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras), beginning with the tonsure (cūḍā), the initiation (upanayana), and the marriage (udvāha), have been described.
For Śūdras—and for those distinct from Śūdras—the sacred thread (upavīta) does not exist.
"For those distinct from Śūdras" means for those who belong to the Śūdra category but are of lower status, such as fishermen (kaivarta) and others.
For those twice-born ones, nine sacraments are prescribed, while ten are traditionally taught;
likewise, all obligatory rites,
occasional rites, and even optional rites, O lady of beautiful hips, should be performed according to the path of Śambhu.
And likewise, for all ritual preparations and other rites,

according to the distinctions of the castes such as the Brahmins and others, the mantras have been shown in their respective order; O Kālikā, they are likewise prescribed for the specific rites of the Satya, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages.

One should employ those mantras beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) in ritual applications; however, O Supreme Goddess, in the Kali age, men shall perform all rites by means of those mantras beginning with *māyā* (hrīṃ), according to the command of Śaṅkara.
In the Nigamas, Āgamas, Tantras, Vedas, and Saṃhitās,
all mantras and their applications have been spoken by me alone according to the distinctions of the Yugas.
Now, O Mahāmāyā, the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) are being described.
In that regard, the seasonal consecration (*ṛtusaṃskāra*) is first described; listen in due order.
Having performed his daily rites and being purified, he should worship five deities:
Brahmā, Durgā, Gaṇeśa, the planets, and likewise the lords of the directions.
One should worship these [deities] in jars located in the directions starting from the northeast (sthāṇḍila) and Indra’s quarter.
Then, the sixteen Mothers beginning with Gaurī should be worshipped in sequence:
Gaurī, Padmā, Śacī, Medhā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā, [Durgā, Bhadrā, Kṣemā, Kriyā, Buddhi, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, and Māyā].
Devasenā, Svadhā, Svāhā, Śānti, Puṣṭi, Dhṛti, Kṣamā, the deity of the self, and likewise the family deity—
may all these Mothers, who bring joy to the thirty gods, come hither.
May all desired fruits of marriages, vows,
and sacrifices be accomplished. May all the Mothers, possessing gentle forms and always mounted upon their vehicles, come for the prosperity of this sacrifice and festival.
Having thus invoked the groups of Mothers and worshipped them according to one's capacity,
one should offer seven or five drops of vermilion and sandalwood paste upon the threshold, which is one span in measure and reaches to the level of the navel.
The wise one, recollecting Kāma, Māyā, and Ramā within each individual drop (*bindu*),
should offer an unbroken stream of clarified butter (*ghṛtadhārā*) and there worship Vasu.
Having thus established the flow of wealth (*vasudhārā*) by the very path described by me, [one should proceed].
Having prepared the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), the wise practitioner, after first establishing the fire,
should consecrate the oblation materials and cook the most excellent caru.
Here, the caru is dedicated to Prajāpati, and the fire is named Vāyu.
Having completed the rites up to the end of the *dhārā-homa*, one should begin the monthly (*ārtava*) ritual.

Having offered three oblations of *caru* with the mantra "Hrīṃ Prajāpataye Svāhā," one should then offer the [final] oblation while reciting this mantra: [The mantra follows: *oṃ hrīṃ prajāpataye svāhā* (Note: The final oblation is to be offered while uttering the above mantra.)
May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ bestow forms.

May Prajāpati sprinkle [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you. Svāhā!—with clarified butter or with sacrificial porridge (caru), one should offer the oblation while meditating upon Sūrya, Prajāpati, and Viṣṇu.
"O Sinīvālī, bestow the embryo; O Sarasvatī, bestow the embryo.
May the two divine Aśvins, adorned with lotus-garlands, place the embryo within you.
Having thus meditated upon the goddess Sinīvālī, as well as Sarasvatī and the Aśvins.
With this mantra ending in "svāhā," one should offer the supreme oblation;
then, reciting "Kāma, Badhū, Māyā, Ramā, Kūrca," one should say:
"O Sadviṭha, place the embryo in this woman who desires a son."
Having spoken thus and meditated upon the Sun and Viṣṇu, one should offer oblations into the consecrated fire with the mantra:
"Just as this goddess Earth, lying supine, has conceived a fetus,
so may you conceive a fetus for birth in the tenth month."
Meditating upon Viṣṇu, one should offer an oblation with this mantra ending in "svāhā.
Then, taking up clarified butter once more and meditating upon Viṣṇu, the Supreme beyond the supreme, [one should pray]:
"O Viṣṇu! By Your most excellent form, [bestow] the most noble [son] upon this woman."
Listen: having uttered the pair of *ṭha* syllables (*ṭha-ṭha*), one should cast the oblation into the fire.
One should enclose the *māyā* (Hrīṃ) with *kāma* (Klīṃ), and the bride (*badhū*) with *māyā*. Having again recited *kāma* and *māyā*, one should touch her head.
Surrounded by women whose sons are living, the husband,
having touched his head with both hands and tied them to the hem of his wife's garment,
should meditate upon Viṣṇu, Durgā, Brahmā, and Sūrya, and then offer three fruits.

Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, one should complete the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Alternatively, by worshipping Gaurī and Śaṅkara at the time of dusk and by offering an *arghya* libation to the Sun, the purification of the couple shall be accomplished.
The rite pertaining to the menstrual period has been described; now hear concerning the rite of conception (garbhādhāna).
On that night or on another night, during an even-numbered night, having gone inside the house with his wife and meditated upon the god Prajāpati,
the husband should touch his wife and recite [the mantra] preceded by the *māyāvīja*.
"May you be the bringer of auspiciousness to our bed for the sake of our noble progeny.
Having ascended the bed with his wife, facing either the east or the north,
he should sit down, touch the woman, and take her hand to place it upon his head.
Embracing with the left hand, one should recite the mantra at each respective place:
having recited "Kāma" (the seed-syllable of desire) one hundred times on the head, "Vāgbhava" (the seed-syllable of speech) one hundred times on the chin,
"Ramā" (the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī) twenty times on the throat, and [the same] one hundred times on each of the two breasts.
Having recited the Māyā-mantra ten times at the heart and twenty-five times at the navel,
and having placed the hand upon the yoni while reciting the Vāgbhava-mantra together with Kāma,
one should likewise perform this for one hundred and eight repetitions at the liṅga.
Having transformed his own womb through *māyā*, the husband should approach his wife for the sake of obtaining a son;
at the moment of the emission of semen, having meditated upon the Lord, the Creator of the Universe,
he should cause it to fall into the bladder, which is the *cit-kuṇḍa* below the navel.
At the moment of the emission of semen, the wise man should recite this mantra:
"As the earth is pregnant with fire, as the sky is pregnant with the wielder of the thunderbolt,
and as the quarters of space are pregnant with the wind, so may you become pregnant."
Thus ends the rite of conception (garbhādhāna).

O Maheśvarī! When the embryo has been conceived during the fertile period, or on the second or third day thereafter, the householder should perform the *puṃsavana* rite in the third month of pregnancy. Having performed his daily obligatory duties, the husband should worship five deities.
The wise man should cause the Gaurī and other Mothers to pour down a stream of wealth (vasordhārā).
Then, having performed the Vṛddhi-śrāddha according to the previously mentioned rule,
and having completed everything up to the Dhārā-homa, he should perform the Puṃsavana rite.
There, a *prājāpatya* oblation is prepared, and the fire there is named Candra.
One should place one barley grain and two black gram (*māṣa*) seeds into cow’s curd.
The husband should ask the wife: "O auspicious lady, what is it that you drink three times?"
Then, having performed the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), one should say: "I have performed the *puṃsavana* rite three times.
The woman should drink three handfuls of curd mixed with barley and black gram.
She should be brought to the place of sacrifice by women whose sons are living.
Having established her on the left side, one should perform the *caru* oblation.
Taking the *caru* as before while reciting the *māyā* and the *kūrca* mantras:
"Those who create obstacles to conception and those who destroy the fetus..."

O Dviṭha, destroy all those spirits, ghosts, piśācas, vetālas, and child-killers; perform the protection of the womb through this mantra. Having visualized the fire as the destroyer of demons, [perform the rite].
Meditating upon Rudra Prajāpati, one should offer twelve oblations; then,
having offered five oblations with the mantra "Māyā-candramase svāhā," and touching his wife to the heart, one should recite the Māyā-Lakṣmī mantra a hundred times.
Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, one should complete the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Thus ends the rite for the birth of a male child (puṃsavana).
Then, in the fifth month, one should give the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) to the woman:
sugar, honey, milk, ghee, and curd, in equal proportions.
This is declared to be the pañcāmṛta; it is prescribed for the purification of the body.
O Śivā! Having recited the Vāgbhava, Madana, Lakṣmī, Māyā, Kūrcaka, and Purandara mantras five times each over the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
the husband should unify them here as nectar and have his beloved consume it.
Thus ends the offering of the five nectars.
One should perform the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) in the sixth or even the eighth month;
this rite of parting the hair continues as long as offspring has not been born.
Having performed the ritual up to the end of the *dhārā-homa* (the stream-offering) as previously described, together with his wife, [he should proceed].

Seated upon his seat, the wise man should offer three oblations to Viṣṇu, Bhāskara, and Dhātṛ, while pronouncing the wife of Agni (Svāhā). Then, having meditated upon the Moon within the sacrificial fire named Śiva—
A person should perform the oblation seven times, dedicating it to Soma;
having meditated upon the Aśvins, Vāsava, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Durgā, and Prajāpati, one should offer five oblations to each one individually, O Śivā!
Taking a golden comb in his right hand,
the husband should place it within the mass of hair at the end of the parted locks above the *sīmanta*;
meditating upon Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, he should utter the seed-syllable of Māyā (*hrīṃ*).
O wife! O auspicious one! O fortunate one! O you of excellent vows! In the tenth month, may you give birth with ease, being well-pleased by the grace of Viśvakarman.
O long-lived one! O comb! May you bestow splendor and bring about prosperity for her.
Then one should conclude the ritual with the offerings to Sviṣṭakṛt and other concluding rites.
Thus ends the parting of the hair ceremony (sīmantonnayana).
Upon seeing his newborn son, the wise man, having placed gold within the house,
should complete the *dhārā-homa* according to the previously mentioned procedure;
thereafter, he should offer five oblations to Agni, Indra, and Prajāpati.
Immediately thereafter, having dedicated [the rite] to all the gods and Brahmā,
the father, having placed equal portions of honey and clarified butter into a vessel of bell-metal,
should recite the Vāgbhava mantra seven times and cause his son to consume it.
Uttering the mantra thus with the ring finger of the right hand:
"O child! May your lifespan, luster, strength, and intelligence always increase!"—having performed this rite for generating longevity, one should assign a secret name.
In the second chapter of the Gandharva Tantra.
Within three days, one should place this *vāgbhava-kūṭa* upon the tongue of the infant using a golden probe, together with honey and white *dūrvā* grass; indeed,
this should be written so that it may persist through future births.
He alone shall become truly wise; he will certainly not remain a fool.
The Vāgbhava-kūṭa is also located right there as follows:
Kāmadeva, then the Yoni, the fourth vowel (Ī), Purandara (H), and Bhuvaneśī;
after that, [the syllable] adorned with five faces (HA).

This is that Vāgbhava [syllable], which bestows the state of Vāgīśvara upon the Goddess. O Dear One! one should place one's hand upon the head of even a fool and recite this Vāgbhava-kūṭa one hundred and eight times until it is mastered.
O Maheśānī! He too indeed composes a verse; of this there is no doubt.

Of the childish and the fool. O Goddess! By placing [this] upon the tongue, even a mute becomes a skilled poet, provided he knows the essence of sound, grammar, logic, the meaning of words and sentences, and poetic ornaments.
In the seventh chapter of the *Vṛhannīlatantra*, concerning the second mantra, the three-syllabled *vidyā*:
"Now listen, O lovely-limbed one! To the supreme practice that brings about poetic inspiration—difficult to obtain and secret, yet revealed to you out of affection."
One should recite the three seed-syllables— Caṇḍī, Cāṇḍālinī, and Tyāginasarvamohana— at night and at midday on the day of the Sun;
one should perform the recitation to the measure of one thousand and eight.
Having consecrated it one hundred times with mantras, one should drink the excellent water.
By practicing this for seven days, poetic skill that delights the mind arises;
there is no doubt in this, O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods! This is the truth.
With his own right hand, he should bring together honey and parched grain;
before the severing of the umbilical cord, the practitioner should perform the consecration for the child.
By this, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, poetic talent and scholarship are born.

O Goddess of gods! having cleansed the tongue, one should draw [the lines] with a golden needle, or else with *dūrvā* grass, O Mahādevī! Having drawn two rows upon the tongue and the lips, one should perform the rite of consecration for the child.
O Goddess of gods! On the eleventh day, or again on the twelfth day,
or even within the month according to the distinctions of caste and class,
one should worship the deity once more with offerings according to one's capacity.
O Maheśvarī! Having worshipped the deity with devotion, one should write down the mantra.
O Parameśānī! When the father is not present in the country, or even the paternal uncle or maternal uncle, one should perform the child's sacramental rites after having written [the mantra].
The practitioner of mantra should write the root mantra with white dūrvā grass upon the lip of a child;
by the utterance of words, that child shall become eloquent and a swift poet.
When a son is born, it is recommended that he be given a name that effects his auspicious birth-consecration.
One should carefully draw the yantra on the tongue using either a wooden splinter or kuśa grass;
having wiped it three times with the right hand alone,
one should recite the mantra for each line and make it very beautiful.
First, the consecration (saṃskāra) must be performed; at its conclusion, one should write the mantra.
O Śivā! One should worship Tāriṇī with perfumes, sandalwood, and flowers, and facing north, one should establish the excellent pedestal (pīṭha).

One should worship the goddess Tāriṇī with various beautiful edibles and with the sixteen types of offerings, worshipping her with a spirit of devotion. One should offer incense made of guggulu, which bestows the fruits of all ritual actions.
Coconut, plantain, jujube, and likewise *vakula*;
*bījapūra*, *karṇikāra*, and sugar combined with fragrance;
honey-water, peas, and prepared food soaked in milk-rice (*pāyasa*).

One should offer black gram, fish, and flour-cakes as a great and most beloved gift. The son shall become wise and eloquent, fulfilling every desire; he is born great, self-controlled, truthful, and righteous.

By the word "should give" (dadyāt), since the recipient is presented through the verbal suffix, even in the absence of the word "brāhmaṇa," the phrase "to the brāhmaṇas" (brāhmaṇebhyaḥ) is understood.
Therefore, there is the conventional usage of giving beans and other items with the brāhmaṇas as the recipients.
In the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra.
Once the initiation ceremony has been performed for the son, one should address him by that name;
having performed the expiatory rites and other duties, one should complete the birth-rite (jātakarman).
Thereafter, the nurse should perform the cutting of the umbilical cord with great enthusiasm.

As long as the umbilical cord is not severed, ritual impurity does not apply; indeed, even before the cutting of the cord, one should perform the rites for the gods and the ancestors. For a girl as well, it should be performed in this very same manner, though without mantras.
Thus concludes the birth rite (jātakarman).
In the sixth or eighth month, one should publicly perform the naming ceremony.
Having bathed the infant and dressed him in auspicious garments, the mother,
having approached her husband, should place the son facing the east.
One should sprinkle the head of the child with water containing gold and kuśa grass,
[reciting]: "The Jāhnavī, Yamunā, Revā, the purifying Sarasvatī,
Narmadā, Varadā, Kumbhī, the oceans, and the lakes."
May these [waters] consecrate you for the attainment of dharma, kama, and artha.
Hrīṃ!
O Waters, you are indeed our source of bliss; grant us strength.
"O Waters, grant us a share here of that most auspicious essence of yours which is for our great delight and vision;
like longing mothers, come to us for our dwelling and quicken us. O Waters, generate us.
Having consecrated [the disciple] with these three mantras, one should perform the purification of the fire as before.
Having performed and completed [the rites] up to the end of the stream, the wise one should offer five oblations:
first to Agni, then to Vāsava,
then to Prajāpati, and likewise to the Viśvedevas.

One should offer an oblation to Brahmā in the fire known as Pārthiva. Then, taking the son onto one's lap, the wise father should announce an auspicious name— composed of few syllables, easy to pronounce, and pleasant— to his right ear.
Having caused the name to be heard three times and having announced it to the Brahmins,
he should then conclude the rite after performing the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and other subsequent duties.
For a girl, there is no formal exit ceremony (*niṣkrama*), nor does the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* exist.
The wise man should perform the naming ceremony (*nāma-karman*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), and the tonsure (*cūḍā*) without the recitation of mantras.
He should perform the infant’s first outing (*niṣkramaṇa*) in the fourth or sixth month. Having performed his daily obligatory rites, the father, O dear one, should worship Gaṇanāyaka.
Having bathed his son and adorned him with garments and ornaments,
the wise man, having seated him before him, should utter this mantra:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Durgā, Gaṇeśa, and likewise Bhāskara."
"May Indra, Rāyu, Kuvera, Varuṇa, Agni, and Bṛhaspati bestow auspiciousness upon the child and protect him always on his path.
Having spoken thus, she took the child onto her lap amidst the accompaniment of songs and musical instruments.
One should bring the child outside together with joyful kinsmen; having gone a short distance on the path, one should have the infant gaze at the sun. Hrīṃ!
That divine eye, beneficial to the gods, rises pure in the east.
"May we see for a hundred autumns, may we live for a hundred autumns,
may we hear for a hundred autumns"—
having thus shown the sun and returned to his own abode.
Having offered the *arghya* to the Sun, the father should feed his own kinsmen.
Thus ends the departure.

O auspicious lady! In the sixth month from the birth of the boy, or even in the eighth month, the paternal uncle or the father himself should perform the rite of first feeding with solid food (annaprāśana). As before, there should be the worship of the deities and likewise the consecration of the fire.
Having thus duly performed the rites concluding the pouring of water,
the father should offer five oblations there into the fire named Śuci;
offering the first directed toward Agni and the second while recollecting Vāsava.

Then, having intended Prajāpati the god, then all the gods, and then Brahmā, he should offer the fifth oblation. Then, having meditated upon the Giver of Food within the fire, the father, having offered the five oblations, [proceeds].
Alternatively, having placed the son, adorned with clothes and ornaments, upon one's lap in that house or another, one should feed him the nectar of milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Having thus fed him five times, one should do so with the mantras for the five *prāṇāhuti* offerings.

Then, having placed a little of the food, condiments, and so forth into the child's mouth, one should complete the rite of atonement with the sounding of conch shells, trumpets, and other instruments.
Thus the Annaprāśana has been described; now hear the procedure for the Cūḍā ceremony.
In the third or fifth year, according to family custom,
the practitioner should perform the *cūḍākarma* (tonsure ceremony) for the child to accomplish the purification (*saṃskāra*) of the infant;
having completed the rites beginning with the worship of the deities and ending with the pouring of water.
To the north of the true fire,
the wise man should place a shallow earthen bowl (śarāva) filled with bull-dung, combined with sesame and wheat;
he should also provide lukewarm water and a single razor well-sharpened.
Having reached his son there, Janaka seated him on his own left side upon his mother’s lap; then, having recited the Vāruṇa mantra ten times over those lukewarm waters, he washed the child’s hair.
One should fashion a single *juṣṭi* from two *kuśa* leaves using the *māyā* mantra;
having recited the *māyā*, *lakṣmī*, and *tridhā* mantras three times and taken an iron razor,
one should cut the root of the *juṣṭi* and place it into the hand of the Mother.
The mother of the boy, taking him with both hands, should place him in a shallow bowl containing cow dung; the father should say to the barber,
"Perform the shaving of the child's head with ease for his well-being," ending with the two syllables *ṭha*.
Having recited [the mantras], while looking at the barber, he should offer three oblations into the fire named Satya, dedicating them to Prajāpati. Then,
having had the child bathed by the barber after the shaving has been performed, [he should proceed].
Having adorned her with garments, ornaments, and garlands, and having placed her to his left side in the presence of the fire, he should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation. Then,
having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the father should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
"O child! May Māyā and the all-pervading Creator of the Universe grant you well-being.
Having recited this into the ear of the child with a golden or iron rod, one should perform the piercing there.

Then, having consecrated the son with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and having performed the rites for peace and the giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should complete the ceremony of tonsure (cūḍākarma).
From conception (garbhādhāna) up to the tonsure, the procedure is the same for all castes.

For Śūdras and those of common castes, all these rites from the birth-ceremony (jātakarman) up to the tonsure (cūḍā) must be performed without mantras; the same applies to the girl. However, the rite of going forth (niṣkramaṇa) is the one exception that must be performed by members of all five castes with mantras.
Now, the procedure for the investiture with the sacred thread (*upavīti*) for the twice-born is described;
once this is performed, the twice-born become entitled to rites for the gods and the ancestors.
One should perform the initiation (*upanayana*) of the child in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year from birth.
One who is more than sixteen years of age should not be initiated, for he is devoid of ritual action.
Having performed his daily obligatory rites, the learned man should worship the five deities,
as well as the Mother-goddesses beginning with Gaurī, and he should perform the rite of Vasudhārā.
Thereafter, one should perform the Vṛddhi-śrāddha for the satisfaction of the deities and the ancestors;
one should carry out the rites up to the end of the Dhārā-homa according to the procedure prescribed in the Kuśaṇḍikā.
Having performed the morning meal, the child, well-bathed and well-adorned, [should be brought].
Having had his hair shaved except for the *śikhā* (topknot), and adorned with silken garments,
he should be brought to the pavilion of shade and seated upon a pure seat to the left of himself, near the sacrificial fire.

The teacher should say to the disciple, "O child, observe the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya)! Then the child should inform the teacher, "I shall observe the vow of celibacy. Thereupon, the teacher, with a gracious soul, [should address] the child whose mind is tranquil.
One should give two saffron-colored garments for the sake of long life and luster.
One should also silently give a girdle made of muñja grass or kusha grass, triple-stranded and provided with a knot, to the one wearing the saffron garment.
Having uttered the *māyā* [syllable], the auspicious girdle (*mekhalā*) should be the bearer of the word "subhagā.
Having spoken thus and tied the girdle, he should remain silent before the Guru.
The supreme, most pure sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), which was innate to Bṛhaspati in former times—
Put on this foremost, auspicious life-prolonging sacred thread; may there be strength and splendor for you.
With this mantra, one should give [the initiation] to the child together with a black antelope skin.
As for the measurement of the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*), it is described in the eleventh chapter of the *Mātṛkābhedatantra*.
O fair-faced one, listen to the measurement of the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra):
the follower of the Ṛgveda should wear the thread above the navel and below the breast.
Now listen to the wonderful measurement of the Yajurvedic thread, O daughter of the mountain!

The sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) should be worn with diligence by the twice-born according to the measurement of the base of the arm; it should never be of any other length. "Of no other [length]" means it should not be of any other measurement.
O lady of excellent complexion, the long thread of the Sāmagas is of three kinds:
the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtraka) extending from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) down to the region of the navel;
or else, having placed it upon the neck, one should let it touch the navel.
Therefore, the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) extends from the back to the spinal column;
or else, O Supreme Goddess! another method is stated:
the sacrificial thread extends from the neck to the right thumb.
One who belongs to the Atharva Veda should wear the sacred thread with effort according to the opinion of the Yajus;
or one may wear the thread according to the authority of the Sāman singer;
or one may wear the sacrificial thread which causes supreme delusion.

The sacrificial thread extends from the wheel of command (ājñācakra) down to the region of the navel. O Goddess, he who wears the thread without knowing this convention is equal to a Caṇḍāla, even if he were equal to Vyāsa himself.
In this context, the cutting of the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) and the placement of life-force (jīvanyāsa) are also written down.
In the fourth Brāhmaṇa-paṭala of the Gāyatrī-tantra.
A maiden, as well as one who has sons and a husband, may spin the thread; likewise, a Brāhmaṇa woman—whether she be a widow or not, or even if she be sonless—may do so.
A Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya wife, and a Śūdra woman, however, must not spin it.
If that Śūdra woman is initiated, she is censured for spinning thread;
O auspicious lady, if she is a true Śūdra, she is pure in the spinning of thread. But if she is an impure Śūdra, O Maheśānī, she is censured for spinning thread.
The sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) is fashioned from cotton thread;
it is exceedingly fine, supreme, and likewise composed of all the gods.
Thus ends the section on emanation.
The minor knot: at the time of tying the knot, one should remember the Brahmins; the thread becomes incarnate as Brahmā, Kāśyapa the Brahmin, Sanaka, and Sanandana.
The Brahmin Sanatsujāta, Nārada, and Kapila; Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Gautama, Kratu;
Bhṛgu, Dakṣa, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Vālmīki.
Dvaipāyana, Bharadvāja, Śukra, and Jaimini;
Vidūratha, Śunaḥśepha, Jātukarṇa, and Raurava;
Aurva, Saṃvartaka, Śukra, and Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods.

May Candra, Sūryya, and the illustrious Budha abide in the knots of my sacred thread (yajñasūtra) on my left side and upon my left shoulder day and night. May all the deities beginning with Brahmā, who are the presiding deities of the sacred thread, likewise [reside there]. Thus:

I shall now proclaim the *jīvanyāsa* (the infusion of life); listen to it regarding the sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*). Having placed the sacred thread in his right hand, the best of the twice-born, having first recited the *gāyatrī*, should then mutter the *praṇava* one hundred times.
Having recited the Gāyatrī once more, O Goddess, one should place it upon the left shoulder;
without the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa), the sacred thread (yajñasūtra) is like an ordinary thread.
In the Mahānirvāṇa [Sūtra].
One should give the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) and a staff made of bamboo, or of khadira wood,
or of palāśa, or originating from a milky sap tree;
this should be done with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," encased by the Māyā-bīja.
Having sprinkled him with water from kusha grass while he holds a staff and sacred thread, and having performed this three times,
one should then fill the child’s cupped hands with water;
that student, offering that handful of water to the Sun, is the giver.
The Guru should show the sun with the mantra "That eye" (*taccakṣuḥ*). Having seen the sun, the Ācārya should then say to the young student (*māṇavaka*):
"Fix your mind on my vow; I give you my heart."
"Be pleased with a single-minded focus, O child! May my words bring you auspiciousness.
Having touched [the disciple's] heart and recited this, he should ask him, "What is your name?
The disciple should say: "I am so-and-so Śarmā; I salute you."
O Pārvatī! When the guru asks, "Whose celibate student (*brahmacārī*) are you?", the disciple should answer attentively: "I am your celibate student. [The guru replies:
"You are the celibate student of Indra; Agni is your preceptor (*ācārya*)."
Having spoken thus, that preceptor should afterwards hand him over to the gods:
"O child! [I offer] you to Prajāpati, to Savitṛ, and to Varuṇa;
to the Earth, to all the gods, and indeed to all the Vedas."
"I offer all this to you; may they protect you constantly.
Then the young student, having circumambulated the fire by moving clockwise and having circumambulated the Guru, should sit down again upon his seat.
O Dear One! When questioned by the disciple during the fire-sacrifice of emergence (samudbhava-hutāśana), the Guru should offer five oblations (pañcāhuti) dedicated to the five deities:
Prajāpati, Śakra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and likewise Śiva.
One should offer oblations with the names of each [deity], beginning with *māyā* (the syllable *hrīm*) and ending with *vahnijāyā* (the syllable *svāhā*).
This rule is proclaimed for all cases where no specific mantra is mentioned.
Then [follow the offerings to] Durgā, Mahālakṣmī, Sundarī, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Having offered oblations to Indra and the other guardians of the ten directions, as well as to the nine planets beginning with the Sun,
each by their individual names, and having clothed the boy with a garment,
the wise preceptor should question the young student who is intent upon the life of celibacy (brahmacarya).
"O son, who is your refuge? Tell me, what is in your heart?
Then the disciple, with focused attention, grasped the two feet of his guru and said:
"By means of instruction in the knowledge of Brahman, please make me an ascetic."
O Śivā! While the child is thus praying, the Guru, having caused the threefold loud recitation of the mantra consisting of all mantras to be heard in the child’s right ear,
should then utter the three *vyāhṛtis* and cause the *Sāvitrī* to be heard.
The seer (ṛṣi) is declared to be Sadāśiva; the meter (chandas) is stated to be Anuṣṭubh;
and the presiding deity (adhiṣṭhātrī) is Sāvitrī, employed for the purpose of liberation (mokṣa). The great splendor contained within is to be chosen by those who seek the Self.
May we meditate upon that true state, all-pervading and eternal; may He who is the effulgence, the witness of all, and our mind, intellect, and senses,
impel and direct us toward virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
O Goddess! Having thus imparted this Brahma-vidyā endowed with its full meaning, the true Guru should enjoin the disciple to the duties of the householder stage of life; he should say:
"My child, now abandon this attire appropriate for the life of a celibate student."
Worship the gods and the ancestors according to the path proclaimed by Śambhu.
Through the instruction of the Brahma-vidyā, your body shall be purified. Having attained the stage of a householder, perform the duties prescribed therein.
Accept two sacred threads, divine garments, and ornaments;
accept sandals and an umbrella along with perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
and thereafter, accept saffron-colored robes together with a black antelope skin.
O Śivā! Having offered to the Guru the sacrificial thread, the girdle, the staff, and the alms-bowl, as well as the alms obtained according to proper conduct,
and having put on a pair of pure sacred threads and auspicious garments;
Bearing perfumes and garlands, he should remain silent in the presence of the teacher. Then the guru should say this to the disciple who belongs to the householder stage of life:
"Be one who has conquered the senses, who speaks at the proper time, and who is devoted to the knowledge of Brahman."
"Accomplish the duties of the stage of Vedic study according to the Dharma," having thus instructed him,
he [then] [offered oblations] into the sacrificial fire with the Māyā-mantra and others ending with the Praṇava, and with the three worlds: Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ.
Having caused the oblation to be offered in three ways, the preceptor should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice;
O auspicious lady, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should complete the rite of the vow.
The nine sacraments, beginning with the impregnation (*bījaseka*) and ending with the vow, are derived from the father.
O beloved! Marriage is established either through the father or even through oneself.
In the thirty-first chapter of the Matsya Purāṇa.
There is no progress for one who lacks a wife; all his actions are fruitless.
One who is destitute of a wife should avoid the worship of the gods and the great sacrifice.
Just as a chariot with only one wheel or a bird with only one wing [cannot move].
Likewise, a man without a wife is unfit for all ritual acts.
There is no sacred rite for one bereft of a wife; how can there be happiness for one bereft of a wife?
To whom does a house belong when bereft of a wife? Therefore, one should take refuge in a wife.
"O Queen of the Gods! One must take a wife even at the cost of one's entire possessions.
Thus, the necessity of taking a wife is stated in that very same [text].
Or else, it may be performed with effort; a third alternative is not possible.
A Brāhmaṇa woman of the same caste is declared to be the lawful wife (dharmapatnī), while a wife of a different caste is declared to be the wife for pleasure (kāmapatnī).
Thus concludes the determination regarding the lawful wife (*dharmapatnī*) in the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*.
Indeed, at a wedding, the performer, having bathed, performed his daily rites, and accomplished his duties,
should worship the five deities as well as Gaurī and the other Mother-goddesses;
then, having prepared the Vasordhārā, he should perform the Vṛddhi-śrāddha.

Having promised the gift of a vessel at night accompanied by song and instrumental music, the donor, having brought it to a pavilion of shade and seated himself on an excellent seat facing Vāsava (the east), should enter while facing west.

The preceptor, together with the Brahmins, should pronounce blessings and prosperity. He should inquire after the welfare of the virtuous and ask about their choice and their inquiry regarding worship. Having received the answer to his question from the chosen one, he should honor that choice with offerings beginning with water for the feet.
One should offer the region and the materials with words;
one should present water for the feet at the feet, and offer the respectful oblation (arghya) upon the head.
One should give water for sipping (ācamya) into the mouth, as well as fragrance, garlands, and fine garments.
One should offer divine ornaments, gems, and a sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*).
Then, having placed curd, clarified butter, and honey into a bronze vessel (*kāṃsya*),
one should offer the *madhuparka* with the appropriate formula and place it in the hand.
The bridegroom, having taken the vessel and placed it in his left hand,
should smell that vessel five times with his right thumb and ring finger while reciting the mantras prescribed for the *prāṇāhuti* offerings, and then hold the vessel in the northern direction.
Having thus completed the *madhuparka*, he should again cause the two of them to sip water (*ācamana*).
Having placed *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) upon the right knee of the bridegroom,
and having remembered Viṣṇu, he should then [state] "tatsat" followed by the month, the fortnight, and the lunar day.
Having observed the auspicious omens, one should choose an excellent bridegroom.

Having pronounced the names of his lineage (*gotra*), *pravara*, and personal name, each ending in the genitive case, starting from the great-grandfather and continuing down to the father of the bridegroom; (p. 157) [one should perform the selection].
The wise man, following the Brāhma marriage rite, should address the bridegroom by his gotra, pravara, and name in the accusative case; likewise, referring to the girl, he should say,
"I choose you as the giver," and then proclaim, "I choose [her]."
"I am chosen," the groom should say; then the giver of the bride should address the groom, saying, "Having said 'as prescribed,' perform the marriage rite.
The groom should reply to that, "I shall do as commanded, according to my knowledge."
Then, having brought the maiden, adorned with garments and ornaments,
and having covered her with another cloth, he should place her facing the groom. Furthermore, he should honor the groom again with clothing, ornaments, and other such gifts.
One should place the bride’s hand in the groom’s right hand;
having placed five gems, or else fruit and betel leaf, between them,
and having honored her, one should bestow the daughter upon the learned groom.
As before, one should recount the narrative of the three ancestors as well as the account of the occasion; then,
with the intention of fulfilling his own desire, he should utter the name of the bridegroom in the dative case and the name of the maiden— worshipped and adorned— in the accusative case.
Reciting the mantra dedicated to Prajāpati, "Sācchādanām," and saying, "I give this to you," the bridegroom should say, "I bestow it.
The giver should say, "May there be well-being! and the bridegroom should accept it by saying, "I receive it."
In matters of dharma, artha, and kāma, you must conduct yourself together with your wife; having spoken these words, the groom should recite the hymn of praise to Kāma:
"Kāma is the giver, Kāma is the receiver, and for the sake of Kāma, he has accepted the loving woman."
"I accept you out of desire; may the desire of both of us be fulfilled. Then the giver should say to the son-in-law regarding the daughter:
"By the grace of Prajāpati, may that which is desired by you both be attained."
"May it be full; may it be auspicious; may you two protect the Dharma.
Then, having covered [the bride] with a cloth, the giver, amidst highly auspicious rites, should cause the bridegroom and the bride to look at each other's faces.

Then, one should give gold and jewels as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the son-in-law according to one’s capacity; one should ensure that the rite is free from defects. The groom, together with his wife, [should perform this] either on that day or on the following day.
One should perform the installation of the fire according to the procedure taught in the *Kuśaṇḍikā*.
Here, the fire is known as *yojaka*, and the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) is prescribed for Prajāpati.
Having completed the ritual up to the pouring of the stream of water, the excellent practitioner should offer five oblations.

Having meditated upon Śiva, Durgā, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā the wielder of the thunderbolt, one should offer oblations into the consecrated fire, addressing each deity individually. Then, while reciting those [mantras], he should take the two hands of his wife.
"I take your hand, O blessed one! Be devoted to your guru and your husband. Practice the duties of the householder’s life according to the dharma.
With the clarified butter given by your lord and the parched grain brought by your brother, O auspicious one!"
The bridegroom, having circumambulated the fire and risen together with his wife, should offer two oblations intended for Prajāpati; he should then worship Durgā,
Śiva, Ramā, Viṣṇu, Brāhmī, and Brahmā.

One should perform the oblation three times for each pair. One should mount the seven stone circles without reciting mantras. If it is at night, one should then see the smoke-colored Arundhatī with women.
Then, having returned and properly seated himself on his seat,
the bridegroom should complete the ritual up to the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and the final *pūrṇāhuti*.
The *brāhma* marriage, performed with a woman of the same caste, is ordained as being free from defects.
According to family custom, a woman born of the same lineage (sapiṇḍa) but of a different clan (gotra) who is to be taken in marriage by the Brāhma rite—
she alone is the wife and mistress of the household;
without her permission, one should not perform the Brāhma marriage again.
O Kuleśvarī! while her offspring or those belonging to her lineage exist, [the family line shall endure].

Now follows the procedure for the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) as taught in the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*. Since one is ineligible to perform rites for the gods or ancestors without these purificatory rites, all castes, beginning with the Brahmins, must perform the purificatory rites prescribed for their respective castes.

The ten sacraments (*saṃskāra*), however, are: the impregnation rite (*bījaseka*), the rite for the male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth rite (*jātakarman*), the naming rite (*nāmakaraṇa*), the rite of first exit (*niṣkramaṇa*), the rite of first feeding (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*cūḍā*), the initiation (*upanayana*), and the marriage (*vivāha*).
Therefore, for Śūdras—and especially for the lowest Śūdras—there is no initiation; they have only nine sacraments.
For Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, however, there are ten sacraments.
Now, the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*).
Having performed the daily obligatory duties (*nityakriyā*) and sat upon his seat, he should establish the water-pots with the mantras to be written in the *Dīkṣāpaddhati*.
Therein, having worshipped Brahmā, Durgā, Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Śiva, Āditya, and the others—the nine planets, Indra and the rest of the ten guardians of the directions—he then...
One should worship the sixteen Mothers, beginning with Gaurī.
As for the sixteen Mothers:
Gaurī, Padmā, Śacī, Medhā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā,
Devasenā, Svadhā, Svāhā, Śānti, Puṣṭi, Dhṛti, and Kṣamā.
The personal deity and the family deity—these are the [deities].
As for the sequence of worship:
Having performed the placement of the *arghya* water and joining his palms in reverence (*baddhāñjali*), [he recites]:
"Hrīṃ! May all the Mothers, who bring joy to the gods, come here.
May they fulfill every desire for this marriage, vow, and sacrifice."
Mounted upon the power of their vehicles and always assuming gentle forms,
may all the Mothers come for the prosperity of this sacrificial festival.

Having thus invoked the group of Mothers (Mātṛkā-gaṇa) and worshipped them according to one's capacity with water for the feet and other offerings using the mantra "Hrīṃ, obeisance to Gaurī Mātā," and having likewise performed the worship of the sixteen Mothers— beginning with "Obeisance to Padmā Mātā" and so forth— according to one's ability,
[one should draw] on a wall reaching the height of the navel, within a space of one span, either with vermilion or red sandalwood paste, seven [lines].

Or one may offer five drops. Then, having offered an unbroken stream of ghee over each individual drop while reciting the three seed-syllables *klīm*, *hrīm*, and *śrīm*, one should worship *vasu* therein.

Then, having performed the rites from the preparation of the sacrificial ground as described in the section on *homa* up to the installation of the fire, and having consecrated the *homa* materials, one should cook the *prājāpatya* *caru*. Then,
having meditated upon and invoked the fire named Vāyu, and having worshipped it with clarified butter, water for the feet (*pādya*), and other offerings;

Having performed the ritual up to the end of the *dhārāhoma*, one should offer oblations three times with the *caru* using the mantra: *hrīṃ prajāpataye svāhā*. Then, [one should offer] with the mantra: *hrīṃ viṣṇur yoniṃ kalpayatu tvaṣṭā rūpāṇi yacchatu*.
"May Prajāpati sprinkle [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you, svāhā!"—with this mantra, one should offer the *caru* oblation once.
Then, having meditated upon Sūrya, Prajāpati, and Viṣṇu, one should offer with clarified butter, or with the *caru* mixed with clarified butter, or with clarified butter alone, [reciting] "hrīṃ."
One should offer oblations with each of the three mantras: "Svāhā to Sūrya, Hrīṃ; Svāhā to Prajāpati, Hrīṃ; Svāhā to Viṣṇu, Hrīṃ.
Then, having meditated upon Sinīvālī, Sarasvatī, and the Aśvins, [one should recite] "Hrīṃ."
May Sinīvālī bestow the embryo; may Sarasvatī bestow the embryo.
May the two divine Aśvins, wreathed with lotuses, place the embryo within you.
One should offer oblations with clarified butter while uttering "svāhā.
Then, having meditated mentally upon the Sun and Viṣṇu, [one should recite]: "klīṃ strīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ huṃ—place the embryo in this woman who desires a son, svāhā!"
With this mantra, one should offer oblations of clarified butter.
Then, having meditated upon Viṣṇu in the mind, [one recites]: "hrīṃ!
Just as this goddess Earth, lying supine, has conceived the embryo..."
In that same way, you must conceive a fetus so that you may give birth in the tenth month.
One should offer oblations with clarified butter using the mantra "svāhā.
Then, having again meditated upon Viṣṇu in the mind, [one recites]: "hrīṃ!
By the most excellent form of Viṣṇu, [may he be] most desirable in this woman."
p. 160) Focus your mind on what has been heard. One should offer oblations with clarified butter while reciting "svāhā.
Then, one should touch the head of the bride with the mantra: *klīṃ hrīṃ strīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ*.

Then, surrounded by women who have sons, the husband, having bound the head of the bride with both hands and meditated upon Viṣṇu, Durgā, Brahmā, and Sūrya, should place three fruits upon the edge of her lap.
Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, he should perform the expiatory (*prāyaścitta*) fire-sacrifice.
Then, at the time of dusk, having worshipped Śaṅkara together with Gaurī, one should offer the *arghya* oblation to the Sun.
Thereafter, on that night or on another even-numbered night, having gone to another room with his wife,
he should meditate upon Prajāpati in his mind, touch his wife, and perform the purification of the bed.
For example:
"O Bed! for the sake of our noble offspring, may you be a bringer of auspiciousness.
Then, having ascended the bed together with his wife and sitting down facing either the east or the north, [he should address] the woman...
Beholding her, placing his hand upon her head, embracing her with his left hand, he should mutter "klīm" one hundred times on her head;
"aim" one hundred times on her chin; "śrīm" twenty times on her throat; "śrīm" one hundred times on her two breasts;
and "hrīm" twenty-five times on her heart. Then, placing his hand upon her yoni, he should mutter "klīm" and "aim" one hundred and eight times.

Having recited [the mantra] upon the *liṅga*, one should also recite "Aiṃ Klīṃ" one hundred and eight times. Then, having opened the womb with the mantra "Hrīṃ," one should approach the woman for the sake of obtaining a son.
Thereafter, at the moment of the emission of semen, having meditated upon Viśvakarman, one should cause the semen to fall into the *cit-kuṇḍa* below the navel.
One should recite this at the moment of the emission of semen:
Hrīṃ!
Just as the earth with its embryo is by fire, and the sky is by the wielder of the thunderbolt.
As the quarters of the sky are pregnant with the wind, so may you become pregnant.
Thus ends the *garbhādhāna*. Now follows the *puṃsavana*.

The husband, having performed his daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*), [should perform] that which is described in the *garbhādhāna* manual, beginning with the worship of the five deities and ending with the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*.

Then, having performed the rites beginning with the installation of the fire (vahnisthāpana), one should meditate upon and invoke the fire named Candra, worship it, and cook the *caru* for Prajāpati. Then, having added one barley grain and two black gram (*māṣa*) beans into cow's curd, one should question the woman.
"O noble lady! Why do you drink this three times?
Then the woman should say, "I am drinking this because the *puṃsavana* rite has been performed by me.
Having said this, she should drink three handfuls (*prasṛti*) of curd mixed with barley and black gram.
Then, he should have her, whose children are living, led to that place of sacrifice by women.
Then, having seated her on his left side and brought the sacrificial porridge (caru), [he recites]: "Hrīṃ Huṃ! And those who are here causing obstacles, and those who are destroyers of the fetus..."
"Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, vetālas, and those who kill children—destroy them all, destroy them! Grant protection to the fetus, svāhā!
Reciting this mantra, one should meditate on Prajāpati while visualizing the destroyer of demons and offering the sacrificial oblation (caru).
One should offer twelve oblations.
One should give five oblations with the mantra "hrīṃ candramase svāhā".
Then, having touched the heart of one's wife, one should recite the mantra "hrīṃ śrīṃ" one hundred times.

Then, having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, and thereafter the rites beginning with the expiatory (*prāyaścitta*) oblations up to the dismissal of the fire, one should perform the rites ending with the determination of the [auspicious] omissions regarding the sacrificial fee; this is the *puṃsavana* ceremony.
Now follows the gift of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
This should be given to the pregnant woman during the fifth month, counting from the month of conception.
The five nectars consist of curd, honey, milk, ghee, and sugar, mixed together with meat.
By this, purification of the woman's body is achieved.

In that regard, having recited "aim klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ huṃ lam" five times over each individual substance and having mixed them together, one should have the pregnant woman consume it; this is the offering of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Now, the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana).
That should be performed in the sixth or eighth month;
if there is an inability [to do so at that time], it should be performed prior to the birth of the child.

Therein, the husband, having performed the rites beginning with the worship of the five deities and ending with the *dhāra-homa* as described in the section on *garbhādhāna*, sits upon a seat together with his wife; having meditated upon the fire named Śiva and invoked it, he worships it according to his capacity and offers three oblations with the mantras: *hrīṃ viṣṇave svāhā*, *hrīṃ bhāsvate svāhā*, and *hrīṃ dhātre svāhā*.
One should give [the offering].
Then, having meditated upon Soma, one should offer oblations seven times with the mantra: *hrīṃ somāya svāhā*.
Having meditated upon the Aśvins, Vāsava, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Durgā, and Prajāpati, [one should offer] for each individually.
One should offer five oblations.
Then the husband, taking a golden comb in his right hand and placing it upon the mass of hair tied at the parting of the woman's hair, while meditating upon Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, [utters] "hrīṃ."
O wife! O auspicious one! O fortunate one! O you of excellent vows, in the tenth month, may you give birth with ease and joy through the grace of Viśvakarman.
O long-lived one! May this comb, full of luster, bring you auspiciousness.
Thus one should recite.

Then, having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and the expiatory (*prāyaścitta*) oblations, one should offer the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), perform the dismissal of the fires (*agnivisarjana*), and so forth; thus concludes the *sīmantonnayana*.
Now, the birth-rite (jātakarman):
as soon as the child is born, the father, having given gold, should look at him.
Then, within the house, he should perform the rites beginning with the worship of the five deities as prescribed in the *Garbhadhāna-paddhati*, up to the end of the *dhārā-homa*.
Having performed five oblations into the heart,
[one should offer]: *hrīm agnaye svāhā*, *hrīṃ indrāya svāhā*, *hrīṃ prajāpataye svāhā*, *hrīṃ viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ svāhā*, *hrīṃ brahmaṇe svāhā*.
"Thus with these mantras.
Then, having brought together honey and clarified butter in equal portions within a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*), one should recite "Aiṃ" over it seven times.
Hrīṃ.
"May longevity, excrement, strength, and intelligence always increase for you, O child!
Reciting this mantra, [the father] should make the child eat [the mixture] with the ring finger of his right hand.
Having thus performed the rite for generating longevity, the father should assign a secret name.
Then, within three days from the date of birth, one should write the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* on the tongue of the child with white *dūrvā* grass or a golden stylus and honey.
By means of this *vāgbhava-kūṭa*, the child becomes learned, a skilled poet, and an expert in verbal ornaments.
If one who has completed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) places this mantra upon the head of a fool and recites it one hundred and eight times,
then even he will compose verses.
And if one places this mantra upon the tongue of a mute, then even he becomes a poet.
Alternatively, having wiped the tongue and lips of the child with *dūrvā* grass using the second [mantra] consisting of three syllables, one should draw two rows [of letters].
The procedure for that is as follows:

Before the severing of the umbilical cord, on the eleventh day, the twelfth day, or at the end of the month, one should worship that deity according to one's ability with ritual offerings and write down the mantra.
If the father is not present in the locality, then an uncle or another relative should perform this.
Alternatively, one should write the mantra of the family deity (*kuladevatā*) upon the child's lip with white *dūrvā* grass; that child will become eloquent and a swift poet.
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual from the *sviṣṭikṛt* oblation up to the dismissal of the fire.
For a girl as well, one should perform everything in this same manner without mantras.
Then, with enthusiasm, the midwife should cut the umbilical cord.
Immediately thereafter, the period of impurity (aśauca) begins; such is the birth-rite (jātakarman).
Now, regarding the naming ceremony: in the sixth or eighth month, one should give the child a name publicly.
For that occasion, the mother, having bathed the infant and dressed him in new garments, [should go] to the side of her husband.
Having approached the left lap-seat, he should place the child facing east.
Then the father, with water containing gold and kuśa grass, should sprinkle the head of the infant with these mantras as follows:
"Hrīṃ! O Jāhnavī, Yamunā, Revā, and the purifying Sarasvatī!"
May the Narmadā, Varadā, Kumbhī, the oceans, and the lakes— may these all consecrate you for the attainment of dharma, desire, and wealth. Hrīṃ.
O Waters, you who are most beneficial and the source of well-being, grant us strength for our nourishment and for our joyful vision. Grant us a share here of that most auspicious essence of yours,
like longing mothers.
"Come to us, O Waters, for whose dwelling you quicken;
give us life.
Having sprinkled [the disciple] with this mantra, he performs the ritual beginning with the installation of the fire as before, up to the end of the *dhārā-homa*.

Having meditated upon the fire named after the [child's] father, and having caused the father to announce three times the name— which consists of few syllables and is easy to pronounce— he should announce it to the Brahmins.
Thereafter, he should complete the ritual up to the conclusion of the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation.
This rite, including the naming ceremony, should be performed for the girl as well, though without the recitation of mantras.
Now, the rite of going out [of the house].
One should perform the going out in the fourth or the sixth month. Therein, the father, having performed his daily obligatory rites and having worshipped Gaṇeśa, should bathe the infant.

Having adorned [the child] with garments and ornaments and placed him before [the deity], one should recite the authoritative passages beginning with "Hrīṃ! Brahmā, Viṣṇu," as stated in the section on proofs; then, placing the boy on one's lap and surrounded by joyful kinsmen, one should lead him outside accompanied by songs and instrumental music.
Then, having gone some distance, one should show the child to the sun while reciting the mantra: *hrīṃ tac cakṣur devahitam*.
Then, having returned home and offered *arghya* to the sun, one should feed one's own kinsmen; this is the *niṣkramaṇa* rite.
Now, the ceremony of first feeding solid food (*annaprāśana*).
In this regard, in the sixth or eighth month, the father, or the paternal uncle, or the father himself, should perform the rite of *annaprāśana*.
Therein, having performed the daily obligatory rites as before, he should worship the Lord of the Gaṇas, Gaurī, and the other deities.
Having consecrated the fire named Śuci and completed the ritual up to the previously mentioned *dhārā-homa* (continuous stream oblation), one should offer five oblations as follows:
*hrīṃ agnaye svāhā*, *hrīṃ indrāya svāhā*, *hrīṃ prajāpataye svāhā*, *hrīṃ*.

Having offered oblations with "To all the gods, svāhā! Hrīṃ, to Brahmā, svāhā!", he should place the child on his lap in another room or house, feed him milk-rice five times with the mantras of the five vital breath offerings (pañcaprāṇāhuti), place some food and condiments in the infant's mouth, and then give him water to rinse his mouth.
Then, preceded by singing and instrumental music, one should complete the expiatory oblations and other rites; such is the ceremony of the first feeding with solid food (*annaprāśana*).
Now follows the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇa).

In the third year, or when the fifth year has arrived according to family custom, the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*) is performed. Therein, having performed the daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*), having conducted the worship of the Lord of the Gaṇas, the Mothers, and others, and having consecrated the fire named Satya, one completes the ritual up to the final oblation of the stream (*dhārāhuti*). To the north of the fire [is placed] an object accompanied by sesame and wheat.
One should place a new earthen bowl filled with bull-dung and lukewarm water, along with a sharpened razor.
Then, the father, having placed the boy on his left side in the lap of the mother, mutters the syllable *vaṃ* ten times;
with that lukewarm water, he washes the hair, and with the mantra *hrīṃ*, [he applies] a single *juṣṭikā* made from two blades of *kuśa* grass.
There he should bind it.
Then, having recited the two seed-syllables of Māyā and Lakṣmī three times, and taking an iron razor, he should cut the hair along with the *juṣṭika* [root] from near the base.

Then the mother of the boy, having grasped him by both hands along with the *saṃjuṣṭika* hair, should place him in a new earthen bowl smeared with cow dung. Then the father should speak to the barber.

Having recited, "O razor-shaven one, perform the shaving of the child's head; accomplish the face, svāhā!", and looking at the boy, he should offer oblations three times into the fire named Satyanāman with the mantra: "Hrīṃ, to Prajāpati, svāhā!"

Then, having placed the child—who has had his hair shaved, bathed, and is well-adorned with ornaments and garlands—on the left side, he should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* and expiatory (*prāyaścitta*) oblations and offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then, having recited: "Hrīṃ! O child! May Viśvakarman grant you well-being," [he should act] with a golden or silver [implement].
One should perform the piercing of the child's two ears with a needle.

Then, having consecrated him with the mantra beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and performed rites for pacification and so forth, one should offer a sacrificial fee; this is the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇa).
The rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and ending with the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā) are common to all castes; however, for Śūdras alone, all of these are performed without mantras.
Now follows the initiation ceremony (upanayana).
The initiation ceremony (upanayana) should be performed either in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year [of age].
Until the sixteenth year, an uninitiated boy has no entitlement to perform rites for the gods or the ancestors.

There, having performed the daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*), and having completed the ritual acts beginning with the worship of the Lord of the Gaṇas and the Mothers, up to the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*,

he should establish the fire named Samudbhava according to the procedure prescribed in the *Kuśaṇḍikā*, perform the rites up to the *dhārā-homa*, and [invite] one who has eaten his morning meal, whose head is shaven except for the topknot (*śikhā*), and who is well-bathed.
Having brought the boy, who is well-adorned and wearing linen garments, outside into the shade of a pavilion, the preceptor should seat him nearby on his left upon a pure seat.
Then the preceptor says: "Hrīṃ! Observe celibacy."
"Hrīṃ. 'I shall practice celibacy,' the disciple should say.
Then the guru should give to that disciple two saffron-colored garments and a girdle made of kuśa grass.
Having recited, 'Hrīṃ! May this auspicious girdle be a bestower of welfare,' the disciple should remain silent."
Having recited the mantra "Hrīṃ, this is the sacrificial thread," the Guru should give the sacrificial thread together with the black antelope skin to the disciple.
Regarding the specific Veda, the measurement of the thread should be understood according to the respective tradition.

Furthermore, he should give a mere sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), a bamboo staff (*vaṃśadaṇḍa*), and one made of *pālāśa* wood. Then, having sprinkled the disciple— who holds a body of water and possesses a garment, girdle, deerskin, sacrificial thread, and staff— with water from a three-leaved *kuśa* blade while reciting the *āpohiṣṭhā* mantra encased by the *māyā* (Hrīm) syllable, he should fill his joined palms with that water.
Then, having caused the child to offer a *añjali* to the Sun, the teacher should show him the Sun while reciting the mantra: *hrīṃ tac cakṣuḥ*.
Thereafter, the teacher, having touched the boy's heart and recited the mantra *hrīṃ mama vrate te*, should ask: "What is your name?"
Then the disciple should say, "I, the disciple named so-and-so, pay homage to you. Then the teacher asks, "Whose brahmacārī are you?
The disciple replies, "I am your brahmacārī."
Then the Guru, having said,
"You are the celibate student of Indra; the Fire-god is your teacher," and having handed over the young boy with the mantra *hrīṃ prajāpataye vatsa*, by means of a clockwise circumambulation—
Having circumambulated the fire clockwise, he should cause [the disciple] to sit upon a seat.
Then, touched by the disciple, the Guru [recites]: *hrīṃ prajāpataye svāhā* | *hrīṃ indrāya svāhā*.
Hrīṃ, svāhā to Viṣṇu! Hrīṃ, svāhā to Brahmā!
Hrīṃ, svāhā to Śiva!

Then, with the name ending in *svāhā* preceded by *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*), one should offer oblations individually to Durgā, Lakṣmī, Sundarī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Indra and the other guardians of the ten directions, and the nine planets beginning with the Sun, each by their own respective names.
Then, having covered the young boy (*māṇavaka*) with a garment, [one asks]: "O son, what is your stage of life (*āśrama*)? Speak! What is in your heart?"
Then, the disciple, having grasped the two feet of the guru, should pray: "By means of the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman, please make me an inhabitant of the spiritual stages (āśramin).
To the disciple thus entreating, the teacher should cause him to hear the *praṇava* three times in his right ear, and then cause him to hear the *Sāvitrī* together with the *Vyāhṛtis*.
This is another Brahmavidyā.
Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi) of the Gāyatrī; Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas); Sāvitrī is the deity (devatā); its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of seeking vision (mīkṣa).
And one should cause that meaning to be known.
Then the young student (māṇavaka) should go for alms.
Then the preceptor (guru) should recite: "Hrīṃ! O celibate student (brahmacārī), [assume] the prescribed attire.
Thereafter, the young student [should take] the ochre-colored garment, along with the black antelope skin, the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra), the girdle (mekhalā), and the staff (daṇḍa).

Having offered the alms-bowl and the alms collected therein to the Guru, and having put on two pure sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*) and two white garments, and wearing perfumes and garlands, he should stand silently in the presence of the Ācārya.
Then the Guru [should proceed].
Having recited "Hrīṃ! One who has conquered the senses, one who speaks the truth," and so forth, the disciple should perform the oblation (hāvayet) with this:
"Hrīṃ oṃ bhūḥ svāhā, Hrīṃ oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā, Hrīṃ oṃ svaḥ svāhā."
Then, one should complete the ritual beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and ending with the sacrificial fee; this concludes the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
Now, the marriage ceremony:

having performed the daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*) and completed the ritual acts ending with the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*— including the worship of the five deities (*pañcadevatāpūjā*) and so forth— the bridegroom, accompanied by song and instrumental music, is led at night to the shadow-pavilion (*chāyā-maṇḍapa*) and seated upon a throne facing the east.
He should cause [the bridegroom] to sit down.
Then, having had the Brahmins recite the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day), he should ask the groom: "Hrīṃ! May you be seated comfortably.
Then the groom [responds].
"Oṃ Hrīṃ, I am a worthy candidate," he should say.
"Oṃ Hrīṃ, we shall worship you," he should ask as his request. "Oṃ Hrīṃ, worship [me]," the candidate should reply.
