Having worshipped the bridegroom with water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), perfume (*gandha*), flowers (*puṣpa*), garments (*vastra*), ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), and the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) by reciting "Hrīṃ, I offer the water for the feet," and so forth, he should offer the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) into the bridegroom's hand, saying: "Hrīṃ, I offer the honey-mixture."

Then the bridegroom, having taken the *madhuparka* and placed it in his left hand, [offers it] with the ring finger and thumb of his right hand while reciting the mantra: "Hrīṃ! Svāhā to Prāṇa! Hrīṃ! Svāhā to Apāna! Hrīṃ! Svāhā to Samāna! Hrīṃ! Svāhā to Udāna! Hrīṃ! Svāhā to Vyāna! (p. 167)

Having struck those materials for the madhuparka five times, he should place that vessel in the northern direction. Then, having again given water for sipping (ācamanīya) to the bridegroom, the giver, touching the bridegroom’s right knee with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), [should say]: "O Viṣṇu! Om Tat Sat! Today, in such-and-such month, when the sun is in such-and-such zodiac sign, in such-and-such fortnight..."
On such-and-such a lunar day, Śrī Amukadevaśarman, belonging to the [Amuka] gotra,

[the great-grandson] of Amukadevaśarman of the [Amuka] gotra and [Amuka] pravara, having again mentioned the gotra and so forth, [the grandson] of Amukadevaśarman, having again mentioned the gotra and so forth, [the son] of Amukadevaśarman...
Having again mentioned the son by his *gotra* and so forth ending in the accusative case— as "the honored bridegroom, the illustrious Amukadevaśarman"—

and having likewise stated the *gotra*, *pravara*, and names of the great-grandfather, grandfather, and father ending in the genitive case, and having stated in due order the great-granddaughter, granddaughter, and daughter as "the illustrious Amukīdevī of such-and-such *gotra* and such-and-such *pravara*," [one should proceed].
He should say, "I choose you to give [your daughter] in the Brāhma marriage rite.
The groom, however, should say, "Hrīṃ, I am chosen.
Then, perform the marriage ritual as prescribed.
The groom says, "Hrīṃ; as you command, I shall do so.
Then, having brought the girl—adorned with garments and ornaments—to the shadow-pavilion (chāyā-maṇḍapa), he should place her facing the groom.
Then, joining the girl's hand to the groom's hand and giving fruits, gems, and so forth, [he should proceed] as before.

After recording the solar month and other details, having mentioned the *gotra*, *pravara*, and name of the great-grandfather, grandfather, and father in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), and having stated "to the great-grandson," "to the grandson," and "to the son" respectively, one should utter:
"To the bridegroom, [named] Śrī-Amukadevaśarman, of such-and-such *gotra* and such-and-such *pravara*; and [to the bride]..."
Having written the names of the great-grandfather, grandfather, and father in the genitive case, along with their lineage (*gotra*) and ancestral lineages (*pravara*),

and having uttered "great-granddaughter," "granddaughter," or "daughter" as applicable, and having recited three times the phrase ending with "the maiden [named] Śrī-Amukī-devī of such-and-such a *gotra* and such-and-such *pravara*s, adorned with her covering and ornaments," [one should offer her].
"Desiring such-and-such [a goal], I give this [gift] to you, whose deity is Prajāpati.
Thus he should give it to the bridegroom.
The bridegroom should accept it, saying, "May there be well-being."
Then the giver [of the bride] should say: "In accordance with dharma, artha, and kāma, you must conduct yourself together with your wife.
The groom, having said "So be it," should recite the hymn of praise to Kāma.
Then the giver, having caused the bride and the son-in-law to hear the mantra beginning with "hrīṃ, by the grace of Prajāpati... and so forth.

Having covered [the couple] with a cloth, he should have the bridegroom and the bride look at each other's faces, preceded by auspicious rites. Then, having given gold or other items as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the bridegroom, he should perform the rite for ensuring the ceremony is without flaw (*acchidrāvadhāraṇa*).
Thereafter, on that night or the following day, the bridegroom, having kindled the fire named Yojaka according to the procedure prescribed in the *Kuśaṇḍikā*, [should proceed].
One should cook a *caru* oblation for Prajāpati.
Then, having performed the ritual up to the *dhārā-homa*, [one offers]: *hrīṃ śivāya svāhā*;
*hrīṃ durgāyai svāhā*; *hrīṃ viṣṇave svāhā*; *hrīṃ brahmaṇe svāhā*; *hrīṃ indrāya*.
One should offer oblations with the word "svāhā.
Then, having recited the mantra "Hrīṃ, I take your hand," one should take the hand of the wife.
Thereafter, [the bride], with the ghee held in her hand by her husband and the parched grains (lāja) brought by her brother or others, [should perform the rite] dedicated to Prajāpati.
One should offer oblations four times with the mantra: *hrīṃ prajāpataye svāhā*.
Then, rising together with one's wife and circumambulating the fire from left to right, one should offer: *hrīṃ durgāśivābhyāṃ svāhā* and *hrīṃ brāhmībrahmabhyāṃ svāhā*.
Having thus offered oblations three times, he should cause her to perform the stepping upon the stone and the taking of the seven steps without mantras.
If the fire-offering takes place at night, then she should look at the moon and the star Arundhatī together with women.
Then, one should complete the ritual from the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation up to the end of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Thus concludes the marriage ceremony.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Forms of Saṃskāras and Granthis," in the second section (Dharmakāṇḍa) of the Śrī Prāṇatoṣiṇī.
Since initiation (*dīkṣā*) also takes the form of a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), it is appropriate that it be discussed among the purificatory rites;
however, because it is rooted in the Guru, the section concerning the Guru is stated first.
Regarding that, the definition of the Guru is found in the second chapter of the Śārādā-tilaka.
Pure by birth on both his mother’s and father’s side, pure in disposition, and having conquered his senses;
knowing the essence of all scriptures and understanding the true meaning of all treatises;
devoted to the welfare of others and intent upon recitation, worship, and other such duties.

One whose speech is unfailing, who is tranquil, who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), who is intent upon the meaning of the path of yoga, and who has reached the heart of the deities—such a guru, endowed with these and other qualities, is approved by the Āgamas. (p. 169)
Like a deity, he is heart-stealing; that is to say, he is captivating.
Also in the second chapter of the Viśvasāra Tantra:
Devoted to all scriptures, skillful, and always knowing the meaning of all treatises;
eloquent, handsome, with well-proportioned limbs, of noble birth, and of auspicious appearance;
one who has conquered the senses, truthful in speech, a Brahmin of peaceful mind.
One who is devoted to the welfare of his father and mother, dedicated to all his duties,
established in the stages of life (āśrama), and residing in his own country— such a person is ordained as a teacher (guru).
The householder is an āśramin;
and so it is stated in the thirteenth chapter of the Matsyasūkta Mahātantra:
Born in the Middle Country, peaceful, endowed with all virtues,
possessed of wife and children, and esteemed by the Āgamas, [he is] the Guru.
The phrase "born in the Middle Country" is intended to demonstrate his excellence.
Since its specific criteria have already been written by the author of the *Tantrasāra*, there is no need to elaborate on them here; such is the definition of the Guru.
In the fifteenth chapter of the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa* and the second chapter of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the *Rudrajāmala*:
"At the outset, the practitioner is a deity, always possessing a mind fixed on right conduct;
thereafter he is a *paśu*, then a *vīra*, and in the evening he possesses the divine state (*divyabhāva*)."
For these groups of entities, the Guru should be one who has reached the further shore of Vedānta,
peaceful, self-controlled, of noble birth, humble, wearing pure attire,
of pure conduct, well-established, clean, dexterous, and highly intelligent.
He is an ascetic devoted to meditation, proficient in the mantras and tantras,
capable of both restraint and grace, self-controlled, and one who recites the meaning of the mantras.
All this beginning with "śānta" is also found in the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*; however, in the section concerning the worship of Śeṣa, the reading is "vaśī" and so forth, where he is designated as "guru."
One who is tranquil is free from intense desire for sense objects and is endowed with qualities such as *śama*.
*Śama* is the restraint of the mind from objects other than hearing [the scriptures] and so forth.
Just as when intense hunger has arisen, no activity other than eating is pleasing to the mind.

He endures delays in eating, and likewise, an extreme delight arises toward objects such as garlands and sandalwood paste, while an extreme delight also arises toward hearing, reflection, and so forth, which are the means for attaining the knowledge of reality.

Or he is renowned for his tranquil form; or he is self-controlled (*dānta*), meaning he endures the hardships of austerity or is endowed with restraint (*dama*). Restraint (*dama*) is the withdrawal of the external senses from objects other than those [pertaining to the Self].

The intention is that *dama* is that specific function by which the external sense organs, such as the ear, which are directed toward objects like sound— objects distinct from the means for attaining knowledge such as hearing and so forth— are withdrawn. For this very reason, one who effects the restraint of the internal organ is called *śānta*, while one who effects the restraint of the external organs is called *dānta*.
This has been stated by those who know the Vedānta.
Also in the third chapter of the *Vṛhannīlamantropaniṣad*:
"A Guru who removes the external senses is difficult to find everywhere;
a Guru who removes the internal senses is auspicious everywhere."

"One who possesses proper conduct, is devoted to the propitiation of Mahāvidyā, is intent upon it, and is thoroughly engaged in its ritual practice— such a person is designated as a Guru. One who is of noble birth is a Kaula.

Not having seen the statements beginning with "of these," some explain by their own intellect that [the candidate] must be of noble birth, of pure origin, or endowed with the nine qualities such as proper conduct; this is extremely weak.
For in the statement of the summary of the essence (*sārasaṃgraha*) which is to be cited later, both "one of pure parents" and "one of noble birth" are mentioned separately.
For one who explains it in this way, there may indeed be a doubt that there is an absence of *kulācāra* (family tradition) in the teacher of the Viṣṇu-mantra;
however, that doubt arises only for someone who has not seen the *Kāmākhyā*, *Kulārṇava*, *Rudrayāmala*, and other such texts.
For in those [texts], there is the teaching on the installation of the *kula* for all—namely, the Saura, Gāṇapatya, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, and Śākta [traditions].

Because it is very clear, that authority should be written hereafter. Since he did not see what will be stated later in the section on those to be avoided during the initiation— that one has black teeth, lacks family tradition, and so forth, being devoid of the fivefold conduct— it was not observed by him.
For this very reason, it is proclaimed that one of noble birth is qualified for all mantras;
"He alone, and no other, is the master of initiation and the self of every mantra"—
thus the citation from the *Tantrasāra* is rightly consistent.
Also in the third chapter of the Kāmākhyātantra:
He who is peaceful, self-controlled, of noble birth, and likewise pure in his inner heart;
who consists of the five principles (pañcatattva), he is proclaimed as the true Guru. Renowned among his kinsmen as a perfected one (siddha), he is the protector of his disciples.
O beloved! A true guru is said to be one who is wondrous through divine power;
he speaks words that are unheard of, yet full of meaning, virtuous, and captivating.
He alone is a true guru who thoroughly understands the tantras and mantras.
And in the tenth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra.
In the Śākta tradition, a Śākta guru is recommended; in the Śaiva, a Śiva-guru is considered best;
in the Vaiṣṇava, a Vaiṣṇava; in the Saura, a Saura guru is declared;
in the Gāṇapa, a Gāṇapa is renowned; but a Kaula is the true guru everywhere.
Therefore, the wise person should, with his whole being, undergo initiation from a Kaula.
The characteristics of the true guru will be described as follows: "One who has destroyed the delusion of various conceptual constructions," and so forth.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the true guru.
Likewise.

One who receives the mantra from the mouth of a *paśu* remains a *paśu* himself; of this there is no doubt. One who receives the mantra from a *vīra* becomes a *vīra*, and from a *kaula* one becomes a knower of Brahman.
Also in the Vṛhannīlatantra:
A Śaiva is undoubtedly a teacher of the higher sciences (paravidyā);
likewise, a Vaiṣṇava is for those established in his own doctrine, and a Saura is for the virtuous who know the Sun.
O Queen of the Gods! One who belongs to the Gāṇapatya [tradition] is the initiator of the Gaṇa-initiation;
he is the master of initiations everywhere, whether in the Śaiva or Śākta [systems], without a doubt. Therefore, a Kaula should with great effort take refuge in a guru of noble lineage (kulīna).
Thus ends the praise of the noble guru.
Is it not so, as stated in the sixth chapter of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the *Rudrayāmala*:

"O God, the state of being (*bhāva*) is threefold, according to the sequence of the Divine (*divya*), the Heroic (*vīra*), and the Fettered (*paśu*). Likewise, here the gurus and the deity of the mantra are also threefold."

If it is asked: "How can such an interpretation be made by accepting the technical term *kulīna*—as found in the words of those who follow the Vāma, Siddhānta, and Kula paths, as well as in the *Āmārcanacandrikā* and other texts—as referring to this [subject] concerning the animal-sacrificing guru (*paśuguru*)?"—the answer is: no.

Since it is clearly stated in the *Mahānirvāṇatantra* that the Kaula is the instructor of all mantras and possesses the status of a true guru (*sadguru*), this refutes the definition of a true guru formulated by moderns, which holds that a true guru is one who, while possessing qualities such as tranquility and so forth, is free from defects such as being falsely accused.
This is because it is stated that only a *kaula* is a true guru.

Now, if it is argued: "What is the harm in using the definition of 'kulīna' as it is well-known among ordinary people—that he is born of a pure lineage and possesses the nine qualities such as proper conduct (*ācāra*) and so forth?"—we say no.
For in the Tantric scriptures, there is heard a censure of the fabrication of artificial meanings (*kūṭārtha*),
as for example in the eleventh chapter of the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*.
In this Śāmbhava scripture, which is expanded by words of clear meaning,
those who imagine a meaning through [arbitrary] code-words fall and go to a downward state.
In the second chapter of the Uttarakhanda of the Rudrajāmala.
Free from disease, devoid of ego, and great, being free from all transformations;
an ascetic, truthful in speech, always devoted to meditation;
distinguished by his knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures, and dedicated to his own duty.
Abiding in unmanifest signs and marks, a practitioner who bestows auspiciousness,
who possesses fortune and steadfastness, is called a Lord and a Guru.
The etymological derivation of the terms *guru*, *nātha*, and *ācārya* is found in the seventeenth chapter of the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava*:

"Because he investigates the reality of the meaning of the secret scriptures and because he provides awakening, and because he possesses the nature of the deities beginning with Rudra, he is designated as a *guru*. (p. 172)

O Dear One! He is called Śrīnātha because he bestows the knowledge of liberation, because he awakens one to the Self as the Sound-Brahman (Nādabrahman), and because he has concealed the outward signs of [worldly] knowledge;
he practices it himself and establishes his disciples in right conduct as well.
For he gathers together the meanings of the scriptures, and thus he is called Ācārya;
he who himself teaches that which is near to all things moving and unmoving,
and who is called Ācārya because of his perfection in the yoga of Yama and the other limbs.
In the *Sārasaṃgraha* as cited in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*.

A twice-born man who has pure parents, has conquered his senses, knows all the scriptures, is distressed by the suffering of others, speaks the truth, is a knower of the Vedas and master of the Vedāṅgas, is peaceful, and is of noble birth— such a one is declared to be a Guru.
By the specific mention of "twice-born" (dvija), it is understood that the reception of mantras does not apply to others;
yet even a twice-born who is devoid of proper conduct remains a teacher for the [other] castes.
Because of this statement,
the word "he" (sa) is connected with the particle "only" (eva).
By the phrase "he alone is the guru," other castes (jātyantara) are excluded.
The particle *eva* is connected with the word *guru* alone, because there is no other [term] to be excluded.
To the Lord of the Nine Chakras, as upheld in the commentary on the Kulamūlāvatārakalpasūtra.
Having assumed the form of Śiva for the sake of liberation from the bonds of worldly existence,
I am the knower of the essence of the Siddhānta and the one who reveals the distinctions within that essence;
I am ever vigilant and unwearied in both bestowing grace and meting out restraint.
O Goddess! Though I am Śiva of divine form, I am not within the range of sight;
nevertheless, O Pārvatī, I shall instruct my disciples in the form of the venerable Guru, generating supreme consciousness and arising from the highest bliss.
O Mistress of the Kula! He by whom that reality is known is the Guru;
O Goddess, Mistress of the Kula! he who always knows the past and future Mantras and Tantras, as well as the sixfold nature of the Creator (Brahmā), is the Guru.
O Mistress of the Kula! He who awakens the six paths—namely, phoneme (varṇa), digit (kalā), word (pada), principle (tattva), mantra, and world-sphere (bhuvana)—is the Guru.
[He knows] the six supports, the nine gates, and the determination of the sixteen supports.
O Mistress of the Kula! He who knows [these] according to the prescribed rule is a Guru.
O Goddess, Mistress of the Kula! he who knows the fivefold—waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the form beyond that, and the state transcending all—is a Guru.
Also in the first chapter of the Sammohanatantra:
He who understands within his own body the six chakras, the sixteen supports, the three lakshas, and the five voids— he is called a Guru by the wise.
These are explained in sequence. (p.
173) The grammatical connection is that he who awakens the disciple to the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) is the Guru. He states the paths beginning with "the phoneme" (*varṇa*), and so forth.
I shall clarify these six paths in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*).
The "six supports" (*ṣaḍādhāra*) are the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*), because they serve as the foundational bases for the elements beginning with earth.
The "nine gates" (*navadvāra*) consist of the apertures of the eyes, ears, mouth, nostrils, anus, and penis.
And it is also stated in the second chapter of the *Sammohana-tantra*:
"The body is proclaimed to be a city with nine gates and nine apertures;
there are nine lotuses, the wheels, the three threads, and the three channels."
The nature of the sixteen supports is also described in that very same place.
The Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and Ājñā cakras; then the Bindu, the Kalāpada, Nibodhikā, Ardhendu, Nāda, and Nādānta.
Unmanī, Viṣṇuvaktra, and then Dhruvamaṇḍalikā—
this is said to be the sixteenfold support, difficult for yogis to attain.
"By means of the prescribed method" (vidhānena) means with effort, that is to say, through breath control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth.
"Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep" constitute the three-fold cycle of the intellect (*buddhi*).
"The Bindu, which transcends that, is the stainless (*nirañjana*)"—this will become clear further on.
Regarding the "three hundred thousand" and so forth, it is stated in that very same place: "The self-existent (*svayambhū*) is the arrow; the other is proclaimed to be three hundred thousand."
The elements beginning with earth and the pentad of spaces have been described.
Among them, the *svayambhū-liṅga* is in the *mūlādhāra*, the *vāṇa-liṅga* is in the *anāhata*, and the other is in the *ājñā-cakra*.
O Sovereign of the Nine Wheels!
He who correctly understands the fourfold— namely, the *piṇḍa*, the *pada*, the *rūpa*, and that which transcends form (*rūpātīta*)— is proclaimed as a Guru.
This fourfold beginning with the *piṇḍa* has been clearly explained in the *Gurugītā*.
The *piṇḍa* is proclaimed to be the power Kuṇḍalinī; the *pada* is celebrated as the Haṃsa.
The *rūpa* should be known as the Bindu, while that which transcends form is the Nirañjana.
O Sovereign of the Nine Wheels!
He who understands the fourfold— whether it be the outward-looking Parā, the Madhyamā, or even the Vaikharī— is proclaimed as a Guru.
Thus ends the specific characteristics of the Guru.
In the Rudrajāmala, in the first chapter of the Uttarakhanda.
The entire world has its root in the Guru; the supreme austerity has its root in the Guru.
By the mere grace of the Guru, the self-controlled person attains liberation.
In the first chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
The Guru alone is Śiva manifest; the Guru is the accomplisher of all aims.
The Guru alone is the supreme reality; the entire universe consists of the Guru.
Without the grace of the Guru, what is the use of ten million rounds of purificatory rites?
Also, in the first chapter of the first section of the *Piñchilātantra*:
"This scripture has the Guru as its root; there is no other Lord more auspicious than Śiva.
Therefore, O Maheśānī, one should take refuge in the Guru with great effort."
Thus ends the majesty of the Guru.
In the fourteenth chapter of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the Rudrajāmala.
O Supreme Goddess! That fool who, without a guru, undertakes the practice of recitation by merely looking at books and the like incurs sin;
O Beloved! neither mother, nor father, nor brother can be his refuge—what indeed is his destiny?
O beautiful lady, the Guru alone destroys sin in an instant;
for without a Guru, there is no entitlement whatsoever to the Tantra.
Therefore, one must with great effort seek out an excellent Guru.
Thus, the necessity of the Guru is established in the scripture,
the Jāmalam.
The Guru alone is declared to be Śiva; O Goddess, I am he, there is no doubt.
You too are the Guru, O Queen of the Gods, and the mantra is also said to be the Guru.
Therefore, no distinction whatsoever arises between the mantra, the Guru, and the Deity.
Sometimes the Guru, who is always to be meditated upon, is visualized within a thousand-petaled lotus;
sometimes in the lotus of the heart, and sometimes within the range of one's vision.
In the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
Contemplating with the intellect the identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra, the mantra then becomes effective; otherwise, there is only failure when it is manifest.
Pārvatī said:
O Mahādeva! O Lord! How does the knowledge of oneness arise?
I consider the Guru in human form to be the deity whose nature is meditation, and the mantra to be of the nature of syllables; how then, O Śiva, can oneness be achieved?
Śiva said:
Because they possess a single nature by virtue of their own essence and originate from a single birth,
when these factors are united as entities, there is indeed only a single means:
the mantra is born from the Guru, and the deity is born from the mantra.
Therefore, O Varārohā! the Grandfather (Brahmā) is the deity’s father;

and because of his devotion, O Goddess, he is as much the father of the father as the father himself. Thus, by being born from him, he attains satisfaction; if it were otherwise, the reverse would occur.
This is the intended meaning:
"in the form of a single genus" means "in a form devoid of specific mental images (nirākāra)."

For it should be understood that these three are formless (*nirākāra*): because Mahākāla alone will be described as the Guru; because the mantra consists of sound (*dhvani*); and because the form of the deity is merely conceptualized.
Alternatively, this may be because they constitute a single mode of practice (*ekaprakārasādhana*).

By the statement "the mantra is born from the guru," it is shown that there is a unity among the triad of guru, mantra, and deity, just as there is a unity between a father and his son or grandson due to their being born of the same lineage.
As it is stated in the tenth chapter of the *Yāmātṛkābhedatantra*:
The illustrious Goddess said:
O Lord! Tell me, how can there be oneness between the Guru who has a human form, who is eternally composed of the syllables of mantra, and the deity who conforms to meditative visualization?
The illustrious Śiva said:
The great mantra is obtained from the mouth of the Guru by the best of practitioners;
from that very source the seed-syllable (bīja) is born, and from it liberation becomes certain.
For, O Dear One, the body of the deity indeed arises from the seed-syllable.
In accordance with the command of the Guru, another form arises;
O Goddess, from the contemplation of the Guru and so forth, the perfection of being (bhāvasiddhi) is produced.
For this very reason, O Maheśānī, oneness is proclaimed.
In the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
For one who does not conceive of any distinction between the mantra, the guru, and the deity,
what indeed will the Mother of the World not bestow day after day?
Thus concludes the explanation of the manner in which the guru, the mantra, and the deity are one.
In the Guru-tantra:
The Guru is the creator, the Guru is the destroyer, and the Guru is the protector upon the earth.
By the mere satisfaction of the Guru, all the deities become pleased.
This statement is also found in the fifty-first chapter of the Vāmakeśvaratantra.
However, in this context, the reading is *pāte gurur dātā*.
When the Guru is pleased, Śiva is pleased; when he is angry, the Three-eyed Lord is angry.
When the Guru is pleased, Śivā is pleased; when she is angry, Sundarī is angry.
Therefore, O Great Goddess! in crossing the ocean of worldly existence, the Guru is the creator, the protector, and the destroyer; the Guru is the bestower of liberation.
Thus ends the section on the fruits such as the satisfaction of the Guru.
In the Rudrajāmala as cited in the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī:
"The letter *ga* is said to bestow perfection; the letter *ra* is the burner of sin;
the letter *u* is called Śambhu; the Guru is remembered as the essence of these three."
In the first chapter of the Kaṅkālamālinī Tantra.
O Great Goddess! The two syllables "Gu-ru" signify the Supreme Brahman devoid of attributes;
this great mantra is the highest of the high and must be kept strictly secret.
In the Guru-tantra:
O Goddess! For him on the tip of whose tongue the syllable "Guru" resides, what delusion can remain? What is the use of the futile recitations of the Vedas?
By the mere utterance of the letter "Ga," even the sin of killing a Brahmin is dispelled.
By the mere utterance of the syllable *u*, one is liberated from the sins of birth;
by the mere utterance of the syllable *r*, and again by the utterance of the syllable *u*;
and by the utterance of the *visarga*, it removes the sin born of ten million births.

O Goddess, for me who was reciting the syllable "Guru," the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa was certainly liberated in the past; this is the truth, there is no doubt. Paraśurāma was freed from the slaughter of his mother, and Devendra from the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
He was liberated even from that sin merely by the utterance of the Guru's name.
Thus is the fruit of uttering the word "guru."
In that very same [text].
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; Pārvatī, the supreme goddess; Indra and the other gods; the Yakṣas and the rest, as well as the ancestral deities;
all rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā; the Gandharvas and the various species of serpents.
The immobile and other moving beings, as well as the mountains composed of all elements—
these and others always abide within the venerable body of the Guru;
by the mere satisfaction of the Śrī Guru, their satisfaction is produced.
Thus ends the description of how the world is satisfied when the Guru is satisfied.
In that very same [text].
There is no scripture superior to the Guru; no austerity superior to the Guru;
no mantra superior to the Guru; no fruit superior to the Guru.
O Goddess, there is nothing superior to the Guru; Śiva himself is not superior to the Guru.
There is no form superior to the Guru; there is no recitation superior to the Guru.
In the *Gurugītā* belonging to the *Viśvasāra-tantra*.
One should always meditate on the form of the Guru and always chant the reality (tattva) of the Guru.
Kāśī is his dwelling place, and the water from the feet of the Jāhnavī is his [offering].
The Guru is directly Viśveśvara himself; he is certainly the Tāraka Brahman.
Likewise:
"The root of meditation is the form of the Guru; the root of worship is the feet of the Guru;
the root of mantra is the word of the Guru; the root of accomplishment is the grace of the Guru."
Likewise,
O Pārvatī, even if one is cursed by sages, serpents, or gods,
or even out of fear of timely death, the Guru protects him.
In the second chapter of the *Guptasādhanatantra*.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru is the sacred ford, the Guru is the sacrifice, the Guru is charity, and the Guru is austerity.
The Guru is fire, the Guru is the sun—the entire world is permeated by the Guru.
Thus ends the exposition on the superiority of the Guru over all [others].

What is the use of charity, what is the use of austerity, and what else is the use of visiting sacred fords? By him who has worshipped the feet of the venerable Guru, the entire world has been worshipped.
Indeed, whatever sacred fords exist within the vessel of the cosmic egg—

"For they indeed dwell perpetually at the soles of the Guru's feet. By this, it is clearly understood that through the worship of the Guru's feet, the accomplishment of the worship of the entire universe is attained.
Thus concludes the exposition on how the worship of the world is accomplished through the worship of the Guru.
In the Piñchilā Tantra.
The Guru is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by initiation (dīkṣā) and instruction (śikṣā). First is declared the initiation-guru; the remaining one is considered the instruction-guru.
From whose mouth the great mantra is heard or even practiced, [he is the guru].
That guru is to be known as supreme; his command bestows accomplishment, according to the Kulāgama held in the commentary on the *Kulamūlāvatārakalpasūtra*.
The instigator, the indicator, the expresser, the demonstrator, the instructor,
and the enlightener— these six are remembered as gurus.
Of these, the first five are the effects, while the enlightener is the cause.
Thus ends the description of the different types of gurus. Likewise:
"Those who have been instructed by those who know reality are themselves knowers of reality; of this there is no doubt."
O Goddess, those who are instructed by the bound souls (paśus) are themselves considered bound souls;
a wise man may uplift a fool, but a fool cannot uplift a fool.
Iron may carry across a stone, but a stone cannot carry across another stone.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Gurutantro*:
There are many gurus who remove the distress of their disciples;
yet I consider that one alone to be rare, who destroys the burning heat within the heart of a disciple.
Among them all, only one may be preeminent, the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the seed-syllable for the hand-gesture of the Guru who knows reality.
In the first chapter of the first section of the Yoginītantra.
The Goddess said:
"O Maheśāna! O Compassionate One! Tell me, who is your guru?
This one whom you have proclaimed as your guru is indeed even greater than you yourself.
Śrī-Īśvara said:
O Great Goddess! He who is known as Mahākāla is indeed the Primordial Lord (Ādinātha).
O Queen of the Gods, he alone is the Guru in all mantras and none other—in those of Śiva, Śakti, Viṣṇu, Gaṇapati, and likewise in those of Indra.

O Girinandini, daughter of the Mountain! At the time of imparting the mantra, he alone—and no other—is the preceptor in both the Mahāśaiva and Saura traditions; of this there is no doubt, O Parameśvarī! He alone shall be the speaker of the mantra, and none else.
O Śaṅkarī, that Mahākāla shall be his presiding deity!
Therefore, O Goddess, there is no heaviness [of status] for a human being here; of this there is no doubt.
Śiva is the giver of the mantra to the Guru, since he performs meditation upon the lotus [of the disciple].
"O Goddess! the disciple also performs that meditation upon the Śīrṣa-śaṅkha;
that meditation is to be imparted upon the head of the disciple and not otherwise.
Thus ends the latter half of the third chapter in the Kāmākhyātantra.

Therefore, O Maheśānī! he alone is remembered as the Guru. O Maheśvarī! by virtue of his being the locus [of the Divine], O Śaṅkarī! his greatness has been proclaimed in all the scriptures regarding that human being.
Also in the third chapter of the Kāmākhyātantra:
Therefore, O Great Goddess! a human has indeed been made the Guru. O Goddess! the status of being a Guru in a human is merely a conceptual construction and not primary;
for liberation does not arise, O Goddess, from the notion of a human as the Guru.
Likewise:
"For this very reason, the Guru is not merely a human being, but rather a mental construction;
just as there is worship of trees and so forth by practitioners during initiation and other rites."

(178) Now, if one objects: "If a human being is not a guru, then what is the status of such statements from the Tantrasāra as 'Whether ignorant or learned, the guru is the supreme deity'? It is true that this was stated [in that context] for the sake of showing respect, just as was previously said regarding trees and so forth.

However, if that were the case in reality, it would not be consistent with the statement to be cited later—"the notion of [the guru] being a human"—nor with the passage from the *Tantrasāra* held by its author, "the notion of humanity regarding the guru.
The wise should reflect upon this: just as a jar has defects such as holes or cracks, so too does a human being have defects such as the great sins (*mahāpātaka*).
Also in the Guru-tantra:
O Goddess, it is proclaimed everywhere that there is but one Guru;
no distinction should be made regarding him, for the entire world is permeated by the Guru.
Because of this statement, those who claim that since the Guru is eternal, there is a three-night period of impurity (*aśauca*) upon the death of the Guru, are indeed fools.
Since impurity and such matters are prescribed by the *Smṛtis*, the impurity due to the death of a Guru refers either to a Guru mentioned in the *Smṛtis* or to a Vedic Guru.
Furthermore, if they accept it as referring even to a Tantric Guru in accordance with statements from the *Matsyasūkta* and other sources, [that too is incorrect].

Some maintain that this [initiation] refers to the lineage of gurus beginning with Preraka as taught in the *Kulāgama*, or that it is prescribed as a duty for a disciple who is still engaged in the conduct of a bound soul (*paśu*); however,
the wise should understand that it does not refer to the guru who imparts awakening (*bodhaka*).
Listen to the distinction; I shall declare the majesty pertaining to the Guru.
In the bestowal of the Paśu-mantra, the limit extends to ten generations;
in the bestowal of the Vīra-mantra, it extends to twenty-five generations.
Among all the great vidyās, it is considered to extend to fifty generations;
however, in the bestowal of the yoga of Brahman, the limit extends to a hundred generations.
This is the intended meaning.

If a mantra belonging to the Pāśupata and other such systems has been received by a disciple from a guru, and subsequently another mantra is received by that disciple’s lineage from a different guru, nevertheless, because [the lineage] is characterized by the negative karma (*duradṛṣṭa*) arising from the abandonment of the paternal guru,
there remains the same status as a guru for ten generations of the paternal line and for ten generations of one’s own line.
It must be done in this way;

otherwise, if the mantra were received individually by each person, then because they would all be [independent] gurus, the conceptualization of a lineage-boundary (vaṃśamaryādā) for all of them would be purposeless— thus is stated the description of the lineage-boundary that has been abandoned [by others].

Alternatively, since the abandonment of a greedy or corrupt guru is prescribed as a rule by the statement found in the upcoming *Kāmākhyātantra*, this [present] statement was made for the sake of maintaining the tradition of that lineage, even if the disciple abandons such a guru.
It will be stated later that even divine (*divya*) or heroic (*vīra*) gurus must be abandoned if they are corrupted by faults.

And thus, the statement cited by the author of the *Tantrasāra*, "By abandoning a guru in this way, death shall occur," should be understood as referring to the abandonment of a guru who is not free from defects and so forth.
In the Mahiṣamardinītantra as cited in the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī.
O Maheśānī! I shall describe to you briefly the lineage of Mānava:
the Guru, the Paraguru, the Parāparaguru, and likewise the Śvaguru; O Parameśānī! he is indeed the manifest [Guru], of this there is no doubt.
His father, the supreme preceptor, is Viṣṇu himself always present on earth;
his father, the preceptor of both the higher and the lower, is always equal to Maheśvara.
This is stated in the second chapter of the Bṛhannīlatantra.
O Pārvatī! Listen now to the determination regarding the supreme and the subordinate gurus. O Goddess of the Gods, in all cases, the one who first imparts the mantra is the supreme guru.
You are indeed the parāpara-guru, while I am the parameṣṭhi-guru.

In the Kulārṇava Tantra: "O Dear One! The lineage of the traditional transmission, the practice of mantras, and so forth—all this must be obtained from the mouth of the Guru; only then does it become fruitful, and not otherwise."
The etymological derivation of the word *pāramparya*, however, is [explained] in the seventeenth chapter (*ullāsa*).
O Goddess, because it severs the bonds, because it is beyond coloring,
and because it cuts through the [notions of] castes, it is called "pāramparya."
Now follows the definition of the female guru.
In the second chapter of the Uttarakhanda and the fifteenth chapter of the Purvakhanda of the Rudrajāmala.
She was virtuous, of good conduct, devoted to her guru, and had conquered her senses;
she knew the true meaning and essence of all mantras, possessed excellent character, and delighted in worship;
she was endowed with all auspicious marks, beautiful, and lotus-eyed.
Adorned with jewel ornaments and decorated with golden finery,
she is peaceful, of noble lineage, born of a good family, moon-faced, and endowed with all wisdom.
Possessed of infinite virtues, she is the beloved who bestows the state of Rudra.

She who is the embodiment of the Guru, the bestower of power, and the form of the knowledge of Śiva—she indeed is fit to be a Guru, for she is free from widowhood. Initiation by a woman is declared auspicious; that by a mother is remembered as being eightfold more meritorious.
A widow who has sons should be accepted as she alone bestows pure bliss;
if the mantra is already accomplished, then one should take it from the mouth of a widow.
In that case, the fruit is considered to be purely excellent and eight times greater than that from a mother.
If she herself, upon the dissolution of her dream, imparts my mantra,
she obtains an eightfold result therein— provided she is a virtuous woman who has borne a son.
And if a mother imparts her own mantra to her daughter, [she likewise gains the same fruit].
Then one attains the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*) on the path of devotion; of this there is no doubt.
O Lord, that very thing is difficult to obtain if it is bestowed by a mother!
Having first attained devotion and then liberation, one assumes a form according to one's desire.
He knows the meaning of ten billion vidyās; there is no doubt in this.
Whether in a dream or in person, if his mother gives him her own mantra, he too, having performed initiation once more, shall attain the state of a Dānava.
If she follows the mother’s will solely by the power of her speech, then she attains success; in that case, one should deliberate upon the mantra.
One should not entertain thoughts of a guru other than through the instruction of one’s own mantra.
Thus ends the discourse on women as teachers.
Regarding what must be avoided when the Guru is to be served, it is stated in the fifteenth chapter of the first part of the second chapter of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Rudrayāmala.
And one should avoid a guru who is devoid of supreme bliss, lacking in beauty,
censured, diseased, cruel, or a great sinner;
as well as one afflicted by the eight types of leprosy or by trickling leprosy.
One who has white leprosy, one who injures people, one who always grasps at wealth for his own sake, a seller of gold, a thief, one devoid of intelligence,
one who is very short, one with black teeth, one lacking family conduct, and one devoid of tranquility— [these are to be avoided].

One who is stained by blemish, afflicted by eye disease, a frequenter of others' wives, a speaker of unrefined words, one conquered by women, one with an extra limb, one who is deceitful by nature, and likewise one who is excessively talkative— [these are to be avoided].
One should not worship anyone who eats excessively, who is wretched, who speaks falsely, who is restless, who lacks inner disposition, who is devoid of the fivefold conduct,
or whose limbs are adorned with a web of faults— unless they are one's own Guru.

Based on the statement that "one should not worship [the deity] without a guru," one may worship someone who has become afflicted by defects such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) once they have been made a guru; however,
the intended meaning of the injunction is that at the very time of being appointed as a guru, one should avoid anyone who already possesses such defects as leprosy.

And as for that statement, "One should avoid a guru who is a great sinner," that too is a figurative expression (upacāra) regarding a future state as if it were already present; it refers to a guru who is to be avoided, otherwise there would be a contradiction between the two parts of this single written work.
In the twelfth chapter of the *Niruttaratantra*.
One who seeks dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa should not honor as a guru a person who is a beast, a fool, a rogue, or especially a flatterer.
In the Jāmalatantra, in the fifteenth chapter of the first section.
The teacher’s deliberation applies everywhere except in the case of his father and maternal grandfather. However, if through negligence he should perform the rite of initiation for them,
he must then perform an expiation and undergo initiation once again.
O Lord of the World, the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred thousand times,
or the Praṇava (Om) one hundred thousand times for Viṣṇu, is recorded in the Smṛtis as the expiation.
O Great Goddess, if one is unable, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
By reciting it ten thousand times,
the Gāyatrī— the mother of all meters and a fire to the scales of heaps of sin— destroys every transgression.
It destroys even the most stubborn enemy, one who is like a brother yet belongs to the side of the foe.
Having excluded his maternal grandfather and his father who is an ascetic living in the forest,
the chief disciple should perform the rite of initiation;
otherwise, by acting in opposition to them, the destruction of the body will certainly occur.
O Bhairavī, one may receive a perfected mantra even from a person of low birth;
however, regarding initiation for both teacher and disciple, there is no restriction concerning dreams.
That which is obtained in a dream or given by a woman is purified solely through the consecration rite.
In the Mahākapilapañcarātra as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
Neither too young nor old, neither lame nor emaciated;
neither with extra limbs nor deficient in limbs, neither bald nor with protruding teeth—
[as stated] in the *Kalpacintāmaṇi* cited in the *Vīramitrodaya*.
One afflicted with consumption, one with skin disease, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who is deaf in one ear, one with discolored eyes, one who is bald, and one who is a cripple.
One blind in one ear is deaf;
a *khañjarīṭa* is lame.

One who is deficient in limbs, one with extra limbs, one with tawny eyes, one with a putrid nose, one with a large scrotum, a dwarf, one who is hunchbacked, one afflicted with vitiligo, and one who is a eunuch; [among these] "one with a putrid nose" means one whose nose has a foul odor.
A teacher who is thus possessed of bodily defects, who is censured,
devoid of purificatory rites, foolish, bereft of the Vedas and Shastras,
lacking in the performance of Shruti and Smriti rituals, dry in speech, and utterly contemptible;
A man who lives by performing sacrifices for others, a physician who is lustful,
one who is cruel, deceitful, envious, addicted to vices, miserly, wicked,
a companion of the base, an atheist, fearful, and marked by great sins;
Averse to the rites of worship for the gods, fire, gurus, and the sciences; devoid of knowledge regarding the mantras for the twilight prayers, libations, and worship;
overcome by laziness, devoted to sensual enjoyments, and lacking in dharma—such a person is merely a nominal listener.
For these and many other reasons, as well as those declared in the scriptures,
the wise should diligently avoid such a teacher when undertaking initiations, installations, and other rites.
In the thirteenth chapter of the Matsyasūkta.

One who is sonless, one whose wife has not borne a child, one who is powerless, or one who is a dwarf; one who is humpbacked, one afflicted with leprosy, one with black teeth, and likewise the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī);
as well as [the sons] of a maternal grandfather, of a younger brother, and of a uterine brother.
One should not receive the mantra from one's father, nor likewise from one who is dependent;
if one should ever receive it from such a person, he must undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) again.
The abandonment of Guru-sāha is taught in the third chapter of the Kāmākhyā [Tantra].
Having stated that in the human realm the notion of "heaviness" is merely a mental construction, [it continues]:
"O Goddess, just as food is not given to an eater directly, but rather in a vessel such as one of gold,
so too is the offering of everything made to Him."
O Mistress of the Family! If that recipient is blameworthy, or even if it be gold, then one should discard that vessel and feed with another vessel;
therefore, a disciple should indeed abandon a greedy and wicked person.
In this world, for all beings, the guru alone is indeed the means for attaining true knowledge;
through knowledge one attains liberation, therefore knowledge is higher than the highest. Consequently, one should abandon that guru who is indeed incapable of bestowing knowledge.

O beloved! Just as one who has no desire for food completely renounces that which is not food, so too does knowledge shine forth therein; such a Guru is indeed Śiva himself. Having abandoned the ignorant, one should seek refuge with those possessed of knowledge.
Just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to another flower,
so a disciple, greedy for knowledge, goes from one teacher to another teacher.
Likewise: "If one who is possessed of the previously mentioned defects is either a divya or a vīra,
even for those two, the disciple must not cultivate the attitude of a guru."
However, one should abandon the desire for personal gain from one's work and the conceit of regarding oneself as a teacher.
But for the Kaulas, it is in that very place.
He who, having bestowed the Great Vidyā, does not impart the conduct of the heroes (vīrācāra),
goes to a terrible hell, and his disciple likewise becomes fallen. For he who, remaining in the state of a bound soul (paśu), [does not practice] the mantra of Kālikā-Tāriṇī...
Having given instruction, one should not speak [of his faults], for he does not turn back from hell;
therefore, O Dear One, a guru who treats a disciple as a mere animal (paśu) must always be abandoned by practitioners.
Even if, by chance, a Śākta practitioner receives initiation from such a beast-like guru...
Having performed the Kaulika rite from the Kaula tradition, one should again touch that mantra.
It will be explained further ahead that, according to the statement "thus it has been said," the Guru must again be appointed through consecration and other rites.
Since the status of being a guru depends upon the existence of a disciple, the section concerning the disciple is stated immediately after the section concerning the guru.
The etymological derivation of the word "disciple" (śiṣya) therein is found in the seventeenth chapter of the fifth section of the Kulārṇava.
He who, having offered his body and vital breaths to the true gurus,
receives the yoga from those gurus, is designated as a "disciple" (śiṣya).
Now, the characteristics of a disciple,
as stated in the second chapter of the Rudrajāmala, in its Uttarakhanda section.
Having described the characteristics of the guru, [it is said]:
"The disciple, having become such as that, should take refuge in a true guru."

From the *Kulamūlāvatārakalpasūtraṭīkā*: One who is endowed with the four primary qualities— possessing faith, having a firm disposition, being free from greed, and having steady limbs— one who acts with discernment and has conquered the senses.
A disciple should be a believer, possessing firm devotion toward the guru, the mantra, and the deity;
one of such character is a true disciple, whereas any other causes suffering to the guru.
The meaning is that he is endowed with the first four [qualities], which are conjoined with the tetrad beginning with tranquility (śama).
In the second chapter of the Śāradātilaka.
The disciple should be of noble birth, pure in soul, and devoted to the goals of human life;
he should have studied the Vedas, be skillful, and have long since cast away the god of love;
he should always seek the welfare of living beings, be a believer, and have abandoned atheism.
Devoted to his own duty with devotion, striving for the welfare of his father and mother,
and intent on serving his guru through speech, mind, body, and wealth—
a disciple endowed with such qualities as these exists, and no other.
In the second chapter of the *Samācāra-tantra*.
The disciple, too, should be endowed with his own virtues, always devoted to service for the guru,
possessed of righteousness, desire, and other [aims], dedicated to the guru’s mantra,
possessing a truthful intellect regarding the guru’s mantra, and intent upon the worship of the deity.
One who possesses noble intelligence and has faith in the path taught by the guru,
and who is endowed with such characteristics, is also a disciple who has been duly examined.
Also, in the thirteenth chapter of the Matsyasūkta Mahātantra:
"The disciple should be of noble birth, pure in soul, devoted to the goals of human existence,
one who has studied the Vedas, skillful, and far removed from the power of passion."
Always seeking the welfare of living beings, ever a believer who has abandoned atheism, devoted to his own duty, striving for the benefit of his father and mother with devotion,
and intent upon serving his guru with speech, mind, body, and wealth.
O Śaṅkarī, such is the disciple who is endowed with these qualities.
Thus ends the characteristics of a disciple.
These are the passages prescribing the methods for honoring the Guru according to the Rudrajāmalatantra,
such as "The Guru is the father," which establishes him as the cause of birth,
and other statements such as "The true Guru [protects] his own dependent," composed by our most venerable great-great-grandfather, Kṛṣṇānandāgamavāgīśa.
Since these have already been written in the *Svakṛtatantrasāra*, there is no need for them here.
The disciple to be avoided is described in the fifteenth chapter of the first part and the second chapter of the latter part of the Rudrayāmala.
One who is lustful, crooked, censured by the world, devoid of truth, undisciplined, incompetent, lacking progeny, fond of enemies,
always engaged in sinful deeds, destitute of learning, and dull-witted.
(184) One whose body is composed of the multitude of defects of the Kali age,
devoid of Vedic rites, lacking the conduct of the stages of life (āśrama), characterized by an impure internal organ, always bereft of faith, base, wrathful, and deluded.

The Guru should avoid that disciple who is of untruthful conduct, devoid of virtue, obsessed with another's wife, whose limbs are bound together, who is fierce toward the assembly, lacking devotion, whose mind is dualistic, and whose body is covered with various censures.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of a censurable disciple.
In the Jāmalam.
If the hero is not released for the sake of granting wealth and other gifts,
that sinful man becomes a denizen of hell like his disciple;
in an instant, he becomes unsuccessful due to the sins incurred by his disciple.
Having fallen unexpectedly into hell solely for the destruction of his purpose,
he should carefully and according to the prescribed rules undertake the gathering of disciples;
otherwise, due to the faults of his disciples, the teacher shall remain in hell.
Thus ends the censure of making [unfit] disciples.

The duties and non-duties of the disciple are stated in the first chapter of the Uttarakhanda of the Rudrayamala as follows: "One should not transgress the command of the guru, nor should one speak back to him."
Day and night, one should carry out the command of the guru like a servant.
Thus concludes the procedure for obeying the command of the Guru.
One should not fail to listen to the words of the guru, nor should one listen while turning away;
whether they be harmful or beneficial, by doing so one shall go to the Raurava hell. O Goddess, he who disregards the command of the guru is a person of deluded intellect.
He goes to a terrible hell and shall attain the state of a pig.
Likewise, in the twenty-first chapter:
For men who transgress the command of their guru, dharma is in vain, conduct is in vain, initiation is in vain, austerity is in vain, and even the reputation for virtuous deeds is in vain.
Thus ends the fault of transgressing the guru’s command.
In the second chapter:
"Violating the command, as well as reviling [the teacher] and speaking unpleasant words of the guru..."
"One who commits treachery against the Guru—one should not associate with him.
In the phrase "one should cause [to do]," the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in its own sense (i.e., reflexively); thus, the meaning is "one should not do so.
This is stated in the eleventh chapter of the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava*.
O beloved! He who covets the property of his guru and is eager to have sexual intercourse with the guru’s wife attains the state of an animal and is devoured by carnivorous beasts.
In the Rudrajāmala:
If one should covet the property of the guru or have sexual intercourse with the guru’s wife,
that constitutes a mortal sin (pātaka), and one should not perform an expiation for it.
By the statement "one should not cause [him] to perform penance," it is implied that this is absolutely prohibited.
For example,
the purport of the statement of Manu— "No expiation is prescribed for the intentional killing of a Brahmin"— has been explained.
In the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa:
That which was stated by Manu regarding the killing of a Brahmin out of desire was spoken solely for the purpose of avoiding the intentional murder of a Brahmin.
In the Jāmalam.
Having treated his guru with malice like an enemy and having departed from him due to slander,
he shall become a brahmarākṣasa in a desolate forest region.
Thus ends the fault of acting against the will of the guru,
as stated in the *Gurugītā*.
For all the gods are powerless, and likewise the sages;
having met death through the preceptor’s curse, they are diminished and go to their destruction—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the section on the fault arising from the preceptor’s curse.
In the fourteenth chapter of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the Rudrajāmala.
If one hears slander or backbiting concerning the Guru on any day,
Sundarī does not accept the worship performed by that person on that day.
Thus ends the fault of hearing disparagement of the guru.
In the Kulārṇava, in the twelfth chapter (ullāsa).

Wherever there may be slander of the venerable Guru, one should place both ears [fingers] over them and immediately depart from that place to a distance so that [the words] are no longer heard. Afterwards, one should remember the name of the Guru; otherwise, there will be a loss of merit in hearing [the teachings].
Thus ends the remedy for hearing disparagement of the guru.
In the Jāmalam.
O Goddess, a man who reviles his guru, having lost his fortune and lost his life,
certainly falls into hell for a hundred billion kalpas.
Likewise: "O Great Goddess! Having heard this, he who reviles his guru goes to a terrible hell for as long as the moon and sun endure."
Thus ends the section on the fault incurred by disparaging the guru.
In the Guru Tantra:
If disciples conceive of their guru as a mere human being,
they shall not attain accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Thus concludes the description of the defects arising from human knowledge regarding the Guru.
In the Kulārṇava:
Disobedience of commands, misappropriation of wealth, and speaking unpleasant words to the guru—these they call "betrayal of the guru" (gurudroha); he who commits such acts is a sinner.
From the guru's anger comes destruction, but from the betrayal of the guru comes sin.
One who reviles his guru incurs death; from what is harmful to the guru come great calamities.
A man might live even after entering fire, or even after drinking poison, or even while held in the grasp of death, but he must never commit an offense against his guru.
Thus ends the section on faults such as offenses against the guru.
In the Rudrajāmala, in the Pūrvakhaṇḍa.
Having abandoned the lineage of one's own guru, one should not take refuge with another guru;
one must never engage in slandering the guru, nor ever listen to such slander.
Thus ends the prohibition against abandoning the lineage of the Guru.
And the manner of honoring the guru and others is found in the tenth chapter of the *Puraścaraṇasollāsa*.
One should always meditate upon the Guru as being eternally identical with Śiva. O lady of beautiful limbs! One should always regard the son of the Guru as equal to Gaṇeśa.
O beloved of excellent hips! The wife of the Guru is like Vāṇī and Lakṣmī.
O Maheśānī! [One should worship] the lineage of the Guru, just as one worships the host of Bhairavas.
In the Kulāgama as cited in the Kalpasūtra-ṭīkā and in the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī.
O lady of beautiful limbs! One should always worship the guru with perfumes and garlands;
likewise, O Goddess, one should worship the guru’s wife according to this same procedure.
The term *gurupatnī* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the wife of a guru;

it does not, however, refer to the husband [of the guru] because of the rule of Pāṇini stating that [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied] "not when there is a connection with a sacrifice. According to the meaning of that sūtra, the substitution of *na* for the final syllable of the word *pati* occurs when a connection with a sacrifice is understood. This indicates one who has been consecrated by the marriage sacrament (*vivāhasaṃskṛta*).

By the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) here, the sacrifice that is an ancillary part of marriage (*vivāhāṅgayajña*) is meant. If it were otherwise, the injunction for the fivefold worship of the Guru’s wife as stated in the *Kulārṇava* would be inconsistent; and so it is said in the first chapter of the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava Tantra*:
One who has been married, one who has been supported, one who has been purchased, one who has been brought for a price,
and one who has once yielded to desire— these are the five kinds of the preceptor’s wives.
The preceptor’s wives are not to be transgressed, are to be honored, and are not to be approached.
In the third chapter of the Vṛhannīlatantra.
Furthermore, a young wife of the guru should not have her feet massaged by one who is twenty years old and capable of discerning virtues and faults;
for this very reason, O Maheśānī, one should not perform the service of massaging her feet.
In the Kulāgama.
O Dear One! One should worship the sons of the guru and their children and so forth every day with devotion, according to this procedure, as one would the guru himself.
The sequence of worship, however, is in that very same [text].
O lovely-limbed one! In the absence of the guru, one should worship the guru’s wife;
"in the absence" means when [the guru] is not available.
And in his absence, O lovely-limbed one! one should worship the preceptor’s son;
in his absence, O beautiful woman! one should worship the preceptor’s daughter;
and in his absence, O lovely-limbed one! one should worship the preceptor’s daughter-in-law.

O lady of beautiful limbs! In their absence, one should worship a member of the Guru’s lineage. O fair lady! In his absence as well, one should worship the maternal grandfather, or else the maternal uncle or his wife, according to this rite.
Thus ends the description of the sequence for the worship of the Guru’s family.
Likewise:
"O lady of beautiful limbs! At the time of worship, you should come to the disciple's abode."
Whether it be the guru, the guru’s wife, or even the son, or even an elder who has arrived during the midst of worship, the disciple should abandon all other worship and worship that person alone;
such is the definitive conclusion of the scripture.
Thus, when the time for worship has arrived and the Guru and others have come, this is the duty to be performed by the disciple; it is explained in that very same place.
O Goddess! O lady of excellent complexion! That day for the disciple is equal to ten million solar eclipses;
indeed, that day is like the time of a lunar eclipse.
Merely by the sight of the Guru, one is liberated from all sins.
Therefore, O lady of tremulous glances, a wise person should give charity at that very moment!
Thus concludes the praise of the day of seeing the Guru.
When the guru has attained pleasure, the deity shall attain pleasure;
and when the deity has attained pleasure, the accomplishment of the mantra will certainly occur.
Thus ends the fruit of pleasing the Guru.
In the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
O Goddess, Bhairava himself takes away the splendors of the mantra of that person who performs the worship of the chosen deity without first performing the worship of the Guru.
In the Rudrajāmala:
O Lord! Without the worship of the Guru, ten million merits are in vain.
Therefore, through the Guru, one shall attain accomplishment, as is renowned among all people.
As cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
Since all ritual acts not instructed by the guru will certainly be fruitless,
therefore the procedures for recitation, fire-offerings, and worship must be performed by those who have received initiation.
Likewise:
"Having bowed to the lotus-feet of the Guru and meditated upon the Guru’s sandals,
he who, having realized the supreme reality, recites the Kulacaṇḍikā mantra..."
O Mahādevī! He becomes one who has accomplished his purpose, he is blessed, he knows his own lineage, he is a wise man, and he understands the true nature of reality; of this there is no doubt.
In the Gurugītā.

I pay homage to the mantra of the Guru, the deity, which is the sole spell for being rescued from the ocean of *saṃsāra*, the perfected mantra served by Brahmā and the other gods and sages, the mantra that destroys poverty, suffering, fear, and grief, and the remover of great terrors.
In the Guru-tantra:

O Goddess! if, by virtue of their past births, service to the guru, meditation on the guru, hymns to the guru, recitation for the guru, worship of the guru, gratification of the guru, and devotion to the guru should ever arise in men;
For them, the mantra shall become perfected, and those men are liberated while living.
Whatever merit a disciple residing in the house of the guru may perform, that merit is declared to be inexhaustible; at a sacred pilgrimage site (puṇyatīrtha), it is said to be a hundredfold greater.
Thus [ends] the fruit of meritorious deeds accomplished in the teacher’s house.
In that very same [text].
The wise person who bears the dust from the feet of the guru upon his head shall obtain ten times the fruit yielded by visiting ten million sacred pilgrimage sites.
He who daily drinks the water from the guru’s feet with devotion [attains the same].
He certainly obtains the fruit of three and a half crores of sacred fords.
In the *Guptasādhanatantra*.
The wise person who drinks the water from the feet of the Guru at the three junctions of the day (trisandhya) shall not be born again in this cycle of existence on the path of delusion.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and all the ancestral deities [are present therein].
While the auspicious water, honored as the lotus of the Śrī Guru’s speech, remains present,
that man who daily drinks the water from the feet of the Preceptor becomes the master of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
In the Yoginītantra.
If one should drink with the sentiment of nectar the water dripping from her feet due to pure devotion, he shall go to the city of the Goddess.
In the Guptasādhanatantra.
That man who bears upon his head the water from the feet of the Guru obtains the merit born of all sacred fords; of this there is no doubt.
In the Guru-tantra:
For one who worships the Teacher of the World with perfumes and flowers at the three junctions of the day,
what need is there for the performance of mantra-worship and the like, or for ritual placements and recitations?
O Great Goddess, as for one who would consume the food of the Guru—
The sin accumulated over ten million lifetimes perishes for him in that very instant.
He need not perform ritual bathing, washing of the feet, nor even the sipping of water (ācamana). Upon its arrival, it should simply be consumed; one should not deliberate upon the location.
There is no consideration of Brahminhood, nor of noble lineage, nor of caste;
there is no thought there for kinsmen, sons, or relatives, nor for the members of the assembly.
For food situated in one place is indeed made into a circle of sacred fords (tīrtha) by that [act].
O Goddess! One should eat that which bestows liberation; one should not even think of food touched by a Śūdra.
If an intelligent man eats the food of his guru with the understanding that it is nectar, O Queen of the Gods, even Śiva becomes pleased with him, and not otherwise.
O Goddess! The remains of the Guru’s meal bestow both devotion and liberation;
it must certainly be consumed day after day by the Vaiṣṇava disciples.
In the first chapter of the Yoginī [Tantra].
O Goddess of the gods! One must eat the remnants of the Guru and likewise the remnants of his son;
of this there is no doubt, for if there is a change of heart, there is a downward fall.
O Great Goddess! Your remnants are very difficult even for Brahmā and the other gods to obtain.
Likewise, that which is the remains of the Guru (gurūcchiṣṭa) is declared to be supremely pure, the highest of the high.
Now, if it be argued that on this account the remains of the Guru’s wife should not be consumed, we say no;
for by the statement, "O Maheśānī! the Guru’s wife is the Guru himself, there is no doubt," she possesses the status of the Guru.

Because the rule for consuming the remnants of that [deity] is established by the rule for consuming the remnants of the Guru; O Dear One! he who eats even a mere handful of food offered by the Guru, the Guru’s wife, or the Guru’s son, [attains the fruit] for twenty days.
He shall become long-lived, free from old age and disease, and auspicious.
In the *Gurutantro*:
If one should smear all one's limbs with the remnants of the Guru’s food,
even a thunderbolt shall never pierce his body.
He who, out of devotion, should eat the food that is the Guru’s remnant—
"Annapūrṇā, the sustainer of the world, bestows sovereignty upon him.
Thus is the fruit of eating the remnants of the Guru, as stated in that very same [text].

O Supreme Goddess! If at any time there should be confusion regarding this, no expiation for it is seen even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. O Beloved! He who, out of delusion, does not eat the remains of the Guru’s meal—
For you would become angry with him, and indeed, calamity would befall you at every step.
Thus concludes the description of the faults arising from not consuming the remains of the Guru's food.
In that very same place.
Upon seeing the sandals, clothing, umbrella, bed, ornaments, or other belongings of the guru, one should offer salutation and must not make use of them for one's own enjoyment.
In the Kulārṇava, in the fifth section, in the twelfth chapter.
Upon seeing the sandals, seat, umbrella, vehicle, garments, or fly-whisks belonging to the guru, one should offer salutation; one must not employ them for one's own enjoyment.
[Likewise, one should not perform] the washing of feet, bathing, oil massage, or brushing the teeth [on behalf of oneself].
Passing urine or spitting, shaving, lying down, indulging in women,
the *vīrāsana* posture, harsh speech, sitting [inappropriately], laughing or weeping, loosening the hair, wearing a turban, wearing a bodice, and likewise clinging [to others].

O Beloved! O Ambika! Stretching out the feet, debate, quarrel, finding fault, stretching the limbs, playing with the body as an instrument, clapping the hands, shaking [the limbs], and wrestling matches such as those involving dice, cocks, and boxers—these and the like [should be avoided].

One should not practice [the rites] at the abodes of the Gurus, Siddhas, Mahāsiddhas, Pīṭhas, Kṣetras, and Āśrayas; if one should practice there out of delusion, one will incur the curse of the deity. One should remain standing in the presence of the Guru without [offering] ritual service (upacāra), and one should not enter [his presence] against his will.
Thus ends the prohibition against washing the feet and so forth in the presence of the Guru or at a great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha) and similar locations.
In the first chapter of the first section of the Yoginītantra.

Even if one should drink unrefined liquor by virtue of a teacher’s command, there is no penance required for that; indeed, this is established even in the Veda. Furthermore, even if something contrary to the Tantras is spoken by the teacher, [it must be followed].
"That which is approved by him shall be as authoritative as the Vedas and the words of Mahārudra.
Thus, there is no fault in performing what is prohibited [by others] when it is done by the command of the Guru.
"Whatever has emerged from the mouth of the Guru is called the entire scripture."
O beloved! One who is himself capable of performing the Guru’s work should not urge another;
even if accompanied by kinsmen, servants, and citizens, he should remain exceedingly devoted. (From the Rudrajāmala)
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, reciting prayers, offering oblations, or performing worship,
one should carry out only the command of the Guru with an inner self absorbed in him.
One should not harbor pride on account of caste, learning, wealth, or the like.
A disciple should always and constantly serve in the presence of the venerable guru.
Thus ends the prohibition against pride in the presence of the Guru.
In that very same [text].
And for that man upon whose tongue-tip the mantra of the sandals always resides,
he shall effortlessly obtain virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
The hero who constantly meditates upon the lotus feet of the glorious Guru for the sake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation—there is no devotee superior to him.
O Lord! [He knows] the limbs of the Vidyā, the seat, the mantra, the mudrā, the tantra, and so forth.
Everything obtained from the mouth of the Guru becomes fruitful; it cannot be otherwise.
The connection [of the words] occurs through a division of the sentence.

One should avoid sitting on the same seat as the Guru, whether it be a woolen blanket, a lotus, a palatial throne, a long wooden plank, or even the back [of a seat]. One should [also refrain from using] the mantra of the Śrī-guru’s sandals, the root-mantra, or one's own sandals [without permission].
O Lord of Gods! one should never speak [this] to just anyone who is not a disciple.
Whatever object is beneficial to oneself, one should certainly not withhold that substance.
O observer of excellent vows! I am pleased with him who has obtained even a single syllable from his guru.
"O Lord! Whatever is performed with devotion according to one's means for the sake of the Guru, the fruit belongs to both of them equally—whether rich or poor;
whether the merit be small or great. Thus it is stated in the Kulārṇava, in the fifth section, the twelfth chapter, in its third quarter-verse.
The recitation.
Even one who might give away his entire possession, if he is devoid of devotion to the Guru, attains hell; for devotion alone is the cause. Thus it is said in the Kulārṇava:
"The disciple does not obtain the fruit"—this is the reading in the third quarter [of the verse].
"Through devotion to the guru one may attain the state of Śakra, but through devotion to me one may even become a pig."
The intended meaning is that it is the devotion directed toward me alone, without [the need for] a guru. In truth, there is nothing superior to devotion to the guru among all the scriptures.
Thus ends the fruit of devotion to the guru.
"Fie on their wealth! Fie on their strength! Fie on their lineage! Fie on their conduct!
O Maheśvarī, devotion to the Guru and the Deity does not arise in them!"—such is the defect regarding the non-arising of devotion.
In the Jāmalam.
One should never disclose the faults of the guru’s wife, sons, or kinsmen;
one should not consume their property, nor should one ever reject what has been given by them.
(From the *Gurugītā*)
Once the path has been shown by the Guru, one should effect purification of the mind. One must not transgress anything spoken by the Guru, whether it be good or bad.
And one should never speak untruth in the presence of the Guru.
In the Picchilā Tantra:
He who, deluded regarding dharma, abandons his father’s house or the teacher’s family,
goes to a terrible hell for as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
In the Kulārṇava, in the fifth section, in the eleventh chapter.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, whatever lineage of gurus one may have—
"He who has reached the firm conviction that 'for me, as a disciple of all, the Kaula is to be worshipped upon the surface of the earth,' he shall be dear to us both."

O Goddess! Having bowed with devotion to the Śrī-guru, the Kula scriptures, and whatever places of worship there may be, one should proclaim them preceded by the word "Śrī. O Beloved! One should not mention the Guru by name, except at the time of recitation (japa).
In a dispute or in the course of a spiritual practice (*sādhana*), one should say, "The venerable Lord Śrīnātha.
Now follows the service to the Guru;
likewise, in the twelfth chapter (*ullāsa*).
Service is fourfold, consisting of one’s own self, wealth, presence, and being.
O Goddess, with such service and with a focused mind, the disciple should satisfy the guru;
at every step he undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
O beloved! Service to the Guru alone brings about Your grace;
if that service is accompanied by devotion to Me, it bestows the fruits of all desires.
All sins are destroyed, and heaps of merit increase.
O beloved, all undertakings are accomplished through service to the guru.
Whatever object is beneficial to oneself, that very thing should be offered as wealth without deception.
The merit of one who worships the guru and the deity cannot be measured.

One should not show contempt toward the teacher’s friends, companions, servants, or slaves; nor should one criticize his commitments (samayas) regarding the Vedas, scriptures, Āgamas, and so forth. Likewise:
Desiring to enter the abode of the Teacher, with a tranquil mind and great devotion,
one should discard one's vehicle, sandals, umbrella, fly-whisk, fan, and so forth, as well as betel and ornaments, and enter very slowly.
The proficiency regarding the Guide (deśika), however, is [discussed] in the seventeenth chapter (ullāsa).
O Dear One! Because he assumes the form of a deity, because he acts for the sake of favoring his disciples, and because his very body consists of compassion, he is called the Teacher.
The "abode of the guide" means the residence of the guru. Likewise:
"One should not approach a king, a deity, or a guru with empty hands."
One should offer fruits, flowers, garments, and so forth, according to one's ability.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Two Branches in the Form of the Section on Guru and Disciple," in the second section (Dharmakāṇḍa) of the illustrious *Prāṇatoṣiṇī*,
as recorded in the *Brahmajāmalatantra* within the *Darapatijayacaryā-svarodaya*.
One should draw a serpent-shaped wheel beginning with Aśvinī, consisting of three channels (nāḍīs).
Therein, the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of marriage and other rites is to be known by means of piercing (vedha).
The nakṣatras for the piercing of the three channels are Aśvinī, Ārdrā, and the pair of Uttaras.
The Hastendra (Jyeṣṭhā), Mūla, Vāruṇī (Śatabhiṣaj), and likewise Pūrvābhādrapadā;
Yāmya (Bharaṇī), Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Guru (Puṣya), Yoni (Āśleṣā), Citrā, Mitra (Anurādhā), and the one called Jala (Pūrvāṣāḍhā);
and Dhaniṣṭhā—these are situated in the middle nāḍīs of Uttarābhādra.
Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Svātī,
Viśākhā, Uttarā, Śravaṇā, and Puṣya are established as the nāḍīs of the breast.
In the nakṣatras that pierce the nāḍīs beginning with Aśvinī, the sixth and second [nāḍīs] follow in sequence.
