One should thus observe the piercing (vedha) in the four [asterisms] beginning with Yāmyā (Bharaṇī), and likewise the four in the group beginning with Kṛttikā, as well as the two sets of six; [one should observe it] regarding a maiden, a mantra, a guru, a deity, a virtuous woman, a master, a friend, a country, a village, a city, and a house.

If the asterisms occupied by the bridegroom and the bride reside within the same single nāḍī, then one should recognize that as a piercing (vedha); this applies likewise to Jupiter and the other planets.
For whichever [person] has a manifest birth-asterism, the piercing is reckoned from that birth-asterism.
One should determine [the suitability of] a woman based on the birth-star of him whose birth-star is auspicious;
however, if there is a piercing (vedha) between the two birth-stars, it should never be done.
If they should reside in the same nāḍī, the woman leads to the destruction of her husband.

Where the Guru, the mantra, and the deity reside within the same channel (nāḍī), one should predict the results in sequence as hatred, illness, and death. [Conversely, if they are in different channels:
the master, a virtuous woman, a friend, the country, the village, the city, and the house.
That which has entered a single channel should be abandoned; that which is auspicious is free from piercing.
From such statements as these, it follows that an examination of the channels (nāḍī) and lunar mansions (nakṣatra) for the teacher, the disciple, and the mantra must necessarily be performed.
When initiation (*dīkṣā*) is to be performed, the necessity of investigating the *cakras* and so forth must be acknowledged.
However, since our most venerable elder Kṣṇānandāgamavāgīśa has written everything regarding this in his own work, the *Tantrasāra*,
there is no need for it here.

As for the statement by those who merely display such words as "there is no need here for [the presence of] Siddhas and so forth," which they claim is intended as praise for the necessity of inquiry everywhere— that is a mockery of the author of the *Tantrasāra*, being a fabrication from his own imagination.
They have neither seen nor heard what is stated in the fourth chapter of the *Rudrayāmalottarakhaṇḍa*, as follows:
One should not examine the *siddha* status and so forth of mantras such as those of Kālī and Tārā;
nevertheless, one should indeed purify the mantra, for that [instruction] is solely for the purpose of praise.
It will be explained later that the statement asserting the absence of such investigation is intended for ascetics (*yati*) and others, and not for householders (*gṛhastha*).
The counter-exception regarding the movement of the *cakra* is stated in the second chapter of the *Annadākālpa*, as follows:
Having spoken of the hells within the wheels, beginning with the wheel of Hara.
The mantra whose essence is purified by the nine wheels is prescribed for one's desired goal,
provided that the ancestral lineage has been worshipped by the ancestors in succession; in that case,
a wise person should not entertain any doubt regarding its acceptance.
If, by the power of fortune, she should take recourse to that mantra,
then her deliberation is through the deliberation of her husband and not of her own accord;
for [the mantras] born in the Kula-cakra were received from the mouths of the heroic Māheśvarīs.
O Bhairava! There is no need for deliberation regarding that which is given out of compassion;
rather, that toward which one has the greatest faith through the functions of one's own internal organ should be diligently worshipped—for in such a case, deliberation is fruitless.

Since the construction of a pavilion is mandatory for the rite of initiation (dīkṣā), and since it is observed that the construction of a pavilion and so forth is prohibited without first examining the ground, the examination of the ground is described at the outset.
That, however, is found in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra preserved at Rāghava-ghaṭṭa.
In that regard, one who is expert in the true principles of site-selection should examine the ground:
ground that is cracked, contains hidden debris, or is overrun by anthills should be avoided from afar, for it takes away the life and wealth of the builder.
If it is cracked, it is not obtained with the letter *ca*;
a cracked [line] causes death, while one that is saline (*ūṣarā*) destroys wealth.
One with a thorn (*saśalyā*) constantly gives distress, and one that is uneven brings fear from enemies.
Thus concludes the explanation of the stages to be avoided.
In that very same [text].

The earth sloping toward the northeast (Īśāna) certainly bestows prosperity upon the builder; according to the sages, that sloping toward the east brings increase, while that sloping toward the north bestows wealth. However, ground sloping toward the southeast (Agni) causes enmity, death, and disease.
The ground sloping toward the northeast (dharmarāja) always brings fear of death;
that ground which slopes toward the southwest (naiṛta) causes the destruction of the household;
and the earth sloping toward the west (varuṇa) is said to cause the loss of wealth.
Likewise, ground that is prone to subsidence from wind is always a cause for anxiety;
thus concludes the section on the auspicious and inauspicious nature of ground prone to shifting in various directions.
In that very same [text]: "White ground is known as Brāhmaṇī; red is indeed remembered as Kṣatriyā;
Vaiśyā should be understood as yellow; and Śūdrā is proclaimed to be black."
The Brāhmaṇī soil has the scent of ghee, the Kṣatriyā has the scent of blood,
the Vaiśyā has the scent of milk, and the Śūdrā earth has the scent of excrement.
The Brāhmaṇī ground is known to be sweet, while the Kṣatriyā is astringent.
The Vaiśya earth should be known as bitter, and the Śūdra earth should be pungent. (p.

194) The Brāhmaṇa earth is covered with *kuśa* grass; the Kṣatriya earth is covered with *śara* grass. The Vaiśya earth is covered with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grasses, and the Śūdra earth is covered with all kinds of grasses.
Thus ends the description of the means for knowing the qualities of the earth, such as its Brāhmaṇa-nature and so forth, in that very [text]:
"White, yellow, red, and likewise endowed with black color;
firm-watered, solid, and smooth—the earth brings all happiness."
When it is cold to the touch during the hot season, when it is hot to the touch at the onset of winter,
and when it possesses both touches during the rainy season— that [wind] is proclaimed to be auspicious.
This is also stated in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*.
O best of beings! There, cows with their calves take delight with their bulls;
there, beautiful women take delight with their men.
It is fragrant with the scent of saffron and sandalwood, and perfumed with camphor and agallochum.
She possesses the fragrance of the lotus and water-lily, the scent of jasmine and campaka;
she has the aroma of trumpet-flower and jasmine, and the scent of nagakesara.
She is rich with the fragrance of curd, milk, and clarified butter, and carries the scent of wine and spirits.
Rich with the fragrance of fragrant rice and endowed with auspicious scents,
that ground is considered common to all castes.
Thus ends the description of the auspicious ground.
From the *Dhṛtahayaśīrṣapañcarātra*, specifically the *Madagrajarāmalocanavidyābhūṣaṇakṛtavāstuyāgapradīpikā*.
Having understood this, one should examine the ground— auspicious, sloping toward the east or north,
free from obstacles, well-covered, and saturated with water. After filling the trench dug in the path with excellent soil that exceeds the amount excavated, one should proceed.
In that [place], a heap of flowers does not wither,
nor does the lamp go out, nor does the flower quickly fade;
white, reddish, yellow, and black [garlands] are especially distinguished for the Brahmins and the other [castes].
The meaning is that it is praised.
Ground that has a salty odor or a putrid smell should be abandoned;
as should ground that is sweet, astringent, sour, or pungent,
and ground that is overgrown with *kuśa*, *śara*, *kāśa*, or *dūrvā* grasses.
Accumulated and extremely crowded.
The explanation of the phrase "likewise, with excessive clay," and so forth, has been stated in the *Prayogasāra*.
Having fashioned a cavity in the ground measuring one *vitasti* in width,
he should deposit that earth into it; among the remaining [earth], it is auspicious if they are equal,
middling if they are even, and it is said to be inferior if they are deficient.
Having thus examined with effort and abandoned a smaller plot of ground,
and having then cleared the surface of the earth of charcoal, husks, hair, and bones—
where "charcoal" and so forth serve as an illustration for all prohibited substances— one should proceed.
By the phrase "having made it inferior," the sequence for extracting the thorn is indicated.
(p. 195) There is also a fault in failing to do so;
therefore, she is wicked in making the *kuṇḍa*.
When the rope is not found while digging the pit in the ground, then there is untimely death; with bones, hair, or charcoal, there is loss of wealth;
with ashes, danger from fire is proclaimed; and with husks, poverty is declared.
Thus he demonstrated the evil result.
That alone is also the auspicious result:
"The cow-horn, the yellow frog, the conch, the pearl-oyster,
the tortoise, the śambūka, and whatever other species of gems there may be— these are to be praised."
Now, [the rites for] extracting the arrow-head and extracting wealth.
In the *Brahmajāmala*, as maintained in the *Svarodaya*.
I shall explain the snake-wheel (*ahicakra*) as it was spoken by the Omniscient One,
by which practitioners come to know substances, thorns, and likewise emptiness;
where on the surface of the earth a treasure is situated, whether stationary or wandering.
Therefore, having established this wheel, one should attend to the gateway of the station.
One should draw eight vertical lines and likewise five horizontal lines;
thus the snake-wheel (ahicakra) consists of twenty-eight squares.
Therein, the asterisms of Revatī, Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Maghā, and Pūrvaphalgunī [are assigned].
Uttarāphālgunī is for writing; there are seven asterisms in the first row.
One should mark Ahibradhna, Ajapa, Dakṣa, Pataṅga, Brahmasarpabha, Puṣya, and Hasta, situated in the second row; as well as Abhijit,
Viṣṇu, Vasu, Saumya, Raudra, and Punarvasu.

One should observe the diagram by placing Citrā, the third lunar mansion, in the seventh position of the third row; then Viśvarkṣa (Śatabhiṣaj), the water asterism (Pūrvāṣāḍhā), Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Maitra (Anurādhā), and the Viśākhā asterism, followed by Svātī, in the fourth row. Thus one should examine the wheel.
Thus the wheel is produced, having the form of a serpent in its configuration.
At the gateway, Maghā and Bharaṇī are situated; Kṛttikā is considered to be at the doorpost.
The triad beginning with Aśvinī, the triad beginning with Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and the tetrad [beginning with Śravaṇa] are likewise placed.
The asterisms of Pauṣṇa (Revatī) and Prauṣṭhapada (Pūrvabhādrapadā and Uttarabhādrapadā) belong to the Moon; the remaining ones belong to the Sun.
Thus for the Moon.
Thus for the Sun.
The nadīs elapsed since sunrise, when divided by sixty, yield a remainder;

this remainder, added to the moon's motion for the day, becomes the moon at that specific time. One should calculate the sun, situated in its asterism, at the desired time in the same manner as the moon.
One should subsequently examine those two [planets] as situated in their respective asterisms or elsewhere:
if the Moon and the lord of the *dāya* (the planet governing the period) are in the Moon's asterism, then a treasure is certainly located there;
however, if those two are situated in the Sun's asterism, one should indicate a thorn (a hidden danger) at that spot.
The two [types of] treasure are to be known as residing in their respective signs; nothing exists otherwise.
A substance situated in a sign joined by a malefic planet cannot be obtained.
When the Moon is waxing, the treasure will be abundant; when the Moon is waning, the treasure will be meager.
That [metal] should also be understood by the wise as being of nine kinds according to the aspect of the planets:
gold, copper, silver, pearl, gem, bell-metal, iron, tin, and lead;
one should know these correspond to the Moon when aspected by the planets beginning with the Sun.
If the mixed substance is found in a mixed [sign], it is empty when devoid of malefic influence;
however, when the Moon is aspected by all the planets, that spot should be known as a great treasure.
[The treasures consist of] gold, silver, copper, iron, stone, earthenware, and iron.
If the Moon is in the house of the Sun or other planets, the acquisition of goods and vessels occurs;
if the Moon is situated in an auspicious sign, there is no doubt that there will be gain of wealth.
If it is in a malefic sign, there will be no gain; this should be understood by the wise among astrologers.
The extent of the land is determined by the number of degrees traversed by the sign, measured in *kārma* cubits.
If [the planet] is in its sign of debilitation (*nīca*), there is an obstacle; if it is in another sign of debilitation, that treasure will be situated in water.
If it is in its exaltation (*ucca*), the wealth is located above ground, according to the sequence of the nine divisions (*navāṃśaka*).
When the other [planet] is in its highest exaltation (paramocca) or its own sign of exaltation (tuṅga), and there is a transit of the asterism upon the wall [of the zodiac],
the number of substances is determined by the measure of the portion of the Moon's rays that has been traversed.
If, from that, an increase occurs through the sequence of strength among the six dignities (ṣaḍvarga), [the result is favorable].
Whatever substance is presided over by the Moon accompanied by the planets,
its presiding deity should be known [by the names] of the Sun and the other planets in sequence.
For there are the planets (grahas), the secondary planets (upagrahas), the Kṣetrapālas, and the Mātṛkās.
Dīpeśa, Bhīṣaṇa, Rudra, Yakṣa, and Nāga are considered [the deities] in sequence.
A fire-oblation (homa) for the planets should be performed, and an offering (bali) at the mouth of Nārāyaṇa;
wine and meat for Kṣetrapāla, and a great offering (mahābali) for Mātṛkā.
In the Dīpa [day], worship consisting of lamps is performed; in the Bhīṣaṇa [day], terrifying worship;
in the Rudra [day], the Rudra-japa is to be recited; in the Yakṣa [day], the pacification of Yakṣas and others;
and in the Nāga [day], the hosts of Nāgas together with Gaṇanātha are to be worshipped.
One should worship Lakṣmī and the principles (tattvas) beginning with Earth in all undertakings.
When this is performed according to the prescribed rite, even a treasure difficult to attain is secured. By obtaining such a treasure, a man is always honored by the wise in this world.
This is its meaning:
The grammatical connection is as follows: "I shall speak of the *ahicakra*," meaning I shall explain it thoroughly—that which was spoken by the Omniscient One and spoken by the illustrious Sadāśiva.
By means of this wheel (*cakra*), the wise [determine] that both the substance (*dravya*) and the thorn (*śalya*) are void; that is, the place is devoid of both substance and thorn.
They know [it] because of the use of the present tense to indicate proximity to the future; the intended meaning is that "they will know."

Regarding "treasure" (*nidhi*): it refers to a place where a treasure is located at a single point of convergence, situated on ground measuring two hundred *hasta*s in length—or rather, two hundred and ten *hasta*s—where one who is confused might wander; it is there that this wheel should be placed.

Regarding the measurement of a *nivartana*, it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi* in the *Līlāvatī*, which is a treatise on arithmetic (*pāṭīgaṇita*), as follows: "A *nivartana* consists of twenty *daśakas* (units of ten), and it is a field bounded by four sides, known as twenty *vaṃśas* (rods) in length."
But the author of the commentary on the *Svarodaya* [states]:
He says that a *nivartana* consists of thirty *daṇḍas*, where a *hasta* is seven *hastas* long.
Both of these views are authoritative. Its length and breadth are fourteen *hastas* and eleven *vārṣikas* (cubits) plus nine *aṅgulas*.
The two measures [of time] are to be determined.
According to the opinion of the author of the *Svarodaya-ṭīkā*, scholars should analyze and apply this starting from the long *prahara* and so forth.
What kind of wheel is it? It is situated at the gates and openings of the locations; thus it arises when the doors of the fields (*kṣetra*) and so on are unknown.

The meaning of the concluding statement, "He made the diagram in the form of a serpent," is as follows: the serpent lies with its head toward the east during the three months beginning with Bhādrapada; therefore, when a question is asked in any given month, one should employ the *Ahibalacakra* by first establishing the position of the *Kṛttikā* nakṣatra in the respective direction. This is the instruction.
"Upwards," it says.
One should draw eight vertical lines and, in sequence, eight horizontal lines;
likewise, one should draw five horizontal lines in sequence.
In this way, there are twenty-eight squares.

In that diagram, within the compartments, the seven lunar mansions—Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Aśvinī, Yāmyarkṣa (Bharaṇī), Kṛttikā, Maghā, Bhāgyabha (Pūrvaphalgunī), and Uttaraphalgunī—are to be written in the first row.
Regarding the phrase "ahibradhna": [it refers to the subsequent arrangement].
The seven constellations— Ahibradhna (Uttarabhādrapadā), Ajapāda (Pūrvabhādrapadā), Śatabhiṣā, Brāhma (Rohiṇī), Sarpabha (Āśleṣā), Puṣyā, and Hastā— are to be drawn situated in the second row.
This is the procedure.
The seven lunar mansions in the third row are: Abhijit, Viṣṇu (Śravaṇā), Saumya (Mṛgaśirā), Raudra (Ārdrā), Punarvasu, Citrā;
and Viśvakṣa (Uttarāṣāḍhā), Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Anurādhā, Viśākhā, and Svātī.
The seven constellations are in the fourth row.
Having done this, one should look at the wheel by means of the implied meaning (*arthāt*).
(p. 198) In this manner, according to the sequential arrangement of the constellations beginning with Kṛttikā, there is the form of a *pannaga*, that is, the form of a serpent.
The two door-frames (dvāraśākhā) are Maghā and Bharaṇī;
the two door-frames are situated on both sides of the door;
Kṛttikā is the serpent’s mouth located at the door.
Regarding the phrase "aśvīśa":

taking Aśvinī, Īśa (Ārdrā), and Pūrvāṣāḍhā as the starting points, there are three, five, and four constellations respectively in sequence; for example, Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and Kṛttikā constitute the first three.
Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣyā, Aśleṣā, and Maghā—these are five.
Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Abhijit, and Śravaṇā—these are four lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
[Furthermore,] Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣyā, Aśleṣā, Maghā, and Pūrvāṣāḍhā.
Uttarāṣāḍhā, Abhijit, Śravaṇā, Revatī, and Pūrvabhādrapadā— these are the lunar mansions belonging to Indra and Candra.
The remaining asterisms are Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśirā, Pūrvaphalgunī, Uttaraphalgunī, Hastā, Citrā, and Svātī.
Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, and those known as Uttarabhādrapadā are to be understood as belonging to Bhāsvat, the Sun.
Regarding "from sunrise, etc.": *udaya* is the time of the commencement of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*); that is the starting point.
And by means of the desired time, as many *daṇḍas* as have been traversed by the moon, those elapsed *nāḍīs* are multiplied.

The [mean] moon should be completed by twenty-seven and divided by sixty. When the quotient obtained and the remainder are both taken, that is the moon at that time. Of what nature is it? It is joined with the daily motion of the moon.

Day by day, it is conjoined with the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) consumed by the moon (indu). Having subtracted twenty-seven from the total exceeding twenty-seven, the remaining number represents the count of lunar mansions consumed starting from Aśvinī. In this same manner, the sun also becomes its current [position] through conjunction with the lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī that it has itself traversed.
In this very manner, it has been explained by Narahari in his commentary on the *Svarodaya*.
Furthermore, the knowledge of the lunar mansion currently being occupied by the sun is stated in the ninth verse of the calculation section of the *Mānasapañjikā*:
"I shall briefly declare the precise moon for that time."
By means of which mere consciousness one perceives the auspicious and the inauspicious;
those two rest within the circle of the celestial sphere in the middle of day and night,
and likewise at the time of inquiry, especially at the time of departure.
The twelve signs of the zodiac correspond respectively to the five *daṇḍas* [of the day] in sequence.
Just as with the ascendant (*lagna*), by discarding the elapsed degrees, the remainder follows the order of direct and reverse sequence.
[The results are: travel, well-being, death, laughter, victory, fever, and pleasure. (p. 199)
Emptiness, diminution, play, sleep, and enjoyment [occur] from Aries;
these are the twelve states of the Moon day by day,
yielding results in accordance with their names in auspicious and inauspicious undertakings.
If twelve moons do not occur at that time according to the sequence of fifteen *daṇḍas* for each single lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*),
then the moon belongs to whichever lunar mansion has its first five *daṇḍas* occupied by the [rising] hour that is to be taken.
That subsequent moon occurs by pervading fifteen *daṇḍas* [of time].
In this manner, twelve moons occur in succession.
According to the view of some, twelve moons occur within a period consisting of sixty *daṇḍas* starting from sunrise.
According to that system, the moon belongs to whichever nakṣatra is current at the five-daṇḍa period following sunrise.
In the subsequent five-daṇḍa periods, the twelve moons for day and night respectively become the current (tātkālika) moons.
"In the journey alone" is the meaning of "situated at the rising point and so forth.
"Obtained by sixty" refers to the remainder obtained by dividing by sixty; [the phrase] "in that remainder obtained by sixty" means in that very remainder obtained by sixty.
By this, it means "when the remainder is divided by sixty and by sixty *daṇḍas*.
In that [remainder], the quotient obtained by dividing by sixty, when added to the [longitude of] the moon's motion for the elapsed days, becomes the moon at that time.
The numerical value which results from adding the elapsed *nāḍīs* since sunrise (or the like) to the remainder of the portion obtained by dividing that [quotient] by sixty—this [value]...
The meaning is that this becomes the *bhogyadaṇḍa* (the arc yet to be traversed) of that Moon.
The suffix *ka* in the word *śeṣaka* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*).
Here, if no remainder (*śeṣa*) is obtained, then the numerical value consisting solely of the *nāḍīs* elapsed since [the previous] sunrise is its *bhogyadaṇḍa*.
This is the intended meaning.
By this, one should understand that the determination of the position of the moon at that time is made from the *khaṇḍana-kṣatra* itself through its [daily] motion.
However, if the reading is *ṣaṣṭyāptaśeṣakaiḥ*, then it refers to the remainder obtained by dividing by sixty—that is, the quotient obtained when divided by sixty.

If the moon at that time is joined with the [daily] motion of the moon, it becomes the moon for that specific moment. By means of the remaining digits— the remainder of the portion obtained by dividing by sixty— added to the number of nāḍīs elapsed since sunrise (or the relevant period),
whatever resulting numerical figure is obtained, that is the *bhogyadaṇḍa* (the duration of the moon's remaining arc) of that moon.
"Like the moon."
Having established the [ascendant] situated in the *ṛkṣa* (asterism) at the time of the query as being located in the desired *daṇḍas* of the moving *nāḍī*,
one should calculate and take the four and a half *daṇḍas* for each day in the sequence of one, two, and three days.
In this manner, according to the order of the asterism, one should take exactly as many *daṇḍas* as have been traversed by the sun at the time of the query.
Having multiplied by the number twenty-seven and divided by sixty, the quotient and the remainder are obtained.

By adding the quotient to the number of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) traversed by the Sun, if the total exceeds twenty-seven, one subtracts twenty-seven; the remainder is the traversed nakṣatra, and its count is reckoned from Aśvinī.
The asterism currently being traversed is the remainder after dividing by sixty.
In that square, the current sun situated in that asterism is to be pierced; subsequently, one should consider the positions of one's own natal asterism and the moon's asterism.

Regarding the completion of sixty *daṇḍas* by the sun in a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the full transit through all the lunar mansions occurs in fourteen days less forty *daṇḍas*. Daily, there are four *daṇḍas* and four *palas* more; thus, due to the remaining portion to be traversed, the *palas* decrease slightly.

Therefore, starting from the time of the commencement of the planet's transit through the asterism until the time of the query, however many *daṇḍas* there may be, for every sixty *daṇḍas* there are four *daṇḍas* and thirty-seven *pala*s according to the measure of sixty; by that proportion, [the correction] for the reduction in the subtle duration is applied when performing the instantaneous calculation (*tātkālikīkaraṇa*) of the solar orb and other planets and asterisms. Two verses of the *Paitāmaha* (Brahmagupta) are written here: [Verse 1] The sun’s daily motion in minutes is one hundred and eighty-one, And its daily decrease in minutes is one hundred and fifty-eight. The daily increase is one hundred and fifty-nine, And the daily decrease is one hundred and fifty-eight. [Verse 2] The daily increase is one hundred and fifty-nine, And the daily decrease is one hundred and fifty-eight. The daily motion in minutes is one hundred and eighty-one, And the daily decrease in minutes is one hundred and fifty-eight. (Note: These verses describe the variations in the sun's daily motion and the resulting corrections for the calculation of the true time.)
The nāḍīs from birth until death, multiplied by sixty and divided by the ghaṭīs from birth until the time of death,
yield the result in daṇḍas and so forth; this is then multiplied by sixty and divided by the solar longitude traversed from Aśvinī onwards.
The sun is reduced to its true value for that specific moment.

Thereafter, following the reduction to the true value for that moment, one should observe whether the sun and the moon are situated in their respective asterisms (*ṛkṣa*) or in another asterism from their own natal asterisms (*svanakṣatra*).

Regarding "Candra": if the Sun and Moon are present at their respective times in the lunar mansion of Candra—that is, in the asterism Aśvinī and so forth as previously described—then a treasure (nidhi) is certainly and definitively present; however, if both the Sun and Moon are situated in the asterism of the Sun (Bharaṇī), then there is a thorn (śalya).
Regarding "svasvabhe": when both the Moon and the Sun are situated in their respective signs and their respective asterisms (nakṣatras), there is a second treasure.
One should declare that the treasure is in the position of the Moon and the thorn (śalya) is in the position of the Sun.

In the opposite case—when the Moon is situated in a lunar mansion belonging to the Sun, or when the Sun is situated in a lunar mansion belonging to the Moon—the meaning is that there is no treasure and no thorn whatsoever. When the Moon at that time is conjoined with malefic planets, wealth is not obtained; by the principle of elimination (pāriśeṣya), it follows that [wealth is obtained] when there is a conjunction with benefic planets.
It is obtained.
"Nourished," it is said.

In the case of *candrapuṣṭa*, from the beginning up until the eleventh day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), the treasure is nourished; therein, it becomes exceedingly abundant. However, when the moon is waning (*kṣīṇacandra*), the treasure is meager.
And the waning moon lasts from the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) until the fifth day of the bright fortnight.
Up until the sixth and tenth [days] of both fortnights, there is no state of intermediate strength;
therefore, the substance must be understood as being of intermediate [strength].
When this arrangement is established, in response to the inquiry "What is that substance?", he says:
Hem! Thus.

The meaning is that one should understand gold and other substances to be present when the moon at that moment is aspected by the Sun and the other planets. In that regard, if aspected by the Sun, there is gold (suvarṇa); if aspected by a large-bodied Moon, silver (tāra); if aspected by Mars, copper (tāmra); if aspected by Mercury, brass (āra); if aspected by Jupiter, gems (ratna); if aspected by Venus, bell-metal (kāṃsya); and if aspected by Saturn, iron (āyasa).
An iron alloy [is produced] when aspected by Rāhu; tin when aspected by Ketu; and "nāga" is the well-known substance called lead.
"Mixed," it is said.
When [the Moon] is aspected by mixed planets of various kinds, one should declare the results to be mixed and of various types.

The essential meaning is that whatever planets aspect it, the substances corresponding to those respective planets come to pass. When the Moon is devoid of aspects, "empty" means there is nothing at all.
When the moon is aspected by all the planets, this great treasure is to be known;
that treasure is to be understood by the wise as being of nine kinds, according to the aspects of the planets beginning with the Sun.
He states the substratum of the substance: "Gold," etc.
The meaning is that when the Moon is situated in a sign such as Aries (the house of the Sun) and so forth, there arises a receptacle for wealth, a vessel, or a container.
For example, gold [is found] in Leo, which is the house of the Sun;
silver [is found] in Cancer, which is the house of the Moon.
Copper is [the metal] in the house of Mars, namely Aries or Scorpio; iron is in the house of Mercury, namely Virgo or Gemini; stone is in the house of Jupiter, namely Sagittarius or Pisces.
In the house of Venus, whether in Taurus or Libra, [the image] should be made of clay;

in the house of Saturn, whether in Capricorn or Aquarius, it should be made of iron or steel. Likewise, the house of Rāhu is Virgo; therein, if devoid of the aspect of Mercury, it should be made of tin.
If Pisces is the ketu-house and is aspected by Jupiter or Mars, it should also be known as "sīsaka."
Regarding "an auspicious field":

The auspicious planets are the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus; when the Moon is in their sign or domain (kṣetra), there is undoubtedly the acquisition of wealth. Likewise, when it is in the sign or domain of a malefic planet, there is no gain.
This means that it should be understood by those who are experts in the science of vowels.

"Having been traversed" (bhukta): by the measure of the signs and degrees traversed by the current moon— that is, by that number of signs and degrees— the measurement of the ground, which is the measurement of the substance held [in the hand], is determined by the hands (karaiḥ) of the artisans with their fists clenched.
The measurement in *hasta*s should be made according to the number of degrees consumed; it should be stated that "the wealth is located within the house.

(p. 202) If the Moon is in its sign of debilitation, namely Scorpio (*nīcarāśi*), that same measure is doubled (*dvighna*). Furthermore, if the Moon is situated in the third degree of Scorpio while in its state of debilitation, that treasure should be declared to be located in water.
One may eat as long as food that has been placed in water is available.
Regarding the term "uccasthe" (situated in exaltation):

when the Moon is situated in the second ninth-part (navāṃśa) of the sign Taurus, as many ninth-parts as have been traversed according to the sequence of ninth-parts [indicate] the upward movement as before; likewise, when the Moon is situated in the third ninth-part of Taurus, it is in its highest exaltation (paramocca).
"There is a substance in a very high place.
When the moon enters the asterism of Ṛkṣa, at the time when the remaining palas of that asterism have elapsed, it becomes situated on the wall.
"O you who possess moonbeams," etc.
The number of substances is determined by the measure of the degrees of the house traversed by the current Moon according to the time elapsed since the Moon's entry into that portion;
furthermore, for each degree traversed, the number ten is applied to the six dignities (ṣaḍvarga) within the house.
In the horā, drekkāṇa, navāṃśa, dvādaśāṃśa, and triṃśāṃśa, there is an increase in strength tenfold according to their sequence.

If [the planet] resides in its own division among the six vargas, then the wealth arising from that degree shall be tenfold. Regarding the question of color: if the Moon shines conjoined with a planet, then the object located there [is indicated].
When combined respectively with the planets beginning with the Sun, the presiding deity of that [planet] should be understood as presiding over the substance:

for instance, when the Moon is conjoined with the Sun, the Upagraha; when conjoined with Mars, the Kṣetrapāla; when conjoined with Mercury, the Mātṛkā; when conjoined with Jupiter, the Dīpeśa; when conjoined with Venus, the Bhīṣaṇa; and when conjoined with Saturn, the Rudra.
When conjoined with Rāhu it is a Yakṣa, and when conjoined with Ketu it is a Nāga, respectively.
Regarding the term *graha*:

when the *graha* is presided over, there is the "seizing by the mouth" (*mukhagraha*) at the very mouth of the golden *graha*; this refers to the offering (*bali*) belonging to Nārāyaṇa, such as the articles for worship and so forth.
When the Kṣetrapāla has been invoked, liquor, wine, and meat should be offered to him.
When the Mātṛkā has been invoked, a great bali-offering is required;
as for the human bali, in its absence, goats and other such animals may also be prepared as the bali-offering, provided they are not prohibited.
When Dīpeśa presides, there is worship centered on lamps, primarily consisting of lamps. When Bhīṣaṇa presides, there is the worship of Bhīṣaṇa, which is worship that produces fear.
When Rudra presides through the offering of red flowers and the like, there is the recitation of Rudra—the chanting of the Rudra-mantra, specifically the Rudrādhyāya which is to be muttered.
When presided over by a Yakṣa, there is the offering of vegetables and the like belonging to the Yakṣas, as well as the worship of the Yakṣas and others.
When presided over by a Nāga, the hosts of Nāgas are to be worshipped. (p.
203) In the *Pratiśāntika* rite, when accompanied by Gaṇanātha, that is, Gaṇeśa, there is the worship of Gaṇeśa.
One should worship twenty-five [deities], beginning with Lakṣmīdhara and Bhūti, in all ritual activities.
"Thus" means:

when this has been performed in the celestial mansion (*vimāna*) according to the rules and in the proper sequence, such as the worship and fire-offerings (*pūjā-homa*), even a treasure difficult to attain is accomplished.
He states the visible purpose for one who describes this: "In this manner, a man—a human being—[attains success] through the acquisition of treasure."
"He becomes worthy of homage, worthy of salutation, or worthy of praise; of this there is no doubt."
Alternatively, the extraction of the "thorn" (śalyoddhāra) should be performed according to the sequence taught in the Mahākapilapañcarātra. That sequence is as follows:
"At the time of commencing the construction of a temple, and especially in the case of a house and so forth..."
If one desires one's own welfare, the extraction of the *śalya* (the core pin) must be performed.
At the time of commencing the construction of a temple, whichever limb of the person touches [the site],
the wise man should firmly insert a *śalya* into that very spot within the body of the *vāstu*.

If a man scratches his head, one should extract a splinter from the head; it should be understood that a splinter exists there at a depth of three handspans when digging. There, a fire-burn, a disease, and loss of wealth will arise.
One who desires their own welfare should extract the splinter with effort;
when there is itching in the arm, one should indicate an iron chain.
Its measurement is two cubits; thus its characteristic has been described to you.
One should know that it portends the death of the master or likewise his departure to a foreign land;
one should diligently extract the thorn if one desires one's own welfare.
Furthermore, when there is itching in the thigh, one should indicate a thorn made of bell-metal.
And it should remain with one hand; this is the characteristic described to you.
If [the mark] is incomplete, the wife will be unfaithful and loss of reputation arises.
One should extract the thorn with effort if one desires one's own welfare.
If the skeleton is indicated while scratching with the hand,
it should be determined to be at a depth of three cubits when being excavated, and not otherwise;
[if otherwise], there will be burning by fire, disease, affliction, and death.
One who desires his own welfare should extract the splinter with effort.
If there is itching on the back, one should indicate a splinter in the arm;
it should remain fixed by means of a single hand—of this there is no doubt.
In that case, there will be the destruction of the husband, or the wife becomes unchaste.
When there is itching on the foot, one should indicate a splinter in the hand;
this characteristic, situated at one and a half cubits [from the navel], has been described to you.
The destruction of women, royal punishment, and loss of crops occur;
one should diligently extract the thorn if one desires success for oneself.
When there is itching in the belly, one should indicate a stone there.
The characteristic signs have been described for you according to the measure of two cubits;
if a snakebite occurs there, one should extract the splinter.
However, if there is itching at the knees, one should indicate that ashes are present there.
It should remain within the span of two cubits; this characteristic has been described to you.
It performs such actions as causing fire-burns, mental anguish, afflictions, suffering, and fears; therefore, one should indeed extract it from there.
In astrology.
Having first carefully dug that site of the temple down to the water-level with effort, one should make it free of debris;
otherwise, there would be no fixed measurement, or rather, O performer of the rite, it depends on the result of the inquiry.
Then, pure and with dūrvā grass, sprouts, unbroken rice, and flowers in hand, he should approach a pure astrologer who knows the divine ordinances.
The master of the house, being humble, should inquire with a sweet voice regarding the truth of the arrow;
then, the first letter of that question must be carefully retained.
From that [letter], the results for the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa are determined in sequence, according to whether they are virtuous or sinful.
By the word "successively" (kramāt), it follows that a Brāhmaṇa should utter the name of a flower, a Kṣatriya the name of a river, a Vaiśya the name of a deity,
and a Śūdra the name of a fruit; [and] the Praṇava [is uttered] on the ground, the word "supporting" (dhāriṇī) on the hands, and immediately after that, [the word] "not" (na).
"Bhūtyai namaḥ" (Salutation to Prosperity)—this mantra ends with "vahnipriyā" (the beloved of fire).
Vahnipriyā is Svāhā. Having consecrated the chalk with this mantra, one should divide it.
One should subsequently draw nine squares for the site of the dwelling with that [line].

If the syllables of the question arise as *va*, *ka*, *ca*, *ta*, *e*, *hā*, *śa*, *pa*, and *ya* within the nine compartments starting from the east, those letters indicate a structural flaw (*śalya*).
In a question, the letter 'va' at the beginning indicates a human bone as a thorn that brings about death. || 1 ||
The letter Ka, when in the fire [element], bestows death caused by the serpent of the king’s rod and produces harsh thorns.
In the southern direction, he saw a house made of monkey bones; the Lord declared it to be a "thorn" that brings about his own destruction. || 3 ||
If they are situated in a house of dog-bones in the direction of the Rakshasas (the south), it certainly indicates great fear. || 4 ||
This [word] "eḥ," belonging to a child whose bones are scattered in the intermediate directions, signifies death, exile, battle, and a dart.
In the northwest (vāyukoṇa), he describes the form of a man: it brings about poverty and causes the destruction of one's beloved. || 6 ||
In the direction of Dhanada (the North), Śakāra spoke, he who causes the destruction of wealth and the loss of the bones of Brahmins.
Then the letter *pa* speaks of the bone of the bear in Śambhu. (8)
Therefore, in this case, it bestows the destruction of the family and the loss of cattle wealth, even for the master of the house who is protected by the gods;
for he who says that there is ash, a skull, or black iron in the middle portion brings about the ruin of the lineage. (9)
Having now diligently set aside other authorities, I shall speak the truth everywhere regarding the *śalya* (the piercing point).

In the directions of Indra, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, and Īśāna, the *śalya* is one and a half cubits from the waist; in the directions of Agni, Yama, Kubera, Puruṣa, and in the middle and the wind directions, it is likewise.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
A structural flaw situated below the human level does not cause harm within the house;
however, a flaw in the upper story causes harm as far as the water's edge.
Thus ends the extraction of the arrow.
One should construct the pavilion and other structures only after ascertaining the directions such as the east; otherwise, a fault is stated in the verse cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"If one should build according to what is [merely] seen [without such ascertainment], being ruined, he shall go to hell."
Having ascertained the directions by the movement of the sun, the preceptor should perform the rites;
however, where the directions cannot be properly known due to irregularities in the site,
he should establish a gnomon there and thereby know the position of the pure cardinal points.
Regarding the measurement of the gnomon, it is stated in the *Jyotistattva*:

"A wooden rod (*kāṣṭhī*) with a needle-pointed tip, twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long and two finger-breadths thick at its base, is known as a 'gnomon' (*śaṅku*); one should calculate its shadow."
As cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
Listen, I shall explain according to the rule how to ascertain the directions by means of that [shadow]:
having drawn a circle on a perfectly level surface by means of rotation,
one should place a twelve-finger-long gnomon at its central point.
Having drawn two circles by means of the sequence of the shadow's tip at the beginning and end of the forenoon and afternoon,
one should then draw two further circles with equal rotation around those marks.
Having placed [the two threads] so that they are situated to the right and left of the center produced by their junction,
one should lay down a thread in the middle between the two junctions, running from east to west.
One should then determine the directions starting from the east using the tips of those threads to the right and left.
Also in the Kriyāsāra:
Having leveled the ground there,
the wise man should place therein a gnomon made of khadira wood— or, if that is unavailable, of sacrificial wood— twelve finger-breadths in height and one cubit in circumference.

Wherever its shadow touches, that point in the middle is known as the center. One should stretch a cord horizontally through the center; these are known as the south and north lines. By stretching four cords, the other four corners are established.
Thus, the thorough understanding of the directions has been clearly explained at all times.
Having understood this, one should properly construct the pavilions and other structures through careful deliberation.
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, however, there is a specific rule:
"When the sun has entered the equinox, one should perform the measurement with a gnomon.
One should set up a gnomon made of *khadira* wood, twelve finger-breadths in width."
Thus concludes the determination of the knowledge of the directions, beginning with the east.
The method for digging out the *śaṅku* (stake) is also described in that very same source:
"Having made [the victim] motionless, one should strike him with an iron mallet;
one should strike eight times, beginning from the most prominent part and proceeding gradually with light blows."
When, while the stake is being struck, the mallet falls from the hand,
then a great and insurmountable grief arises for the striker.
Thus ends the method for digging the Śaṅku.
The method for constructing the pegs and the cord is also [described] in that very same place.
One should wrap a cord around the peg; the cord may be made of muñja grass, silk, cotton, or even animal hair, and its thickness should be four barley-corns.
When the cord being wrapped leaves a mark on the peg, that is the characteristic.
One should know that the death of a son occurs [therein], while in the Chinnā [constellation], there is the destruction of a Vaiśya.
Even there, the destruction of inauspiciousness occurs through the Nārasiṃha oblation.
Likewise.
The gnomon is said to be the essence of the earth; its tip is described as having a variegated circle.
One should place it on level ground at the beginning of the circle and so forth.
With a measurement double that of the gnomon, one should draw a circle in its center.

When the shadow at the forenoon and afternoon enters the center of that circle, the line passing through those two points is considered the east-west direction. A line drawn from the tail of an arrow rotated between the two points passes through the center.
In this manner, one should lay down two threads running from south to north;
then, one should cast forth threads from their tips toward the western end.
The wise person should place the threads facing either eastward or northward.
Also in the Hayashirsha Pancaratra:
Having made the ground level like water and as smooth as the surface of a mirror,
one should draw a circle there with a measurement of twelve finger-breadths.
Then, having fixed an immovable gnomon (śaṅku) in the center, one should observe its shadow.
The line of the circle situated on the outside is assumed to be the shadow of the gnomon (śaṅku).
One should determine the entry and exit points upon that gnomon-shadow.
From the two marks of the tips of the gnomon-shadow, one should establish the east and west directions.
Now, the method for determining the east at night is as follows.
The space between the constellations Kṛttikā, Śravaṇā, Puṣyā, Citrā,
and Svāti is the form of the eastern direction when the sun has risen to the height of a yoke.
Also in the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍala*.
When Śravaṇa rises in the east, and likewise when Kṛttikā rises;
and when the moon and sun are between Citrā and Svātī. Thus ends the section on the gnomon.
Now begins the section on the mandala,
from the second chapter of the Viśvasāra.
For the sake of initiation, one should construct a pavilion that is beautiful and highly enchanting;
it should be painted with various colors and variegated hues, making it most captivating,
and its walls, pillars, and all other parts should be adorned with gold and jewels.
One should decorate the jeweled pavilion, variegated with various colors and diverse hues, according to the prescribed rite with canopies, leaf-patterned ornaments, and the like;
one should also fashion a beautiful banner in the four directions with flags.
The wise one should construct eight jars in the eight directions and arrange the pavilion.
The procedure for this has been stated in the second chapter of the Śāradātilaka.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day, one should construct a beautiful pavilion.

"An auspicious day" is for the sacrificer. "May you declare it an auspicious day," "Likewise, may you [declare] well-being," and "May you [declare] success"— with these three, the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) is performed.
This has been stated by Baudhāyana as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
"Having caused [the officiants] to pronounce each blessing three times, preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*, beginning with 'Auspicious day!', 'Welfare!', and 'Success!'";
because of this instruction to "cause [them] to pronounce the blessing," the mention of the name of the sacrificer follows all the more clearly.
Therefore, to utter merely the words "Auspicious day! and so forth without mentioning the name is contrary to established practice.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
The distance between them should be measured at five, seven, or nine cubits.
It is joined with sixteen pillars, four of which are situated in the middle;
having established those eight cubits in height, twelve [pillars] are placed around them.
They should be five cubits in length, without holes, straight, and auspicious.
The central pillar is eight cubits in measure, while the other twelve are five cubits in measure.
The best of those who know the mantras should bury one-fifth of that in the earth.
One should cover it on all sides with coconut leaves and bamboo.

By the use of the plural number in both instances— such as "with bamboos" (*vaṃśaiḥ*) and "with bamboo slats" (*vaṃśadalaiḥ*)— it follows from the maxim that "words ending in the plural indicate a group," whereby other materials suitable for covering are also obtained.
At the doors, there should be arches (*toraṇa*) made, in order, from trees that yield milky sap.
The height of those pillars is prescribed as seven cubits each;
their circumference is said to be ten finger-breadths [per cubit]. The measurement of the horizontal beam should correspond to the vertical height of the pillars.
One should fashion the central pillars at the gateway measuring one cubit;
one should tie banners to the cardinal directions possessing splendor equal to that of the world-protectors (lokapālas),
and one should adorn the pavilion with canopies, darbha grass, and other ornaments.
"Of milk-exuding trees" refers to the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa*.
This has been stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa as follows:
A gateway made of *nyagrodha* wood is prescribed for the east; an *uḍumbara* gateway is considered appropriate for the south;
one produced from *aśvattha* wood for the west; and a *plakṣa* gateway for the north.
It is held that the Plakṣa tree is located in the east, and the Nyagrodha tree in the north.
Regarding the purpose of constructing the archway (toraṇa), it is stated in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra:
"The gods are united in the form of the archway within the sacrificial pavilion,
for the sake of destroying obstacles and for the protection of the sacrifice."
"Of the *adhvara*, that is, of the sacrifice.
Thus ends the section on the construction of the pavilion and so forth.
Now, the *Aṅkurārṇava-pana* from the fifth chapter of the *Prapañcasāra*.
Whether seven days or nine days prior, and certainly before the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth,

one should prepare a mandala on a pure spot on the ground in another house, extending from the east to the west (the direction of Varuṇa), using four clay bowls with five faces and provided with seeds and water.

At the four corners of the square is the rising of the sun; yellow, reddish, white, and black [are the colors] at each step, beginning with fire (the southeast) and ending with the seven (the northwest). Other practitioners of that mantra also declare it to be extended from south to north.
Now, the Vaiṣṇava *pālikās* should measure twenty-four finger-breadths; the Vairiñca *ghaṭikās* should have five faces and a height of eight finger-breadths;
and the Śaiva *śarāvas* should be twelve finger-breadths wide. These should be washed with water, arranged in rows, and aligned with threads.
And one should place those [syllables] according to the stated sequence.
Furthermore, there are vessels filled with rice grains, each containing a bundle of darbha grass tied with a cord;
these vessels are filled respectively with earth, sand, and dried cow-dung.
Śāli rice, kaṅgu millet, śyāmāka millet, sesame, mustard, mung beans, black gram, and niṣpāva beans,
together with khalva and āḍhakī— these they know as seeds fit for germination.
Having washed them, the excellent practitioner should offer them into the vessels while consecrating them with the root mantra;
this should be done according to the rules, accompanied by the blessings of the Brahmins and the sounds of the five most excellent instruments, such as the conch shell.
Having thoroughly sprinkled [the image] with turmeric water and covered it with cloths, let it be bathed with water accompanied by the five sounds.
At evening and at dawn during the nights, the lord of practitioners should offer that bali-oblation with the aforementioned substances.

To the spirits (bhūta), ancestors (pitṛ), yakṣas, nāgas, Brahmā, Śiva, and the deities ending with Viṣṇu— on those nights, one should offer oblations (bali) to them in sequence, seven times, eight times, or according to their respective strength.

The offering called *bhūtakrūra* consists of parched grain, oil, red turmeric, curd, flour-cakes, and rice; that for the ancestors (*paitrya*) consists of sesame and rice along with cakes and food; and that for the Yakṣas (*yākṣa*) consists of *karambha*, parched grain, and rice.
Coconut water and powdered sesame for Nāga; lotus seeds and rice for Vairiñca; cooked food and cakes for Śiva; and milk-rice for Vaiṣṇava.
If the bali offering is prescribed for nine nights in succession,
the mantra for the bali consists of their respective names, beginning with "Tārā" and ending with "namaḥ.
Furthermore, the arrangement of the bali offerings is made in the eight directions around the three types of vessels.

This well-known rite of sowing the seed (vījāropaṇa) is "all-fulfilling" (sārvakāmika). Because of the use of the term "all-fulfilling" and because of statements such as "in the initiation [to be] described hereafter," its necessity is established.
The meaning of these points will become clear through the authorities cited from the Viśvasāra and the Śāradā; therefore, [they are not elaborated] here.
No commentary has been made [on this].
And in the third chapter of the *Viśvasāra-tantra*:
"One should prepare seed-vessels (*pālikā*) in the four directions where sprouts have grown."
The *pālikās*, the principal vessel, and the shallow bowls (*śarāvas*) follow in sequence;
these are respectively sixteen, twelve, and eight finger-breadths in size.
It is declared that they should be filled with fragrant water and contain sprouted seeds.

The preceptor, who has mastered the meaning of all scriptures, should, according to the prescribed rite, scatter seeds there on all sides using the *sudhā* seed-mantra. *Śyāmāka*, black gram (*māṣa*), *kaṅgu*, and rice (*vrīhi*) are prescribed for all sides.
On the seventh day prior to the initiation, being always self-restrained,
one should perform worship of all the deities during the seven nights; O Supreme Goddess, one should worship with various offerings and oblations.
The wise preceptor should worship all [the elements] from beginning to end with the *praṇava* at the start and *namaḥ* at the conclusion;
he should worship the spirits (*bhūta*), ancestors (*pitṛ*), yakṣas, nāgas, Brahmā, Śiva,
and Hari in sequence over seven nights.
One should worship with offerings those deities who are honored by all for the seven nights; O Pārvatī, I shall describe them to you.
One should worship the Bhūtas with parched grain, perfumes, flowers, sandalwood, and other such offerings.

One should worship those— the Lord of Beings (Bhūtādhipa), the Host of Beings (Bhūtagaṇa), and the Master of Beings (Bhūteśa)— in succession with offerings for worship consisting of oil, turmeric, curd, and parched grain; and one should worship them with rice mixed with sesame seeds, along with cooked rice and cakes.
One should always worship the ancestors, as declared by the Lotus-born One;
one should worship the Yakṣas with *karambha* and parched grain (*lāja*) accompanied by coconut water, and the Nāgas with groats and flour, according to this rite.
(210) O Goddess! One should worship with lotuses, rice, dūrvā grass, and śāli rice; this is declared by you to be the supreme form of worship for Brahmā, approved by all.
For Viṣṇu, food accompanied by cakes is approved in all tantras.
One should offer molasses-water and molasses-rice endowed with various flavors,
as well as curd, milk, and milk-rice pudding (pāyasa), which is most beloved and great;
and by offering these to Viṣṇu, a person shall obtain all perfections.
In this context, because of the observation of an abundance of offering materials (balidravya), the previously mentioned offerings for the *prapañcasāra* are merely illustrative,
or intended for those who are either capable or incapable [of obtaining more].
This is also stated in the third chapter of the *Śāradātilaka*.
Even before the initiation and other rites, one should perform the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) according to the rules over seven days for the attainment of all auspiciousness;
this should be done in a hall extending from east to west on the northern side of the mandala.
Then, having kept it secret, the wise one should fashion a maṇḍala within it;
he should lay down five lines, each measuring five cubits,
extending from east to west, with an interval of twelve finger-breadths between them.
In that same manner, one should lay down eleven threads from south to north;
forty squares are thus produced there, which one should then wipe clean.
Along the rows, there are four pathways at the ends on both sides of the two quadrants.
There are two pathways and one four-square grid remaining here;
the wise man should color those squares with white, yellow, red, and black powders,
and then fill the pathways with dark blue powder.
Regarding the rite of planting the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), they say there are three types of vessels:
the *pālikās*, the five-faced ones (*pañcamukhī*), and the shallow bowls (*śarāva*); these are declared in all Tantras to be, respectively, the essence of Hari, Brahmā, and Śiva.
Having wrapped those auspicious vessels, which measure sixteen, twelve, and eight finger-breadths respectively in height, with a thread,
the preceptor washes them and places rice within those pedestals.
One who knows the reality should place [the vessels] upon bunches of fragrant *darbha* grass starting from the west;
one should fill those vessels with dried cow dung, sand, and clay,
having washed the seeds with milk using the seed-syllable of *sudhā*.
Having recited the root mantra three times preceded by the five sounds,
and following the auspicious customs of the twice-born with words of benediction,
the preceptor, with a restrained mind, should offer [the oblation] into those vessels.
Rice, black gram, pigeon pea,
mung bean, sesame, flat bean, mustard, horse gram, millet, and black lentils— these seeds are for the rite of germination.
Having sprinkled them with water mixed with turmeric and covered them with *varuṇa* grass, the preceptor [proceeds].
One should cast the bali offering for the various vessels into the directions starting from the east,
using mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, and at night, using the names of the lords of the night:
the spirits (*bhūta*), the ancestors (*pitṛ*), the yakṣas, the nāgas, Brahmā, Śiva, and Hari.
The deities for all seven nights have been proclaimed.
For the *bhūtas*, there should be parched grain (*lāja*), sesame seeds, turmeric, curd, and flour; for the ancestors (*pitṛs*), rice and sesame-seeded grains are prescribed.
One should offer *karambha* and parched rice (*lāja*) along with coconut water to the Yakṣas; flour and ground meal to the Nāgas; lotus-shaped unbroken rice (*akṣata*) to Brahmā;
food with cakes to Sarva; and rice cooked with jaggery (*guḍaudana*) to Viṣṇu.
Then, one should duly offer bali-oblations even to the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras).
For the sake of prosperity during initiation, consecrations, the entry into a new house,
and festivals, one should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
The meaning of these is as follows.

By the phrase "due to the power of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth, [the ripening occurs] in seven days," it is stated that the procedure must be performed in such a way that the eighth day coincides with the day of initiation. By the term "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), it follows that [the ripening may occur] in nine, five, or three days, and so on.
This has been stated in the Siddhāntaśekhara:

One should perform the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) for the purpose of pacification during the consecration of a deity, the initiation ceremony, the installation of an image, a festival, the ritual sprinkling, a marriage, the tying of the sacred thread,
and indeed in all auspicious undertakings.
Also in the Mahākapilapañcarātra:
Having performed the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhaghoṣaṇa*) together with the Brahmins,
the preceptor should perform the auspicious rite of the sprouts (*maṅgalāṅkura-yajña*) on that very same day.
On the seventh or ninth auspicious day prior to the day of the recommended sacrifice,
or on the fifth or eighth, at an excellent moment (muhūrta), one should perform the rite for the auspicious sprouts (maṅgalāṅkura).
The preceptor, having already been purified, should fast on the seventh day prior to the day of the rite;

having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), he should perform the auspicious planting of sprouts (aṅkurāropaṇa). On the preceding day, he should perform the Nāndīmukha Śrāddha and the recitation of benedictions (svastivācana).
One should indeed perform this very rite according to the method prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra; it is also stated in the Saṃhitā.
One should perform the Abhyudaya-śrāddha at the very beginning of every rite of an auspicious nature, for it is like the production of a sprout.
"A hall" (*śālā*) refers to a measurement of twenty cubits in length and ten in width; this is the maximum measurement for a hall.
Since there is no purpose for such a large one here, the hall should be made with half that, which is the medium measurement.
Therefore, a hall measuring ten cubits in length and five cubits in width should be constructed here; [one should use] that very [hall].
Regarding the phrase "extending from east to west":

one should construct it long, with broad hands (sides), and square in shape; it should be concealed, enclosed by doors and the like, provided with a single gate on the south side, and protected from drafts.
As it has been stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
Having made that firm hut windless and situated toward the north from the front,
he describes the method for constructing the mandala therein:
"With five cubits," meaning having cast five lines in the sequence from east to west.
One should lay down eleven threads from south to north, each separated by twelve finger-breadths; by this, forty squares are formed.
The word "one should erase" follows later [in the text].
Having invoked [the deities] in rows, one should sweep the four paths; as for the method of sweeping:
First, one should clear away one path consisting of four squares in the east; then another consisting of eight squares in the south; then yet another consisting of four squares in the west;
and finally the other one consisting of eight squares in the north.
Then, one should erase two paths on both sides within the central square, each consisting of two squares.
By doing so, three sets of four squares remain in this mandala.
Those remaining twelve squares situated in the three sets of four squares [should be treated] as individual four-squared units.
One should color [the mandala] with powders, white and so forth.
Therein, it is white in the quarter of Vāyu, yellow in the quarter of Agni, reddish-brown in the quarter of Nairṛti, and black in the quarter of Īśāna.
Then, one should fill the pathways (vīthī) with dark-green powder.
The term *patrāṇi* refers to thick, high shallow bowls (*śarāva*) which are designated by the word *pālikā*.
These same *pālikās*, when low and provided with five openings, are called *pañcamukhī*; these are well-known as shallow bowls (*śarāva*).
The *pālikās* are the form of Hari, the *pañcamukhīs* are the form of Brahmā, and the *śarāvas* are the form of Śiva.
By this, it is stated that Hari, Brahmā, and Īśa are to be worshipped in these vessels.
This has been said in the Sārasvata-tantra:
One should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva in those vessels that have been mentioned.
Also in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
One should worship Rudra with sandalwood and flowers in shallow bowls (śarāva),
Viṣṇu in small cups (pālikā), and Brahmā in water-jars (ghaṭikā);
"by height" means by their vertical elevation.
In the Mahākapilapañcarātra.
The mouth-opening of the vessel is said to be sixteen finger-breadths wide;
its neck-cavity should be eight finger-breadths wide at the base.
The width of the foot-stand is declared to be six finger-breadths.
The height [of the base] shall be four finger-breadths (aṅgulas), and its joint two finger-breadths;
the circumference of that joint shall be equal to half the footstool.
Thus, the water-clock (ghaṭikā) shall have five openings and shall grant all desires.
They say that the five faces indeed have a width of four finger-breadths each;
four are in the four directions and one above, according to the rule.
The length and width of the water-clock (ghaṭikā) is said to be twelve finger-breadths.
Some teachers say that the mouth of the *śarāva* is remembered as being sixteen *aṅgulas* in length,
or twelve *aṅgulas* in width;
its base at the bottom is said to be four *aṅgulas* in width.
As cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:

The five-faced [vessel] should be only one tāla in height; the water-clock (ghaṭikā) should be measured according to the width of Vyāsa. Its four faces should be directed toward the cardinal directions, while the one in the middle should be turned evenly toward the center.
A shallow bowl with a wide mouth should have its height and width measured by four finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
Its handle should be one finger-breadth in thickness, and its tip should be devoid of a hollow in the middle of the neck.
These may be made of gold, silver, or copper, or otherwise they may be of fresh clay.
But in the Siddhāntaśekhara, however:
It has been stated that one should perform the rites with vessels such as the *pālikā* and others as far as possible.
Regarding the term "auspicious," Rāghavabhaṭṭa explains it as meaning free from black spots, scars, and the like.
As for the phrase "with thread," it refers to a triple-stranded thread; first there is the washing, and afterwards the wrapping with the triple-stranded thread.
The *darbhakūrca* will be described further on.

Regarding the phrase "starting from the west," one should place four *pālikās* in the western group of four, four five-faced vessels (*pañcamukhī*) in the central group of four, and four *śarāvas* in the eastern group of four.
The installation of [the deities] starting from the southeast (āgneya) in the midst of that is stated by the word "deśika" (the preceptor).
This has been stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
Having done thus, the practitioner should place the vessels there individually in the four corners, starting from the southeast (vahni) and ending with the northeast (īśāna),
beginning with "karīṣa" and so forth.
*Karīṣa* is the powder of pure cow dung.
With these, one should fill all the vessels in successive order.
This has been stated in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*:
"One should fill them higher and higher. Also, in the *Prayogasāra*:
"One should fill the vessels from above with earth, sand, and dried cow-dung."
The specific detail regarding this is found in the Siddhāntaśekhara.
Having worshipped the spade with perfumes and other offerings on another day,
accompanied by song and dance and attended by elephants and horses,
the preceptor and others shall mount chariots, while others likewise mount elephants.
Having gone to the bank of a pond, a river, or a flower garden,
one should there sweep a pure portion of ground with *darbha* grass or a cloth,
and sprinkle it with water for the *arghya* offering while recollecting the respective mantras.
Having invoked the Earth with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers.
Then, having dug the ground with the *kuddālī* mantra,
one should take the earth from the northern side and fill a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*) with it.
Having cleansed it with the heart-mantra and wiped it dry, one should cover it with a cloth and maintain it.
Then, while sounding all auspicious instruments, the Guru should circumambulate the city or the residence, and subsequently lead [the deity] to the pavilion.
A wise person should perform those respective rites during the day and not at night;
regarding the sowing of seeds in them, he says "sudhā" (the nectar).
"With the seed-syllable of nectar, by means of the mantra 'vami'";
"having washed with milk"—
this is the specific detail found in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra.
Having washed it with water by means of the twelve-syllable mantra.
This is also the case in the opinion of Sārasvata.

"Having washed those seeds with water and milk in succession"—all this is indicated by the phrase "one who knows the tantra. "With the root" means consecrated (*abhijapta*) with the root mantra one hundred and eight times; such is the meaning.
This has been stated in the Mahākapilapañcarātra:
"If friendship is not mentioned, one should perform a hundred or a thousand repetitions, plus eight, in japa and other such rites."
But the fivefold sound, however...
"Conch shells, drums, gongs, clay drums,
and mouth-instruments [are played] as auspicious rites.
By "fourfold forces," one refers to those well-known sounds such as the *hula-hula* cries and so forth.
Then, having gathered those seeds together, one should sow them at night—facing either east or north—into the *pālikā* vessels and so forth with the root mantra; thus it is said.
This has been stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:

Facing either the east or the north, one should sow all the seeds in sequence into the *pālikās* and other vessels using the primary root-mantra. Since Soma is the lord of seeds, one should perform the sowing at night.
This is also the case in the opinion of Sārasvata.
Since he was radiant at night due to the seeds and the deities,
the preceptor should therefore sow the seeds only during the night.
He mentions the seeds with the words "śālī" and so forth. *Śālayaḥ* are winter rice; *śyāmāḥ* are *śyāmāka* grains, known as *sāmbā* in the Kānyakubja dialect.
In the Gauḍa language, it is well known as *śāmā*.
*Āḍhakī* is known in the Gauḍa language as *tuvarī* or *arahara*. *Niṣpāvā* is known in the Gauḍa language as *vorā*.
In the opinion of Sārasvata, the worship of the deities for each seed is stated as follows:
Skanda in *priyaṅgu*, Vāyu and Agni in *niṣpāva*,
Nirṛti in *kulattha*, Soma in *āḍhakī*, and Vaivasvata in sesame (*tila*), O beautiful one!
"One should worship Prajāpati with rice grains, Ananta with mustard seeds, [Brahmā] with this [term] in the case of black [grains], and Varuṇa with beans, O Daughter of the Mountain!
(p. 215). However, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, the daily worship and recitation of Soma is stated as follows:
One should worship Soma daily until the day of the preparatory rite (adhivāsa).
When the day of the preparatory rite has arrived, the Guru should cause Soma to be brought forth;
this is stated in the respective mantra beginning with "Hariḥ indra".
In the *Prayogasāra*: "Homage again and again to the one who possesses the three five-fold bodies, to Śaṅkara, to Śiva, the preeminent among all worlds, the eternal."
Having scattered [the seeds] with this mantra, one should rain down water mixed with turmeric powder upon them; one should sprinkle them with water every day—
this is the meaning of "daily."
"With garments" means with new garments;
the plural number, according to the principle of the *kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa*, results in the sense of three.
"Having covered"—the syntactical connection is that one should offer the *bali* at night, placing [the offering] upon each of the four vessels with one garment each.

In the morning, having again performed the cleaning of the ground and other rites, the offering of the *bali* at the beginning of the second night and so forth is performed with mantras beginning with the *praṇava*.
The mantra for that is:
"Oṃ, salutation to the spirits (*bhūtas*). The mantra is likewise [to be applied] elsewhere as well.
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, however, there is a specific distinction:
"Then one should sprinkle [the vessel] with pure water mixed with fragrant scents for three nights or even five nights, according to the prescribed rule."
According to the tradition of Sarasvata, however:
"When the sprouts have fully emerged, no one else should ever look at them;
only the preceptor or the disciple may enter, as it should then be known."
Also in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
Having carefully covered them with cloths, one should cause them to be well-guarded.
Regarding the sacrificial offerings for the spirits (*bhūta*) over seven nights, he says: "To the spirits [be this offering]"; *karambha* is curd mixed with parched grain flour.

"Akṣatāḥ" refers to unbroken rice grains, according to Rāghavabhaṭṭa; however, in the statement cited in the *Śrāddhatattva*, "akṣatāḥ" refers to barley (*yava*). When the offering of the *bali* occurs over nine nights, then the offering of the *bali* takes place during two nights.
The substance and the deity have already been mentioned. An offering (bali) consisting of milk-rice and other items should be presented in their respective directions.
Among them, an offering should be given to Brahmā between the northeast and the east, and to Ananta between the southwest and the west.
Now follows the examination of the sprout.
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"For the sake of the prosperity of the patron, one should examine the sprouts—
those that have properly grown halfway, being tender and white."
One should avoid those that are smoke-colored, unprecedented, moving horizontally, dark-blue, or humpbacked, for they are inauspicious;
a black one brings lack of rain, while one with a smoky luster likewise causes strife.
There will be unprecedented events, the destruction of progeny, bad alms, and dark sprouts;
if [the moon] goes into the *tiryag* position, there will be disease, and likewise, if it is in the *kubja* position, there is fear of enemies.
This is also according to the *Sārasvata-mata*.
One should indicate the auspicious or inauspicious results for the agent by the fully developed sprouts:

with dark or black sprouts there is loss of wealth; with those growing horizontally, disease; with those swaying, suffering; with those that are bent, misery; with those that fail to grow properly, death; and with those that are crooked, illness and loss of one's position, country, or desired objects.
If an inauspicious sprout has emerged, one should perform a propitiatory *homa*;

the preceptor, together with the Brahmins, should offer oblations with the root mantra, using either the Aghora-weapon mantra or the Astra-mantra, one hundred or one thousand times. Thus concludes the ritual for sowing the sprouts.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Sprouts," consisting of the narration of the rites beginning with the examination of the Guru and the disciple and ending with the ritual of sowing the seed-sprout, in the second section on Dharma within the illustrious *Prāṇatoṣiṇī*.
The etymology of *dīkṣā* is found in the *Rudrajāmala*:
"It bestows identity with Śiva (*śivatādātmya*) and destroys the three impurities (*malatraya*);
therefore, it is called *dīkṣā* by those who know the meaning of the *Dīkṣātantra*."
And in the Laghukalpasūtra:
Supreme knowledge is bestowed and the path of sin is destroyed;
therefore, initiation (dīkṣā) is so called with respect to the mantra, according to the strength or weakness of the meaning of one's own scripture.
This is also stated in the third part of the Yoginītantra, in the sixth chapter.
Knowledge is bestowed and the bondage of the fetters is utterly destroyed;
therefore, O Goddess of gods, it is called *dīkṣā* by those who contemplate the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
Whatever sin has been accumulated through mind, action, or speech—
Because she bestows supreme knowledge and effects their distinction,
she is therefore celebrated in this world as "Dīkṣā" by those who know the scriptures;
she alone is the giver of the fruit of realization and is the second [form] which brings about dissolution.
The third indeed bestows liberation; therefore, it is known as dikṣā (initiation).
And in the second chapter of the Viśvasāra-tantra:
Now, O lotus-faced one, listen as I shall explain the initiation (dīkṣā),
by the mere knowledge of which a person attains divinity;
for it bestows divine wisdom and thereby effects the destruction of sins.
Therefore, that is declared to be initiation (dīkṣā), as agreed upon by the Savatantra.
Now, regarding the greatness of initiation (dīkṣā),
as stated in the third chapter of the first section of the Rudrayāmala:
O Goddess! For one devoid of initiation, there is neither spiritual perfection nor communion.
Therefore, with every effort, one should be initiated by a Guru.
One must certainly perform the contemplation on the essence of the Cakra.
Even one who is uninitiated shall go to the Raurava hell at the time of death;
therefore, one should always diligently perform the Tantric initiation.
In the fifteenth chapter.

O Dear One! Those who perform rites such as recitation (japa) and worship without having been initiated do not attain results; it is like seeds sown upon a stone. (As stated in the Kulārṇava-tantra cited in the Kalpasūtra-ṭīkā.)
Just as iron pierced by the best of mercury attains the state of gold,
so too, O beloved, the self pierced by initiation attains the state of Śiva.
With his karma burnt by the fire of initiation, he goes forth, his bonds severed.
For him who has gone [to that state], the bondage of karma is gone and he becomes Śiva, devoid of life (nirjīva).
The status of a Śūdra is gone for the Śūdra, and the status of a Brāhmaṇa is gone for the Brāhmaṇa as well;
when one is permeated by the purificatory rite of initiation (dīkṣā-saṃskāra), no distinction of caste exists.
One incurs the same sin as that which one would incur by perceiving a Śiva-liṅga as a mere stone;
likewise, one incurs that same sin by recollecting the former state [of being a common object] even regarding a consecrated liṅga.
[This applies to] a liṅga made of wood, stone, metal, clay, or precious gems, once it has been installed.
