As it has been said, all castes are pure once they have received initiation;
by merely worshipping one who has been initiated, everything as far as the world of Brahmā becomes worshipped— of this there is no doubt.
For one who has been initiated, there should be no need for austerities, restrictive vows,
nor even for visiting sacred pilgrimage sites or physical disciplines.
Also in the sixth chapter of the fifth section:
"The ghee residing within the body of cows does not nourish itself;
rather, it nourishes only that [cow] through the rod of its own past actions."
Thus, O Supreme Goddess! like clarified butter situated within every body, it does not yield fruit for men without worship, O Devi!
In the first chapter of the *Puraścaraṇarasollāsa*:
"There is no knowledge superior to initiation, no austerity superior to initiation, and no time superior to initiation; therefore, initiation is most weighty."
Thus ends the praise of initiation.
Regarding the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of the day, lunar date, asterism, month, and so forth for initiation (*dīkṣā*),
these may be seen there in the *Tantrasāra* written by our very venerable great-great-grandfather, Kṛṣṇānandāgamavāgīśa.
The specific details, however, are found in the *Puraścaraṇarasollāsa*.
O lady of tremulous glances! In initiation, there is no restriction of time whatsoever.
From the mere sight of a true Guru, it is always like a solar eclipse.
If the Guru, out of compassion, summons the disciple and bestows [the initiation], [it is accomplished].
In that regard, one should never consider anything such as the ascendant (lagna) and so forth;
all of this pertains to the divine hero (divyavīra).
And likewise, prior to this:
"Having obtained a divine heroic guru and having received initiation, the wise one,
then becoming composed, shall perform the *puraścaryā*.
By this statement, it follows that everything regarding initiation from a *paśu*-guru must be investigated.
In the Kulārṇava as maintained in the commentary on the Kalpasūtra.

Even if a twice-born man is initiated later while an outcaste was initiated earlier, that twice-born man is the junior and the other is the senior; such is the determination of the scripture. By virtue of their seniority, they are to be honored and must never be treated with contempt under any circumstances.
Thus concludes the exposition on seniority based on initiation and other such matters.
Also in the Kulārṇava:
According to the teaching of Śiva, there can be no liberation for living beings without initiation (dīkṣā);
and that initiation cannot exist without a preceptor (ācārya)—thus there is a lineage of preceptors.
Without such a lineage, one does not achieve success even through a hundred forms of worship.
One should diligently take recourse in that initiation from the venerable Guru for the sake of attaining success in mantra.
In the Mahākapila-pañcarātra and the Nārāyaṇīya.
A mantra which one might accomplish by means of a single [deity] through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth—
by whose manifold rituals other [mantras] are mastered with little effort—
for one who has correctly perfected a single mantra, there is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished.
"What need is there to speak of a man possessing many mantras? He is indeed nothing but loss. This is the fruit of accomplishing even a single mantra, as recorded by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
O beautiful one! For him by whom a mantra written in a book is recited, no accomplishment arises; rather, there is loss at every step.
It is also cited in the *Ṣaṭkarmadīpikā*.
O beautiful one! He by whom the vidyā written in a book is recited does not attain accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
(Cited from Rāghavabhaṭṭa).

Just as those twice-born who have not undergone initiation possess no entitlement here to the six duties, study, and so forth, according to their respective capacities, so too those who have not been initiated possess no entitlement to the recitation of mantras, the worship of deities, and the like.
"Therefore, one has no authority [to perform rites for others]; thus, one should make oneself consecrated by Śiva."
The description of the faults incurred by not performing initiation.
In the Nārāyaṇīya [section].
A mantra heard by chance, or even one seen on paper through concealment or deception, is inferior and brings about misfortune if not practiced according to the proper rules.
Thus ends the description of censurable initiation.
Also in Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
Having heard the ritual initiation according to rule and the *avratānika* consecration from a preceptor, and having received the *tantra*, one who has been initiated should accomplish the mantra;
all the primary rites performed by the preceptor bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Therefore, for the sake of liberation, those who are well-composed should always serve the guru; for all rites not instructed by the guru will certainly be fruitless. Recitation, fire-offerings, and the ritual of worship must be performed by men who have received initiation.
Thus concludes the exposition of the procedure for initiation.
The Root Sūtra.
There are three initiations: the Śākta, the Śāmbhavī, and the Māntrī.

Among these, the Śākta [initiation] is from the entry of power (śakti), the Śāmbhavī from the placement of the feet, and the Māntrī is that which is taught through mantras. Some say that one should perform all of them, while others say one should perform each one individually.
The venerable Śaṅkarācārya explains this as follows:

"Śākti" refers to Śakti, who is Kuṇḍalinī, whose nature is supreme consciousness (paracit). Through the association with her activity, the union with Supreme Śambhu within the Brahma-nāḍī—due to the distinction between Kula and Akula—is the entry of Śakti.
"Śāmbhavī is the placement of the feet"—thus are your four feet, which consist of the white, red, mixed, and supreme natures.
"Māntrī is that taught by the mantra. This has been stated in the Rudrajāmala:
Initiation born of Śakti arises from Śakti; that Śakti is the venerable Parakuṇḍalī. Through the reverse order of her vital breaths, there is entry into the supreme Śāmbhava state.
Born from the two feet [of the Guru], the Śāmbhavī [initiation] bestows swift accomplishment.
The initiation pertaining to mantra (*māntrī dīkṣā*) arises from mantra; its power is born of one's own self.
Through the aforementioned rites of mantra, yantra, and worship, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The two feet are the very form of Śiva and Śakti.
In this regard, that which is dominated by *sattva* is white; that dominated by *rajas* is red; and that dominated by *tamas* is mixed.
That which transcends the *guṇas* is *nirvāṇa*;
it is directly filled with supreme bliss and is the very nature of Sadāśiva.
They should be meditated upon as being bathed by streams of nectar situated within the lunar disc located at the center of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus.
And it was said by the Blessed One Dattātreya:

Brahmā and Śiva, white and red respectively, reside between your eyebrows; indeed, your feet, possessing the qualities of passion (rajas) and inertia (tamas), perform the creation and maintenance [of the world] when served.
The fierce one, worshipping the third [foot], destroys the entire exalted universe;
I perpetually bow to that fourth noble foot of yours, which is to be known as free from limiting conditions, dense with nectar, and situated in the state of Śiva.
In the Rudrajāmala:
That initiation (dīkṣā) is threefold: the first is the Āṇavī;
the other is the Śāktī; and the third is the Śāmbhavī, which bestows immediate liberation.
[The Āṇavī is performed] by means of mantra, worship, placement of the seats (āsana), ritual deposition (nyāsa), meditation, and the various services (upacāra).
That initiation (dīkṣā) is declared to be the Āṇavī, having the form described according to the scriptures.
And for the sake of attaining perfection, when the Guru perceives the power (śakti) in the disciple,
the initiation performed by that power alone is proclaimed as the Śākta.
Even without formal initiation, for both teacher and disciple,
the status of being a disciple that brings about [spiritual] pervasion occurs solely through the grace of the Guru.
Also in the *Ṣaḍanvayamahāratna*:
That initiation (dīkṣā) is threefold: the first is the Āṇavī;
the other two are the Śākteyī and the Śāmbhavī, which bestow immediate liberation.
[The Āṇavī is accomplished] through mantra, worship, postures, meditation, installation, ritual service, and so forth.

That initiation which is performed according to the form prescribed in the scriptures is called *āṇavī*. When, having perceived the disciple's own power (*śakti*) for the sake of accomplishment, initiation is performed by that power alone without any external means, it is proclaimed as *śākteyī*.
Without any prior intention on the part of either the teacher or the disciple,
this Śāmbhavī initiation— which brings about the manifestation of Śiva-nature solely through the grace of the Guru and effects the command of Śiva— is indeed [the supreme].
Also in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā: "In the Śiva-āgama, initiation is taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as threefold: the Śāmbhavī, the Śākta, and the Māntrī."

Through the mere sight of the Guru, or even by touch or conversation, consciousness arises immediately in the person; that initiation is considered Śāmbhavī. The Śākta initiation, however, occurs when [the Guru], possessing knowledge, enters the body of the disciple.
By means of the path of knowledge, the Guru, with the eye of wisdom,
performs the initiation consisting of mantra and ritual action, preceded by the water-pot and the mandala.
Thus ends the explanation of the different types of initiation according to the differences in the act of naming.
The other distinctions regarding initiation (dīkṣā), however, are found in the fourth chapter of the Śāradā.
That [mantra] is declared to be fourfold, according to the divisions of *kriyāvatī* and so forth:
it is *kriyāvatī*, *varṇamayī*, *kalātmā*, and also *vedhamayī*.
In the *Prayogasāra*:
Having directly realized the chosen deity according to the path of mantra, the guru awakens the disciple; this is called "mantra-initiation" (mantradīkṣā).
He cites another sūtra: "One should perform all [the rites], or each one individually," so say some.
In the Rudrajāmala:
The *āṇavī* initiation is manifold, and likewise the *śāmbhavī*;
each one is taught by the learned who are experts in the scriptures.
[This occurs] through the auspicious conjunction of Śiva and Śakti brought about in a previous birth.
"When, through the continuous practice of Śiva-worship, the equilibrium of karma is attained,
then one becomes Śiva himself directly through the *āṇava* initiation.
This is the statement regarding the fruit of initiation.
In the Viśvasāra Tantra:
That initiation was declared by Brahmā in four types in ancient times:
the Kriyāvatī, the Kalāvatī, the Varṇavedhamayī, and the Guṇavatī.
(p. 221) These auspicious initiations, which bestow all prosperity, are now described in their proper order.
Thus, for all initiations, from the mental one up to that which culminates in liberation, the fruit is exactly the same.
That has been stated in the Rudrajāmala:
The unimpeded fruit of all initiations is liberation;
this occurs without contradiction, while the various forms of devotion are merely incidental.
Now follows the procedure for the formal acceptance.

Therein, first, immediately after entering the house, one should perform the installation of the jar (ghaṭasthāpana) preceded by the removal of obstacles, having recited the hymns beginning with "Sūryaḥ somādi" and the mantras beginning with "Bhūrasi.
This is stated in the third chapter of the Viśvasāra Tantra:
The disciple should perform everything according to the prescribed rules under the guidance of the Guru;
the wise disciple should have all the rites performed by the Guru and receive everything [from him].
He should fumigate the sacrificial pavilion with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
Having entered the house according to the prescribed rite, one should destroy the obstacles therein;
with palms joined in reverence, one should recite this mantra:
"Oṃ! Sūrya, Soma, Yama, Kāla, and the five great elements."
These nine are the witnesses here of one's auspicious and inauspicious karma.
The preceptor should perform the ritual placement of the jar (ghaṭāropaṇa) with this mantra;
this mantra for the placement of the jar is approved in all Tantras.

Oṃ, you are Bhūḥ, you are the Earth, you are Aditi, the sustainer of all; you who support the entire world, uphold the earth, make the earth firm, do not harm the earth. This, O Goddess of Gods, is called the purification of the ground, endowed with the authority of all Tantras, performed with this mantra.
One should scatter white grain [with the mantra]:
*oṃ dhānyam asi dhinuhi devān dhinuhi yajñaṃ dhinuhi yajñapatiṃ dhinuhi māṃ yajñanam*.
Oṃ! Breath is the mantra; I give you, having considered you for my desire. Indeed, this state of measurement is long for them.
May the divine Savitṛ, the golden-handed, accept you with an unbroken [vessel]. For the sake of the stone-eyed one, I take you; you are the great earth, you are milk.
Having fashioned a jar one cubit in measure with nine gems inside,
the preceptor should place the jar there with this mantra:
*Oṃ ājighra kalaśaṃ mahyātmā viśantu devāḥ*.
Return again with vigor; may you be ours.
"May the thousand-streamed, milk-abounding cow yield for me; may wealth enter me again.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should then establish the jar with this mantra.
[One should place] pearls, rubies, lapis lazuli, gomedaka, diamonds, and corals.
One should place ruby, emerald, and sapphire, respectively, as the nine gems there, until the dissolution of the world. Also in the *Merutantra*:
Blue sapphire, lapis lazuli, coral, pearl, as well as emerald,
diamond, hessonite, and ruby—
these are declared to be the nine gems by the preceptors who are most proficient in mantras.
Oṃ, may you swell; may [the waters] come to you from all sides, O Soma; be a shower of rain for the gathering of strength.
With this mantra, O Goddess of the Gods, one should offer water upon the jar:
Oṃ, with wealth we shall conquer, with wealth we shall overcome, with wealth we shall conquer the fierce in battle.
"May the bow of the enemy be rendered useless; may we conquer all the quarters with our strength.
O Queen of the Gods! With this mantra, one should place a branch upon the jar, and specifically offer betel leaf, a bilva fruit, or a plantain.

Oṃ! Śrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives; day and night are your two sides; the stars are your form; the Aśvins are your eyes. He is the pervasive, beloved, and sovereign Lord; may he, the Great Lord of all worlds, be my Lord.
O Goddess of the Gods! With this mantra, one should cast a flower into the jar;
then, having placed a shallow bowl (śarāva) containing rice flour along with fruit upon the jar, one should perform the rite according to the rules, accompanied by a milky tree.
The practitioner should offer clothing and garments with this mantra:
"Oṃ! This garment is purifying, white, and woven from many threads;
it is offered by me with devotion—please accept this garment."
Having boiled [the ingredients] with jambu powder and the leaf of indravallī,
and having wrapped the jar according to the prescribed rite and adorned it with vermilion and other substances,
the wise practitioner should carefully place that jar there while reciting the mantra.
The statement "boiled with jambū powder" is said for the sake of illustration; its specific details regarding other [substances] are also found in the third chapter of the Merutantra.
Immediately thereafter, one should fill [the vessel] with decoctions of fifty medicinal herbs;
these color-enhancing herbs (varṇauṣadhi) together with that one [base herb] are as follows in sequence:
sandalwood, red sandalwood, and likewise agallochum (aguru).
Camphor, uśīra, kuṣṭha, bālaka, keśara,
kakkolaka, jātiphala, jaṭāmāṃsī, murā,
granthika, rocanā, jātīpatra, pippalī, and vilvaka.
Pṛśniparṇī, Citraka, Karaṅga, Kattṛṇa,
as well as Kaṭphala, Guñjā, Dadruha, Vaka,
Kāśmarī, Padmakoṣa, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, and likewise the crest of a peacock.
Plakṣa, agnimantha, as well as mudgaparṇī,
kuśa grass, pāṣāṇabhedaka, black śaṅkhapuṣpī, rohiṇī, śyoṇāka, bṛhatī, pāṭalī, and mukhakarṇikā.
Tulasī, Śikharā, Indravallī, and again that called Bhṛṅgā; then Aparājitā, Tālamūlī, and Kṛtāñjalī;
Dūrvā, the one named Śrīdevakanyā, the one named Bhārgī, and Bhadramustaka.
And these fifty in number are devoid of cloves.

Although fifty medicinal herbs were described in the first section, they are shown again here for the purpose of reaching a total of fifty-one, to eliminate the difficulty of what has already been stated, and to make known the difference in their sequence.
"With decoctions of the bark of milk-exuding trees (*dugdhavṛkṣa*), as well as those produced from the *brahmavṛkṣa*,
or with boiled waters scented with fragrant paste, flowers, and the like;
then one should stabilize the jar until the ritual of initiation takes place."
Oṃ, be firm, O Viḍaṅga; be swift, O Vāyu; be broad, O Earth; be a good seat, O Agni!
By this mantra, O Goddess of Devas, the supreme stabilization is accomplished.
Then, having joined his palms in reverence, he should recite this mantra:
"Oṃ, salutations to the gurus and to the Gaṇapatis; salutations to you who are multiformed and to you who possess universal forms;
salutations to the hosts and to the lords of the hosts."
Homage to you, the domestic deities and the lords of the household;
at the outset, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited, preceded by the invocation of well-being.
Oṃ! May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya with his uninjured wheel grant us well-being;
may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
With the mantra *astrāya phaṭ*, one should shatter terrestrial obstacles;

and with a divine gaze (*divyadṛṣṭi*), one should drive away celestial obstacles in the four directions. Regarding the characteristics of the divine gaze in that very same source: "The divine gaze is proclaimed to be the gaze of unblinking eyes."
One should offer a bali of black gram flour mixed with rice and barley gruel,
along with the blood of a goat's ear,
milk, and honey, to the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.

Oṃ! May all the spirits, ghosts, and piśācas who dwell in the netherworld and upon the earth, as well as those situated on mountain peaks, in trees, and in houses, fields, and so forth—may they all be satisfied; may they accept this bali offering from me.
One should worship with red flowers and the blood of a red buffalo,
along with fried fish, meat, and other offerings, as well as with milk, according to this ritual procedure; and there too, one should present the bali offering, and then begin the auspicious rite.
Since initiation (*dīkṣā*) consists of religious duties and rituals, the removal of obstacles therein is described in the eighth chapter of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the *Yoginītantra*:
"Especially at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), in the construction of a temple, and at the commencement of a religious act..."
(224) Obstacles indeed dwell at the commencement of a vow or a sacrifice;
one should first worship them with offerings such as *balis* and sweetmeats (*modakas*). Know this from me, O beloved: otherwise, an obstacle will arise.
Moreover, other obstacles indeed dwell within the body;
they are the removals of mental ignorance—listen to them from me, my beloved!
O Goddess, some are obstructive, while others are likewise impelling.
Whether it be proximity or distance, a thousandfold fruit or even the pursuit of sin; whether it be corruption through laziness,
or the affliction of grief, delusion, fever, and disease, or the craving for wealth.
He experienced quarrels with his wife, famine,

and domestic entanglements; though his mind was filled with various vows and the thought "I am a righteous man," he nevertheless encountered sorrow on account of his dharma, being deprived of his wife.
A leaf of the *vṛkṣa* tree and *tulasī*, as well as the fruit of the *dhātrī* tree;
a fragment of *śālagrāma* stone, an image carved from wood,
a human being who is a Brāhmaṇa, and a self-manifested circular stone.
A conch, a variety of shellfish, and the flesh of a rhinoceros—
these may appear as such in the sight [of the observer]; likewise, water born at a sacred ford (tīrtha),
or the form of a river like the Gaṅgā, or even a plot of land that is a field of merit.
These obstacles arise again and again;
therefore, having worshipped according to the prescribed rite at the entrance, one should not perform the practice there.
One should do so by reciting the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) as the seed-syllable seven times.
Having expelled all those obstacles, one should then again bestow protection.
In the Viśvasāra Tantra.
One should protect oneself there by means of the enclosure of fire;
one should mentally visualize the enclosure of fire in the four directions within the seed-syllable of fire.
Then the preceptor should perform the triple *tāla* gesture with the seed-syllable of fire.
Then, by means of the yoga of ascending step-by-step, one should bow to the gurus:
"Oṃ, perpetual salutation to the gurus; and then to the guru’s sandals—O Goddess!
the supreme, the both-supreme-and-non-supreme, and that which is even beyond the supreme."
The wise one should prostrate in sequence to those [deities] beginning with Oṃ as they are invoked;
having bowed to Gaṇeśa on the right and to the presiding deity (Iṣṭavat) in front,
the intelligent one should establish Gaṇeśa in the previously mentioned jar.
I invoke the god Gaṇeśa, the son of Śiva,
who wears a tiger-skin garment, has a serpent as his sacred thread,
is surrounded by ten million attendants, and whose food consists of sweetmeats.

I invoke the formidable Lord of Obstacles (Avighneśa), who possesses a great body, who is uniquely worshipped by all the worlds, and who is powerful for the sake of universal pacification. Come, come, O Blessed One! O God, destroyer of all obstacles!
"Accept this offering; make all of mine fruitful.
One should worship the son of Śiva with vermilion, red flowers, and other offerings.
First, one should invoke him with joined palms (añjali); this is remembered as the procedure for all instances.

Then, having offered a welcome and so forth, along with questions and their respective answers, one should provide a seat and then present water for the feet (*pādya*) and the respectful offering (*arghya*). "Oṃ! O God, this fragrant water for the feet brings happiness to all beings."
"Please accept this water for washing the feet (*pādya*), which removes the fatigue of a long journey.
*Namaḥ* (obeisance) to the pair of feet; *svāhā* to the water for the feet; *svadhā* to the water for the head (*arghya*) which is placed upon the head;
then the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and again the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*)."
One should say "namas" for the bathing water, and then again for the perfumes and other offerings;
one should assign the garment and the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) at the end of the word "namas.
Then, one should offer food and edibles with the word "svadhā," followed by incense and a lamp according to the prescribed rite.
One should gradually place [the offerings] there for the deity according to this rite;
having offered the *arghya* into the *arghya* vessel, then listen, O fair-faced one!
The *arghya* water should be in a conch shell, along with *syāmāka*, barley, and *dūrvā* grass.
Combined with various fragrances, along with *kuśa* grass, sesame, mustard seeds,
*viṣṇukrāntā*, and barley— this is proclaimed as the sixfold *arghya*.
The practitioner should offer the *arghya* while reciting the mantra beginning with "Oṃ kāṇḍāt."
One should perform the offering of water for the feet with the *pādya* mantra, and likewise the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*).
Joined with "Oṃ Namaḥ Svāhā," it is for the sake of attaining the fruit of Brahmanhood.
"Accept from me with devotion this *madhuparka* which has been offered by me."
In all cases, the root mantra is preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and followed by *namaḥ*.
Due to its Vedic character (*chāndasa*), there is no loss of phonemes; the meaning is that [the offering is made] with the root mantra accompanied by *oṃ* and *namaḥ*.
The *madhuparka* is proclaimed to consist of curd, honey, and clarified butter.
One should offer the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) with the *yajñopavīta* mantra.
The *yajñopavīta* mantra is as follows:
Oṃ, this sacred thread, the supreme purifier, which was born together with Bṛhaspati in the beginning—put on this bright, life-prolonging thread; may it be strength and splendor for you.
Oṃ! Crafted from various jewels and fashioned by Viśvakarman and others, you who are the ornament adorning every limb—accept this for the sake of the fruit [of my merit].
Oṃ! This supreme fragrance, rich in scent, is produced from the essence of trees.

May this incense, to be smelled by all the gods, be accepted. Oṃ, may this great lamp, brilliantly shining and dispelling darkness on all sides, this lamp which is light both internal and external, be accepted.
One should place rows of lamps nearby, along with incense and oil-lamps.
Afterward, the wise one should set down a vessel for the washing of the hands.
Then, the wise one should construct a pavilion filled with gold.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, as well as Arka, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā,
the practitioner should worship them there in the jar according to the prescribed rite for the sake of all prosperity;
first, the practitioner should throw a handful of *kūrca* grass with the *phaṭ* mantra.
Sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and mustard seeds constitute what is proclaimed as a "handful of kūrca";
one should scatter these *vikira* offerings there seven by seven with the *śara* mantra.
The *vikirās* will be explained in the context of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
With the *śarāṇu* weapon-mantra,
the Guru, having gone to the altar, shall sit upon his own seat.
In the third chapter of the Merutantra.
Having thus invoked the form [of the deity] into that [image] by means of the *sañcintya* mantra, the most excellent guru should worship his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) within that image;
then, the practitioner, having properly recollected the root mantra, [should draw the deity] from the opening of the channel (*nāḍīmukha*).
The Guru, having brought forth the consciousness of the exit [of the breath] that has emerged at the tip of the nose—
the splendor within the *mātṛkā*-lotus accompanied by flowers— into his joined palms (*añjali*),
should then raise it from the head and invoke it into that [flower].
Then one should perform the rites of stabilization (*saṃsthāpana*), bringing [the deity] near (*sannidhāna*), and complete restraint (*sannirodha*).
Then also the facing [of the deity] (*sammukhīkaraṇa*) and the ritual of making [the body] whole (*sakalīkaraṇa*).
After that, the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*) should be performed, and then the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*).
One should perform the act of perfection (*paramīkaraṇa*) sequentially with each respective mudrā; thereafter, one should duly arrange the ritual services (*upacāra*),
having prepared the extensive services beginning with the seat (*āsana*).
Then, within the ritual procedures for mantras, the limbs and enclosures that have been prescribed [should also be arranged].

Furthermore, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas), beginning with the Weapon-deity (Astra), in order within the directions starting from the east, either in the mandalas or upon the water-jars (kumbhas) therein:
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, and Añjana.
One should worship Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka at the forefront; at the very end of all the world-protectors (lokapālas), the worship of their weapons;
and prior to the worship of Indra and the others, also the worship of Brāhmī and the other goddesses.
And likewise, in the Viśvasāra:
In the eight directions, one should place eight jars filled with decoction water;
the Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, who are endowed with all the Tantras,
should be worshipped according to the procedure for knowledge, using perfumes, flowers, and fresh water.
Brahmī, possessing a golden luster and radiant with a black antelope skin, holds a staff, a water-pot in her hand, a rosary, and likewise the gesture of fearlessness.
Carrying a trident, a skull-bowl, an axe, and a beautiful boat for men, the auspicious Māheśvarī, resembling gold in complexion, should be meditated upon. (2)
Holding a goad, a staff, a skull-topped club, and a noose in her hands, Kaumārī—resembling the bandhūka flower in hue and bestowing happiness—is to be meditated upon. (3)
Bearing a discus, a bell, a mace, and a sword, she is most enchanting;
dark as the tamāla tree, the Vaiṣṇavī goddess, the bestower of bliss, is to be meditated upon. || 4 ||
Vārāhī, possessing the complexion of a dark cloud at the time of dissolution, should be meditated upon as holding a pestle, a sword, a shield, and a plough with her four hands. || 5 ||
Indrāṇī, who resembles a sapphire, holding a goad, a javelin, lightning, and a thunderbolt in her hands, should be meditated upon as the bestower of all prosperity.
Holding a trident, a skull, and a human head-skull in her hands, adorned with a garland of severed heads, Cāmuṇḍā, whose body is red, should be meditated upon. (7)
Holding a rosary of beads, a citron, a skull-cup, and a lotus in her hands,
Mahālakṣmī, who resembles gold, is the beloved of Hari.
In the Merutantra: "Having thus performed the worship with incense, lamps, and food offerings,
and having presented the offering, one should then [draw] the mandala around it in due order."

The officiating priest (mantrin) should place sprouts and leaves of coral upon an excellent sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) prepared on the southern side of the altar (vedikā). Having established the fire and performed its consecration (saṃskāra), he should commence the Vaiśvadeva rite.
Then, according to the prescribed rule, one should worship the deity there with perfumes and other offerings.
Thereafter, having first offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the *praṇava*,
one should offer milk-rice and clarified butter with the root mantra.
Having first offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* twenty-five times,
and having worshipped her with sandalwood paste and other offerings, one should unite her with the form on the pedestal.
Having dismissed the fire, one should present the *bali* offering with the remaining milk-rice (*pāyasa*).

Then, having lifted the food offering (naivedya) from the side-attendants along with sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken rice (akṣata), the wise practitioner should cleanse that spot. He should then worship again with the five services (upacāras) and subsequently show [the deity] [the prasāda].
The practitioner, with a concentrated mind, should recite the root mantra one thousand times while holding a mirror, a fan, an umbrella, a chowrie, and mouth-perfume.
In the Viśvasāra:
Having offered water according to the prescribed rite, one should then perform auspicious acts;
having received the blessings of the Brahmin women and Brahmins, and having gratified the Brahmins with shouts of "Victory! and Vedic chants.
Then, having satisfied the circle of kinsmen,
the best of preceptors should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) for the disciple with careful attention, using these substances and this mantra in the proper sequence.
Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, one should offer [the materials] ending with *namaḥ*.
Then, one should cast down the earth with the mantra *oṃ bhūrasi*.
[And then: *oṃ gandhadvārāṃ durādharṣāṃ nityapuṣṭāṃ karīṣiṇīm*.
I invoke here Śrī, the sovereign of all beings.
The practitioner should offer fragrance according to the prescribed rite with this mantra:
"Oṃ, she who moves about, nourished by the bull of the mountain, has come from the moon."
Thou hast placed the turned-back [earth] on the north.
Thou art the follower of the serpent Vṛdhna; thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, thou art the step of Viṣṇu, thou art the pace of Viṣṇu;
for Viṣṇu’s sake, I take thee.
With this mantra and according to this procedure, the wise one should offer a stone.
The offering of grain with the grain-mantra is approved in the Tantras:
*Oṃ, growing from stalk to stalk, O purifier, [purify] man after man.*
"O Dūrvā! Spread these out by the hundreds and thousands. O Goddess of Devas! With this mantra, one should offer the Dūrvā grass according to the prescribed rite.
And with the mantra "oṃ śrīśca te," one should offer a flower according to the prescribed rite.
The wise practitioner should offer fruit with the mantra beginning "oṃ yāḥ phalinī. [He should recite:

"oṃ dadhikrāvṇo'kārṣaṃ jiṣṇoraśvasya vājinaḥ | surabhi no mukhākarat praṇa āyūṃṣi tāriṣat ||" (Oṃ, I have performed the service for Dadhikrāvan, the victorious and spirited horse; may he make our mouths fragrant and extend our lifespans.)
Having meditated upon that with this mantra, one should perform the consecration (*adhivāsa*):

*Oṃ ghṛtavatī bhuvanānām abhitrīyorvī pṛthvī madhudughe supeśasā | dyāvāpṛthivī varuṇasya dharmaṇā viṣkambhite ajare bhūriretasā ||* [Oṃ! The two, Heaven and Earth, are rich in ghee, the protectors of all beings, wide and vast, yielding sweetness, and well-formed. By the law of Varuṇa, the two are propped apart—unaging and possessing abundant seed.]
O Queen of Gods! With this mantra, one should place [the mark] upon the head of the disciple.
With the mantra "Oṃ svasti naḥ," one should present the svastika.
"Oṃ, like the stream of the Sindhu, the thick-flowing tongue of ghee falls like a wind-swift steed; it is like the red [sun]."
With the mantra: "The vigorous one, breaking through the heights, swelling with waves," one should place vermilion upon the head of the disciple. Then:
"O Conch! You are the most auspicious among all auspicious things and the merit of the conch."
Viṣṇu-nature is eternally sustained; be the bestower of peace upon me.
This mantra for touching the conch is approved by all Tantras:
"Oṃ, O Agni, making the fuel the abode of my thoughts, may you be anointed with honeyed ghee."
"Like a horse carrying its rider, Jātavedas, the beloved speech of the gods, has brought [the offering].
O Goddess of the Gods! With this mantra, one should prepare the collyrium. (p.
229) *Oṃ yuñjanti bradhnam aruṣaṃ carantaṃ pari tasthuṣaḥ.*
The luminous ones shine in the sky. O beautiful one, one should place the luminous substance all around with this mantra:
"Oṃ! Giver of food, grant us food; [grant us] the food of the powerful and vigorous enemy."
"O Savior, bestow strength upon us—upon our bipeds and our quadrupeds!
Svāhā to Viśvakarman!
O Goddess of the Gods, by means of this mantra, the ritual touching is fully described.
"Oṃ! In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists.
He supported this earth and yonder heaven. To which god shall we offer our oblation with our speech?
O Goddess of the Gods, one should place gold around [the vessel] while reciting this mantra.
Oṃ! May Puthumā, the all-knowing, distribute the form of mortals by means of form;

as he knows the highest [realm], where the moon, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and the sun are seen, and the intermediate space is well-seated on high—by this mantra, O Goddess of Gods, one should give silver according to the prescribed rite.
Oṃ! He who is copper-colored, ruddy, and tawny, the most auspicious one;
and those Rudras who dwell around him in the various directions by the thousands—him indeed we implore for favor.
O Goddess of the Gods! With this mantra, one should offer the copper according to the prescribed rite:
*oṃ rakṣohano valagahanaḥ prokṣayāmi vaiṣṇavān; rakṣohano valagahano balayāmi vaiṣṇavān; rakṣohano valagahano vastṛṇāmi vaiṣṇavān; rakṣohano valagahana upadadhāmi.*
"O slayer of Rākṣasas, slayer of Vṛtra, I purify the Vaiṣṇava [substance]; they are Vaiṣṇavī; you are Vaiṣṇava; you are Vaiṣṇavas.
Having offered the *siddhārtha* (white mustard seeds) upon the child's head with this mantra:
"Oṃ, moving through the dark space, establishing the immortal and the mortal..."
"O Goddess of the Gods! With this mantra, one should present the mirror: 'Savitar, the god, goes upon his golden chariot, beholding all beings.
Om! May the mind, through the light, enjoy the clarified butter; may Bṛhaspati extend this sacrifice.'"

"May all the gods grant this sacrifice to be free from obstacles; may they rejoice here; O Goddess of Gods, establish yourself with this mantra. With this mantra, one should offer the lamp according to the prescribed rite.

Oṃ, you are the first step; for the sake of the first step, I take you. You are the following step; for the sake of the following step, I take you. You are the perfect attainment; for the sake of the perfect attainment, I take you.
You are splendor; for the sake of splendor, I take you.
Endow me with splendor. Oṃ, you are the measure of praise; in this vessel of reality, fulfill all my purposes, including the pair of the Goddess’s feet.
Worthy of veneration.
In the fourth chapter of the Śāradātilaka.
Having washed a new vessel made of copper or another metal with the Astra-mantra,
one should place ten handfuls of rice grains produced from the *śāli* variety, consecrated by the root mantra, into it, and then mutter the Antram mantra.
Having washed the mouth of the vessel and performed the rite of armor (*kavaca*) with the *anunā* mantra,
the preeminent teacher, facing east, should cook the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Once it has been thoroughly steamed, he should pour hot clarified butter (*ājya*) over it with the *śruva* ladle while reciting the *taptābhimarśana* mantra.
Afterwards, with the root mantra, he should lower that vessel with the armor mantra (*kavaca*).

Having divided it into three parts according to the rules upon a mandala strewn with *kuśa* grass over which the weapon mantra (*astra*) has been recited, the Guru should assign one portion to the deity.
The preceptor himself should offer another oblation into the fire, and then,

having performed the prescribed ritual rinsing (ācamana), he should eat together with the disciple. Then, taking the disciple who has rinsed his mouth and having rendered him complete through the sakalīkaraṇa rite, the preceptor [should proceed].

Then, one should give a tooth-stick made from a milk-tree or similar source, measuring the height of a palm tree, which has been empowered by reciting [the mantra] over it while focused on the heart; this should be given to the disciple who is self-restrained. Having cleansed his teeth with it, the disciple should then rinse it and discard it.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) for him according to the rules and protected him by tying the topknot (śikhā),
the Guru should lie down upon that altar amidst the darbha grass together with him; that night is declared to be the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).
The specific details, however, should be sought in the third chapter of the Merutantra.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the consecration.
Now follows the procedure for the installation of the *aṅkurāḥ* (germinating seeds).

Therein, due to the influence of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other factors, on an auspicious day— either the ninth, seventh, or fifth day prior [to the ceremony]— one should cast five threads, each measuring five cubits, across the interior of the fire-pavilion (*vahni-maṇḍapa*) in the order from east to west, and then in the order from south to north.
One should drop eleven lines at intervals of twelve finger-breadths; by this, forty squares are formed.
One should erase four paths outside of them.
As for the method of erasure: first, one path consisting of four squares in the east, and then—
One should erase another [line] consisting of eight squares in the south, another consisting of four squares in the west, another consisting of eight squares in the north, and yet another.
Then, one should again erase two paths consisting of two squares each on the eastern and western sides of the inner group of four.
By that, three sets of four squares remain within the mandala.
Then, one should color each of the twelve squares situated in those three sets of four squares with powders, beginning with white.
Therein, in the square of Vāyu [the northwest], it is white; in that of Agni [the southeast], yellow; in that of Nairṛti [the southwest], reddish-brown; and in that of Īśāna [the northeast], black.
Then, one should fill the paths (vīthī) that have been wiped with dark-blue [pigment].
In those squares, there should be *pālikās*, five-mouthed vessels (*pañcamukhī*), and bowls (*śarāva*), which have been well-washed and wrapped with a triple-stranded thread.
Filled respectively with dry cow-dung powder,
sand, and earth, having the forms of Hari, Brahmā, and Rudra, black in color and free from wounds or other defects,
[these are placed] in each of the four squares starting from the southwest corner and ending at the northeast corner, proceeding in order from the west.
One should establish them.

Then, having meditated upon and invoked Viṣṇu in the four *pālikās* in the western direction, Brahmā in the four *pālikās* in the center, and Rudra in the four *śarāvas* in the east, one should worship them.

Then, with the mantra *vaṃ*, and for the sake of Viṣṇu with the mantra *oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya*, one should wash the seeds with milk and water; over the seeds, one should recite the seed-mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, one should place Skanda upon the *kaṅku* grain, Vāyu upon the *niṣpāva*, Agni upon the *kulattha*, Nirṛti upon the *āḍhakī*, and [Varuṇa] upon the *mudga*.

Having worshipped Soma in sesame seeds, Vaivasvata in Śāli rice, Prajāpati in mustard seeds, Ananta in Śyāmāka grains, Sūrya in Māṣa beans, and Varuṇa in [other] grains, and having mixed those seeds together, one should worship Soma therein while facing either the east or the north.

"Oṃ, salutation again and again to the one who possesses the three five-fold bodies, to the all-pervading Śaṅkara and Śiva, the preeminent lord of all worlds, the eternal. With this mantra, one should scatter seeds into those vessels.
Then, one should sprinkle those vessels with water mixed with turmeric powder and water mixed with fragrant substances.
One should perform the sprinkling with the aforementioned types of water and the worship of Soma every day until the day of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*).
Then, having covered those vessels with three new cloths, one should offer an oblation (*bali*) to the deities every night.
One should give [the offering].

There, on the first night, having offered scents and flowers with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the spirits (bhūta)," one should present the bali-offering consisting of parched grain, sesame seeds, curd, and barley flour.
Then one should perform the cleaning of the site and other preliminary rites.
On the second night, having offered scents and flowers with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the Pitṛs," one should present the bali offering consisting of rice mixed with sesame seeds.
On the third night, having offered scents and flowers with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the Yakṣas," one should present the bali offering consisting of curd, parched barley flour, and fried grain.

On the fourth night, having offered scents and flowers with the mantra "Oṃ, homage to the Nāgas," one should present the bali-offering consisting of coconut water, sugar, and flour cakes. On the fifth night, having offered scents and flowers with the mantra "Oṃ, homage to Brahmā," [one should offer] with lotus-leaves, unbroken rice grains, and raw rice.
One should offer the bali.
On the sixth night, having offered scents and flowers with "Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva," one should offer a bali of food with cakes.
On the seventh night, having offered scents and flowers with "Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu," one should offer a bali of rice mixed with jaggery.
Then, an offering (bali) consisting of milk-rice and other items should be presented to the world-protectors (lokapālas). Among them, an offering should be given to Brahmā between Īśāna and the East,
and an offering should be given to Ananta between Nairṛta and Varuṇa.
Another would not see the sprouts once they have fully grown;
one should perform rites such as pacification regarding these inauspicious sprouts—this is the "planting of sprouts."
Now follows the ritual procedure for the formal acceptance (*adhivāsa*).

Therein, first the Guru, having entered the house and made the interior well-perfumed with sandalwood, agallochum, incense, and so forth, and having destroyed the obstacles while reciting "oṃ sūryyaḥ somaḥ" and so on, should perform the installation of the water-pot (ghaṭasthāpana).
As for its sequence: "oṃ bhūrasi" is for the purification of the ground. || 1 ||
With the mantra "oṃ dhānyam asi," one should place white grain there. || 2 ||
With the mantra "Oṃ prāṇa," one should place the nine jewels within the interior of a jar measuring one cubit.
Its installation there is performed with the mantra beginning with "oṃ ājighra," and so forth. || 4 ||
The pouring of water upon the jar with the mantra "oṃ āpyāyasva" (Oṃ, may you swell). || 5 ||
Oṃ dhanna neti; with this, the placing of the branch upon it. || 6 ||
Above that, one should offer betel leaf, a bilva fruit, or a plantain fruit. || 7 ||
"Oṃ śrīśca te," with this [mantra], one offers flowers upon that. || 8 ||
Then, one should place a shallow bowl filled with rice flour and fruit upon a jar. || 9 ||
Oṃ vastram; thus [ends] the offering of cloth together with a branch of the milk-tree (kṣīraśākhin). || 10 ||
The filling of a jar with the decoction of fifty medicinal herbs from the Jambu tree. || 11 ||
The wrapping of the jar with *indravallī* [creeper]. || 12 ||
The offering of vermilion into the jar. || 13 ||
"Oṃ, be firm"—this is the stabilization of the disciple up until the point of initiation. || 14 ||
Having thus established the water-pot, and having recited "Oṃ, obeisance to the Gurus," and so forth,

and having caused the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made with "Oṃ, may there be an auspicious day for the patron," and so forth, and having performed the recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*) with "Oṃ, may there be well-being for us," [he should ward off] terrestrial obstacles with the mantra "Oṃ, phaṭ to the weapon (*astra*") by means of a divine gaze consisting of an unblinking eye-vision directed toward the four directions.

Having removed the obstacles with the mantra "oṃ bhūtāḥ pretāḥ," one should offer a bali-oblation consisting of meat, cooked rice, barley gruel, goat's ear-blood, milk, or sweet substances, and worship them with red flowers.

Then, having expelled all obstacles with a scattering of grains over which *hūṃ* has been recited seven times, one should fashion a wall of fire in the four directions with a stream of water accompanied by *raṃ*.
Then, having struck the triple *tāla* gesture upward in successive order with *vaṃ*, [one should say]: *Oṃ, homage to the Gurus.* Thus.

Having bowed to the left to the *gurupādukās*, the supreme gurus (*paramaguru*s), and the higher-lower gurus (*parāparaguru*s) in ascending order, one should bow to the right saying "Oṃ, salutation to Gaṇeśa," and in the center saying "Salutation to the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevī*).
Then, having meditated upon Gaṇeśa with the mantra beginning "Oṃ, I invoke... and having invoked him into the jar with the mantra beginning "Come, come... [one should proceed].
One should worship him with vermilion, red flowers, and other offerings.
The sequence for this is as follows: after answering the question of welcome, the offering of a seat is made.
Then, saying "Oṃ, pādya," one offers water for the feet, saying "namaḥ" (salutation) over the feet. This is the offering of the *pādya*.
Having placed the sixfold *arghya*— consisting of conch-water, *śyāmāka* grain, *dūrvā* grass, *kuśa* grass, sesame, mustard, and *aparājitā* flower, along with barley and scents— into a conch,
one offers the *arghya* upon the head with the mantra beginning with "oṃ kāṇḍāt" and ending with "svāhā."
The offering of water for sipping (ācamanīya) is performed with the *pādya* mantra.
With the words "Oṃ namaḥ," the offering of the *madhuparka*—consisting of curd, honey, and clarified butter—is given with the word "svadhā.
Again, with the root mantra, the offering of water for sipping is given with the word "svadhā."
The offering of bathing powder is made with the root mantra followed by "namaḥ.
The offering of the sacred thread is made with "oṃ yajñopavītam.
The offering of ornaments, beginning with "oṃ nānāratnaiśca," is performed.
The offering of perfume with the root mantra followed by *namaḥ*. The offering of flowers with the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*. The offering of incense with the mantra beginning *vanaspate*.

Oṃ suprakāśa—thus is the offering of the lamp. With the root mantra and the words "dīpābalibhir namaḥ," the waving of lights (nīrājana) is performed. With the root mantra and the words "nivedayāmi," the offering of food (naivedya) is presented.
Then, having performed the salutation "Obeisance to the Gurus" as previously stated,
and having thus fully worshipped Gaṇeśa,
one should worship the Sun, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Durgā in the jars in this sequence.

Then, with the mantra *oṃ phaṭ*, one should throw a handful of sesame seeds, kuśa grass, mustard seeds, and *rūpaka* stalks. Then, having recited the mantra *oṃ astrāya phaṭ* seven times, one should perform the scattering of the "dispeller of obstacles" (*vighnavināśaka*) materials consisting of parched grain, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, and *dūrvā* grass.
Then the Guru, having sat upon his own seat on the pedestal, should fashion the form with the root mantra and invoke [the deity].
Having displayed the *āvāhanī* and other mudrās, he should worship the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) beginning with the seat and ending with flowers.
Then, he should worship the limbs (*aṅga*), the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), and so forth.
The sequence for that should be sought in the *Tantrasāra*.
Then, having placed eight jars filled with decoction-water in the eight directions using the previously mentioned mantras,
one should worship them after first performing the meditation upon and invocation of the eight Mothers (*mātṛkā*).

Then, having worshipped Indra and the other world-protectors in the ten directions, as well as the eight elephants beginning with Airāvata and the weapons beginning with the thunderbolt, and having offered incense, lamps, and food offerings to one's chosen deity, one should prepare a mandala on the right side of the altar and place the vessels for the sprouts (aṅkura).

Then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) to the south and consecrated the sprouts (*aṅkura*), one should worship the deity there and offer oblations of clarified butter with the *vyāhṛtis*: "Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā," "Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā," and "Oṃ svaḥ svāhā. Thereafter, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) twenty-five times with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Having again offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* and worshipped the fire with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should dismiss the fire.
Then, one should present the *bali* offering to the attendant deities with the remaining milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Next, having lifted up the food offering (*naivedya*) and performed the cleansing of the place, one should again worship the chosen deity in the water-pot with the ten services (*daśopacāra*).
Having worshipped [the deity], one should show him a mirror, a fly-whisk, a fan, an umbrella, and betel-leaf for refreshing the mouth; then,
having recited the root mantra a thousand times and completed the recitation, one should prostrate, gratify the Brahmins,
and perform the consecration (adhivāsa) preceded by auspicious sounds, dance, and song.
Just as, with the mantra "Oṃ bhūr asi," there is the touching of clay upon the head of the disciple. || 1 ||
Oṃ gandhadvārām; thus is the perfume. 2.
Oṃ *praparvatasya*—thus [is consecrated] the stone. 3.
"Oṃ, you are grain," [with these words] he places the grain. || 4 ||
Oṃ, "From the joint," [is the mantra for] dūrvā grass. || 5 ||
Oṃ śrīścate, [this is] the flower. || 6 ||
Oṃ yāḥ kalinī, thus [is] the fruit. || 7 ||
Oṃ dadhi; thus, curd. || 8 ||
Oṃ; it is called *ghṛta* because it sustains (*dhṛtavat*). || 9 ||
Oṃ svasti na iti svastikam || 10 || "Oṃ, may there be well-being for us," thus [is] the Svastika.
Oṃ sindhoriva iti [the mantra for] vermilion. || 11 ||
"Oṃ, you are the conch," thus [he addresses] the conch. || 12 ||
Oṃ *samidhaḥ*—this refers to soot (*kajjala*). || 13 ||
Oṃ, "They yoke," is the illuminating [verse]. 14.
Oṃ anna, [this is] prepared food. || 15 ||
"Oṃ hiraṇya" [is used] for gold. || 16 ||
Oṃ, that which is characterized by form is "rūpya. || 17 ||
Oṃ asau ya iti refers to copper. 18.
"Oṃ rakṣohana" is for white mustard seeds. || 19 ||
Oṃ, with the mantra "ākṛṣṇena," [he offers] the mirror. || 20 ||
Oṃ, "The mind is the light," thus [is] the lamp. || 21 ||
Oṃ, "on the first lunar day," [this is] a Praśasta vessel. || 22 ||
One should place all of these upon the head of the disciple.

Then, having washed a new vessel with the mantra "phaṭ" and having placed ten handfuls of rice grains consecrated by the root mantra into it, one should wash the mouth of the vessel with the mantra "huṃ" and cook the *caru*.
Once the sacrificial porridge (caru) is well-cooked, one should perform the sprinkling of clarified butter over it with the Mūla-mantra.
Then, saying "Hūm," one should remove the vessel and place it upon a mandala strewn with kuśa grass, using the mantra "Phaṭ.
Having divided that caru into three parts, one should offer one portion to the deity and sacrifice another into the fire.
The teacher should eat the other portion together with the disciple.

Then, having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) upon the disciple who has sipped water and is standing before him, the teacher should give him a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) twelve finger-breadths long.

The disciple, having cleansed his teeth with that tooth-stick and washed it, should discard it. Then, the teacher should sleep for that night upon a bed of *darbha* grass on the altar together with the disciple who has performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). This is the procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*).
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Adhivāsa and Puṣpa," in the second section, the Dharmakāṇḍa, of the Śrī Prāṇatoṣiṇī.
Now begins the Initiation (Dīkṣā).
In the Viśvasāra Tantra.
Having invited the Guru, the practitioner on the following day,

according to the prescribed rule, [should honor him] with garments, ornaments, colors and the like, and with cows; then, having bathed according to the rule in a river or similar place, the best of practitioners—

In the ritual procedure of Tantric practice, such as the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and so forth, it is stated that the solar month should be mentioned at the beginning of the resolve and other rites;
this is found in the fifth chapter of the *Picchilātantra*.
Initiation is auspicious in the solar month, and not in the lunar or stellar months;
one should perform all ritual applications and the like according to the solar reckoning alone.
In the second chapter of the Viśvasāra, following the planting of the sprouts:
One should worship the Mātṛkās there, beginning with Gaurī, who are honored by all;
one should worship Gaṇeśa and the others, and say "forgive me" to ask for forgiveness.
The matrices (mātṛkā) have been explained previously.
Then the Vasordhārā offering, which destroys all obstacles, should be given;
the wise man should worship King Uparicara with supreme devotion and likewise perform the Nāndīmukha Śrāddha according to this procedure.
If the father is alive, one should perform that *śrāddha* beginning with the paternal grandfather, and likewise for the great-grandfather; thereafter,
[one performs it] for the maternal grandfather, the maternal great-grandfather, and the maternal great-great-grandfather.

O Goddess! Having worshipped those six lumps of food, the excellent practitioner should perform the śrāddha rite according to the rules, in accordance with the names and lineages [of the ancestors]. He should first perform the śrāddha for the deities, and thereafter the nāndīmukha śrāddha.
Purūravas and Mādravas are the deities for all rites;
Nāndīmukha Vasu and Satyā are proclaimed as the deities.
In the Śrāddha ceremony, one should offer water and all other items strictly according to the sequence of the deities.
As for that which is stated in the tenth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra:

O fair-faced one, in the *nāndī* or *ābhyudayika* śrāddha, one should mention the Nāndīmukha ancestors and the Nāndīmukha mothers, as well as the paternal grandfathers and others, and the maternal grandfathers and others.
Likewise:
"In that regard, first listen to the statement concerning the side of the gods, O lady of pure smiles! Having first mentioned the time and other such causal factors, thereafter—"

O Dear One! Having spoken for the sake of the prosperity resulting from those various rites, the most excellent practitioner [should perform them] for the three ancestors beginning with the father, likewise for the three beginning with the mother,
and also for the maternal grandfather and the maternal grandmother.
One should pronounce the name ending in the genitive case, preceded by the utterance of the lineage (gotra).
Then one should utter the word "śrāddham" for all the gods (viśve devāḥ),
followed by the words "aham" for the two Brahmins made of kuśa grass.

"I shall perform [the rite], O Supreme Sovereign"— this is declared to be the sentence of permission. O Pārvatī, having set aside the Viśvedevas, permission is proclaimed for the paternal side as well as for the maternal grandfather's side.
Thus, the *śrāddha* for the mother and others, as well as for the maternal grandmother and others, has been described; that refers specifically to the *śrāddha* for twelve deities (*dvādaśadaivika*).
However, the statement cited from the *Viśvasāra* refers to the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha*.
Furthermore, even that [latter] applies only to the Sāmavedins.
According to the *Ṛgveda* and *Yajurveda*, however, there is the *navadaivata* (nine-deity) *śrāddha*.

Thus, because the aforementioned authorities are seen for both the twelve-deity *abhyudayika* (prosperity) *śrāddha* and the nine-deity *śrāddha*, one may choose between them according to one's preference.
Likewise, in the Viśvasāra:
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should then declare the purpose of all the rites.
Thus concludes the Vṛddhi-śrāddha.
The worship of the five deities is also performed in that very place.

In all matters and for all undertakings, one should diligently worship Gaṇeśa first, preceded by the ritual of the water-pot (ghaṭa-pūjā); thereafter, one should worship Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Śivā, and Śiva, and finally Viṣṇu, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of every endeavor.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, and likewise Yamunā;
the guardians of the quarters, the elephants of the directions, the gods, the sages, and thereafter Vighnavāsinī and the planets;
O Pārvatī! [He should worship] the months, the zodiac signs, the lunar days, the yogas, and the karaṇas.
One should worship them with supreme devotion, together with all the Tantras.
The worship of the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and others has been previously described; their specific details, however, are to be understood from what follows.
Now, for the purpose of the worship of the planets (grahas), the mantras of the planets are first stated.
In the fourth chapter of the *Grahajāmalatantra*.

The Praṇava mounted upon Vahni (Ra), joined with Śiva (Sa) and the Moon in the mouth (Au), followed by the seventh creation of Māyā (Ha); this four-syllabled mantra of the Sun is: Oṃ Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Saḥ. || 1 ||
The Praṇava (Oṃ) with *ka* as the fourth [consonant], that mantra is endowed with the vowel and the nasal drop (*bindu*).
Mounted upon the fire of the *ha*-series and joined with the fourteenth vowel,
it is the mantra of the Moon consisting of the syllables of the Vedas, with *ra* as the sixth and the *ṣa* of creation.
The mantra, however, is: Oṃ ghauṃ srauṃ saḥ. || 2 ||
The letter *tā* (ta) mounted upon the letter *śi* (śa), joined with the letter *mukha* (ma),
enriched by the *bindu*, and encased by this [syllable], followed by *māṣāha* and so forth along with the conjunction—
this, O Goddess, is said to be the five-syllabled mantra of Bhauma (Mars).
The mantra, however, is: Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ. || 3 ||
The syllable *Tāra* mounted upon the sound (*nāda*), together with the fourth vowel and the *anusvāra*,
and the *bindu*— these two, O Goddess, consisting of five letters along with the two and four [syllables], are declared to be the mantra of Budha.
The mantra, however, is: Oṃ hrauṃ hrauṃ hrāṃ saḥ || 4 ||
*Tāra* (Om), *kadaśama* (the tenth letter, Ta), and the nasalized vowel (*anusvāra*) with the *bindu* (M)—
these three, together with the Sun (Ra) and the fourth [of the vowels] (I), constitute the five-syllabled mantra of the Guru.
The mantra, however, is: Oṃ ñauṃ ñauṃ ñauṃ saḥ. || 5 ||

O Dear One! The four-syllabled mantra of Śukra, consisting of the second [syllable] beginning with Candraja (Candra), and the third and fourth [syllables] of Dinanātha (Dina), has been declared. The mantra is: Oṃ Hrauṃ Hrīṃ Saḥ. || 6 ||
The Praṇava (Oṃ) with the fourth vowel (Au), accompanied by the anusvāra and bindu, forms two [syllables];
this pair, together with the fourth vowel of Sūrya (Ra), constitutes the four-syllabled mantra of Śani:
Oṃ Śauṃ Śauṃ Saḥ. || 7 ||

O Dear One! The mantra of Śrī Rāhu is declared to consist of four syllables: it begins with the letter 'ma' (the king of vowels), followed by the fourth vowel 'ī', and is encapsulated by the nasal bindu; then comes the sixth consonant 'kha', enriched by the nasal bindu at its mouth, followed by the eighth letter of the fourth group [the letter 'ta'], and finally the sun, which is the letter 'ra'. Thus, O Beloved, the four-syllabled mantra is proclaimed.
The mantra, however, is: Oṃ chīṃ chāṃ chauṃ saḥ. || 8 ||
The fifth letter of the vowels is *tāra* (the syllable *om*), joined with the nasal (*anusvāra*) and the sky (*nabhaḥ*, the letter *ha*).

The sixth letter of the sky (*kha*) is accompanied by the dot (*bindu*). O Maheśānī! The eighth [letter] with the dot is the fifth letter of Ketu; this is the five-syllabled mantra of Ketu, consisting of the fourth [letter] of the Sun (*sūrya*).
Manu: The mantra, however, is *oṃ phauṃ phāṃ phauṃ saḥ*. || 9 ||

As for the sequence of worship: first one should utter the mantra, then declare the substance, then the word of dedication (*sampradāna*), and after that the word consisting of renunciation (*tyāga*). According to this statement from the *Rudrayāmala*, having uttered the root mantra, [one says]: "This water for the feet (*pādya*)—Oṃ, to Sūrya, the planet..."
One should worship with "Namaḥ" and so forth.
This sequence should be understood to apply to all [deities]. In this context, their preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and so on are now written down.
As stated in the Brahmajāmalatantra, these are the words of Śiva:
But when the planet is devoid of its qualities, O Goddess—when there is affliction by disease, enemies, or the king;
when a terrible calamity befalls the kingdom; when the destruction of life approaches; when the ruin of one's lineage and the extinction of the family occur; and when total destruction is imminent.
And for the desire of wealth, sons, and so forth,
one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) with a thousand recitations for each of the ten stated years;
this is prescribed as the preliminary rite for all those who move through the sky.

One should offer oblations into the fire ten times [the number of recitations] using the best of sacrificial woods smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu). O Goddess, one should then satisfy the deity with water mixed with perfumes and camphor, according to the sequence of ten parts of that [number].
One should consecrate [the deity] with water scented with camphor in a tenth part of that [number];

and in the same sequence of tenth parts, one should provide a feast for Brahmins. At the beginning and the end, there should be a grand worship, with sacrificial fees according to one's wealth and according to the prescribed rule.
Thus concludes the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for the planets,
according to the third chapter of the Varadā Tantra.
Therefore, the practitioner must also perform the worship of the planets;
otherwise, due to the affliction of the planets, the fruit will never be attained.
For even after performing all the spiritual practices here according to the rules with devotion, one will not be a partaker of the fruits of this world without [this worship].
The Worship of the Planets:
I shall describe, in brief, the supreme accomplishment of the planets. Indeed, a day favorable to the moon and the stars should be selected by the wise.
One should worship with great effort those planets that have become malevolent;
one should cause all garments and flowers of their respective colors to be offered.
One should perform oblations according to one's capacity for the sake of attaining the desired success regarding the planets.
Having given the substances prescribed for each respective planet to those [deities], one should direct them to the twice-born [brahmins].
The granting of the planets, however, is [described] in the sixth chapter of the *Grahajāmalatantra*.
The auspicious Goddess said:
O Friend of the Wretched! O Ocean of Compassion! If you are pleased with me, then, O Lord, please graciously tell me the practice that destroys all calamities.
The Lord said:
O beloved! Just as a lamp that has received its wick and oil may be extinguished by the wind, even so occurs the destruction of life at an untimely hour.
Therefore, for the sake of averting calamities and for the cause of long life, I shall declare one essential method: one should diligently practice the giving of gifts.
O beautiful lady, he who bestows the gift of the scales (tulādāna) upon a Brahmin who is an astrologer—
He too shall be liberated from calamity and shall rejoice happily upon this earth. || 1 ||

O beloved! He who gives a balance of gold to a Brāhmaṇa presiding over a planetary rite, the preceptor of the gods, being pleased with him, increases his lifespan. And he who gives a gift of a balance of silver to a Brāhmaṇa presiding over a planetary rite—
Being satisfied with him, Śukra, being pleased, would grant him long life. || 2 ||
O Pārvatī, he who gives a balance made of copper to a Brāhmaṇa who is a planet-worshipper—Maṅgala, being well-pleased, indeed grants him long life. (3)
O Dear One, if one gives whatever [is desired] to a Brāhmaṇa who is a planet-possessor and is of bilious temperament (pittala),
then Budha, being pleased with him, shall bestow longevity, nourishment, and great dignity.
To him who gives a balance of iron to a Brahmin who is a planet-worshipper,
the pleased Śanaiścara bestows abundant longevity.
O beloved! To him who gives a *tulā* of lead to a Brāhmaṇa who is an astrologer, Rāhu, being well-pleased, swiftly bestows good fortune and long life.
O beautiful one, if someone gives a skull as a gift equal in weight to a householder Brahmin,
the blessed Ketu, being well-pleased, shall increase his life-span with happiness.
O beautiful one, he who gives a balance of copper to a brahmin afflicted by a planetary affliction,
the Sun-god becomes well-pleased with him and bestows long life.
O beautiful one, to him who gives a balance made of bell-metal to a Brahmin astrologer,
the Lord of Night (the Moon), being well-pleased, bestows prosperity and long life.
O beloved! One should give to a Brahmin and wear upon one's own hand the lapis lazuli, the sapphire, the ruby, the emerald, the diamond, the coral, the go-meda, and likewise the emerald.
Thus concludes the gift for the planets.
Now follows the armor of the planets (grahakavaca).
In the eighteenth chapter.
Pārvatī said: O Śrī Īśāna! O Knower of all scriptures! O Lord of the deities! O Sovereign!
O All-pervading One! [Please grant] the divine, imperishable armor [protecting against] the planets and other celestial bodies.
This secret, which was previously indicated, brings about imperishable merit for those who possess true devotion.
If you have compassion for me, O illustrious Maheśvara, please speak!
The illustrious Śiva said:

Listen, O Goddess, my most beloved! To this armor, difficult even for the gods to obtain, by wearing which all the deities became immortal, O fair-faced one! Out of affection for you, I shall speak it; it must not be given to just anyone.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ soḥ, may the illustrious Sun, the lord of planets, protect my head. Oṃ ghrauṃ sauṃ oṃ, may the illustrious Moon, the king of planets, protect my face.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrāṃ saḥ, may Mars, the commander of the planetary army, protect my two hands.
May *hrauṃ hrāṃ saḥ* protect the two feet; may *jña*, the prince, protect the feet. (p.
240) May *oṃ ñauṃ ñauṃ ñauṃ saḥ* protect the waist; may he who is worshipped by the immortals protect [it].
May *oṃ hrauṃ hrīṃ so*, who is worshipped by the Daityas, thoroughly protect the heart.

Oṃ śauṃ śauṃ saḥ! May Śanaiścara, the servant of the planets, protect my navel. Oṃ chauṃ chāṃ chauṃ saḥ! May the illustrious Rāhu, the crusher of gods, protect the region of my throat. Oṃ phauṃ phāṃ phauṃ saḥ! May Ketu, the crested one, protect my entire body; may he guard me on all sides.
These planets, which are the bodies of experience, are indeed eternal, yet their manifested forms are subject to change.
May those born from the minute portions of these [planets] protect me eternally from the wicked.
This meritorious, inexhaustible armor has the Sun and other planets as its presiding deities.
The person who, being pure, either recites this, causes it to be recited, or retains it in memory, shall attain their desired success, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Out of affection for you, I have spoken this which brings about the welfare of the world.
Bhairava is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra], and Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed as its meter (chandas).
The deities (devatās) therein are proclaimed to be the auspicious planets, beginning with the Sun.
For the complete attainment of all desires and goals, the application (viniyoga) has been declared by me.
Having constructed it together with the planetary yantras, one shall obtain one's desired goal inexhaustibly.
Thus ends the armor-yantra named "Inexhaustible and Hard to Obtain in the World," from the *Grajamālā*, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara.
Now follows the worship of the lunar days (tithis).
In the Gāyatrī Tantra,
the illustrious Mahādeva said:

O Goddess! O Supreme Sovereign! For one who performs the daily rites without knowing the lunar day (tithi), its meditative absorption (dhyāna), and likewise its mantra, all that daily ritual activity shall become fruitless, O fair-faced one.
That lunar day (tithi) is Mahāmāyā, the primordial form who pervades the universe;
in the dark fortnight she is black in color, and in the bright fortnight she has a radiance like the moon.
She is two-armed, white in appearance, and moves with the playful gait of a wagtail.
She has two eyes, wears a digit of the moon, and is radiant with a vermilion tilaka;
she is adorned with various ornaments fashioned from molten gold,
and is beautiful with the luster of teeth resembling pomegranate seeds.
One should meditate upon the Goddess at every step for the purification of recitation and worship.
The mantra is as follows:
*grīṃ* to the first days of the lunar fortnights, *svāhā*! (1)
Thus, she has two eyes, a crescent moon, and is as beautiful as pure crystal;
she is enriched with the splendor of pure ornaments, draped in white garments,
and graced by creeper-like eyebrows joined with various sidelong glances.

O lovely-limbed one! Having meditated upon the second [form], who is radiant with a vermilion tilaka, whose eyes are tremulous like those of a wagtail, two-armed, beautiful of body, a young maiden in the bloom of fresh youth— listen now to how you should recite the mantra.
Aiṃ, svāhā to the second [digit]. || 2 ||
Resembling a white lotus, draped in white garments,
and enriched with the splendor of white ornaments, she stands upon a white lotus;
she has two eyes, possesses the crescent moon, and is radiant with a tilaka mark of vermilion.
One should worship the third [form], who has two arms and is endowed with side-glances as her arrows:
Oṃ Aiṃ, svāhā to the Third! || 3 ||
Having known her, who is the fourth [form], beautiful-limbed and white, one attains perfection—
she who has the luster of a *kunda* flower, possesses two arms and tremulous eyes,
is clothed in white garments, and is adorned with white ornaments.
She was radiant with a tilaka of vermilion, and her eyes were like those of a wagtail.
Aiṃ Huṃ, svāhā to Caturthī. || 4 ||
O lady of beautiful limbs! Listen now to the fifth [tithi], which bestows all perfections;
by knowing it, O Supreme Goddess, one shall obtain the fruit of the lunar day.
Resembling pure crystal, seated upon a white lotus,
endowed with a smile and a serene countenance, radiant with the arrows of her sidelong glances,
and graced by creeper-like eyebrows shaped like the bow of Kandarpa.
Having two arms, white in color, and adorned with white ornaments.
Adorned with two eyes, radiant with a tilaka mark of vermilion,
graced by vine-like arms resembling lotus stalks,
possessing the gait of a playful wagtail, and resplendent with a beautiful crest;
Hrīṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ, svāhā to Pañcamī. Hrīṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ, this is the special [mantra].
On the day of Śrīpañcamī, the great worship must be performed.
Having gazed upon the Lord of the South (Dakṣiṇanātha), one should perform meditation, worship, and so forth;
one should meditate with supreme effort upon her who has the form of the fifth lunar day (Pañcamī).
Having meditated and offered water for the feet and other offerings, one should mutter the mantra ten times.
Then one should worship the Goddess Śāradā, who delights in speech.
Resembling a *kundapuṣpa* flower in luster, she has two arms and tremulous eyes;
she is radiant with the arrows of her sidelong glances and brilliant with a vermilion tilaka;
she possesses the brilliant radiance of teeth resembling pomegranate seeds.
For the sake of one's own spiritual power, one should meditate upon her who is beautiful with white ornaments, who dwells upon a white seat,
who is arrayed in white garments,
who delights in white necklaces, who has two arms, and whose face is like the moon.
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī. || 6 ||
Resembling the autumnal moon, with two arms and the moon as her crest-jewel,
endowed with two eyes, she moves with the playful gait of a khañjana bird;
she is radiant with a vermilion tilaka and her eyes are adorned with collyrium.

One should meditate upon her for the sake of one's own spiritual power— she who is endowed with side-glances as her arrows, adorned with creeper-like eyebrows, seated upon a white throne, decorated with white ornaments, and clothed in white garments.
Hrīṃ oṃ, svāhā to Saptamī; oṃ hrīṃ. || 7 ||
Resembling the full moon, she has two arms and bears the moon upon her crest;
her face is like a row of full moons, adorned with curling locks of hair;
she is endowed with a smile, possesses a gracious countenance, and is clothed in white garments.
Abundantly adorned with the splendor of white ornaments, she is a young maiden in the bloom of fresh youth;
she is endowed with flower garlands and side-long glances, graced by creeper-like eyebrows,
radiant with a vermilion tilaka mark, and her eyes are anointed with collyrium.
KṚĪṂ HŪṂ AIṂ AṢṬAMYAI SVĀHĀ AIṂ HŪṂ KṚĪṂ || 8 ||
Resembling a white lotus, with two arms and tremulous eyes,
her row of teeth is as bright as pomegranate seeds;
she wears garments of white silk and has a white cloth as an upper garment.
On her forehead she wears a pure fillet, radiant with a mark of vermilion;
her limbs shine with various ornaments and are anointed with yellow sandalwood paste;
her conch-like neck is beautified by a pearl necklace that curls like a whirlpool.
Adorned with various garlands and resplendent with diverse royal ornaments:
Oṃ hūṃ, svāhā to the Ninth One, hūṃ oṃ! 9.
Resembling a *mallikā* flower, with two arms and tremulous eyes, seated upon a white throne, draped in white garments,
adorned with white ornaments, and anointed with white perfumes.
She was radiant with a tilaka of vermilion, and her eyes were adorned with collyrium.
Aiṃ Oṃ, svāhā to the tenth [tithi], Oṃ Aiṃ. 10.
Resembling a *ketakī* flower, adorned with creeper-like eyebrows,
endowed with various side-long glances, moving with the gait of an elephant in rut,
beautiful with diverse ornaments, and clothed in yellow garments.

I bow to the beautiful two-armed goddess for the sake of my own spiritual prosperity— she whose limbs are smeared with yellow sandalwood paste, who is radiant with a tilaka mark of vermilion, and who possesses a most excellent row of teeth resembling pomegranate seeds.
Oṃ krīṃ oṃ, svāhā to Ekādaśī! Oṃ krīṃ oṃ. || 11 ||
Resplendent with the luster of a yellow lotus, draped in white garments,
her limbs anointed with white sandalwood paste, she has two arms and tremulous eyes;
she is enriched by the beauty of white ornaments and rests upon a white seat.
To her whose splendor is beautified by teeth resembling pomegranate seeds, whose auspicious forehead-plate is illuminated by a mark of vermilion:
Hrīṃ Oṃ Hrīṃ, Svāhā to the Twelfth! Hrīṃ Oṃ Hrīṃ. 12.
Resembling a red moon, a young maiden in the bloom of fresh youth,
clad in red garments and adorned with curling locks of hair;
two-armed, beautiful, pure, and possessing the radiance of a full moon’s face.
She has two eyes and the crescent moon [upon her brow], is worshipped by Viṣṇu, and possesses broad hips; she is radiant with a tilaka of vermilion, her eyes are adorned with collyrium,
she is endowed with various side-long glances, and she is beautified by manifold amorous charms.
Having meditated upon the thirteenth goddess, one should recite the supreme mantra.
Oṃ aiṃ, svāhā to the Thirteenth [Tithi], aiṃ oṃ. || 13 ||
Resembling pure crystal, delighting in green garments,
beautiful with various ornaments, adorned with yellow garlands and raiment,
seated upon a white lotus, two-armed, and with tremulous eyes.
She is radiant with the arrows of her sidelong glances, brilliant with a tilaka mark of vermilion,
and glowing with the luster of teeth resembling pomegranate seeds;
she is enchanting with a pair of breasts shaped like *kadamba* buds.
She was endowed with a smile, possessed a serene countenance, and was a young maiden in the bloom of fresh youth.
KṚĪM OṂ HRĪṂ CATURDAŚYAI SVĀHĀ HRĪṂ OṂ KṚĪM || 14 ||
In the seventh chapter.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
