Listen, O lady of beautiful limbs, to [the description of] Pūrṇimā, by whom one becomes filled with spiritual perfection (siddhi):
she has the form of ten million streaks of lightning, is endowed with four arms, is clothed in yellow garments, and is resplendent with necklaces of jewels.
Adorned with various ornaments such as anklets, bracelets,
and armlets, her cheeks were made enchanting by shimmering jeweled earrings;
she possessed a graceful form with the three-fold bend (tribhaṅga) and was radiant with a vermilion tilaka.
Adorned with hundreds of thousands of sidelong glances and graced by creeper-like eyebrows.
Hrīṃ oṃ krīṃ oṃ, svāhā to Pūrṇimā; oṃ krīṃ oṃ hrīṃ. || 15 ||
This, O Goddess, has been told to you—the supreme mantra beyond the supreme.
These lunar days (tithis), O Goddess of beautiful countenance, are auspicious in the bright fortnight;
and in the dark fortnight, O Maheśānī, these lunar days are likewise most excellent.
The young maidens, resembling heaps of blue collyrium and in the bloom of fresh youth—their meditation I shall now describe; listen attentively.
Resembling crushed collyrium, she was clothed in yellow garments;
her limbs were anointed with yellow perfumes and adorned with yellow ornaments;
seated upon a yellow lotus, she was a young maiden in the bloom of fresh youth.
She has two eyes, a crescent moon [on her forehead], two arms, and breasts like flower buds.
Her forehead-slab is pure and radiant with a tilaka of vermilion;
she moves with the gait of a playful wagtail, her form graced by the three-fold bend (tribhaṅgi);
and she shines with the brilliance of teeth resembling the seeds of a pomegranate.
O Maheśānī! During the dark fortnight, this meditation is praised.
O Parameśānī! O beloved! By means of this single [meditation], [the goal] for all [deities] is attained.
O Śivā! For all [of them], the mantra is as before, except on the new moon day (amāvāsyā).
O Goddess, O lady of excellent complexion! Listen now to the mantra for the new moon day (Amāvāsyā).
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ oṃ, svāhā to Amāvāsyā; oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ oṃ.
Now, O fair-faced one, I shall explain the meditation on the wings along with its fruit.
Resplendent like a conch shell or a jasmine flower, endowed with fresh youth,
four-armed and three-eyed, she moves with the gait of an elephant in rut;
upon the middle of her forehead rests a tilaka mark of vermilion.
Her eyes were dark as collyrium and shone like wandering bees;
she was clothed in yellow garments with a black upper robe;
beautiful with various ornaments, she sat upon a blue lotus.
Her eyes were rolling, and she held a blue lotus;
she was eternally sixteen years of age, with breasts like *kadamba* buds,
and radiant with the brilliance of teeth resembling the luster of diamonds.
Every day, one should meditate upon the Goddess, who embodies the nature of the bright fortnight, as being composed of various flowers and supreme with various fragrances.
Aiṃ aiṃ krīṃ krīṃ, svāhā to the bright fortnight; aiṃ aiṃ krīṃ krīṃ.
O Maheśānī! Now, during the dark fortnight, I shall describe her to you:
she is as dark as a great emerald, endowed with four arms, possessing full and lofty breasts, beautiful, and delighting in variegated garments.
Richly adorned with various elegant ornaments, her eyes quivering and startled,
radiant with a tilaka of vermilion and her eyes anointed with collyrium,
she was graced by creeper-like eyebrows shaped like the bow of Kandarpa.
Adorned with a necklace of jewels together with a serpent-necklace,
seated upon a yellow lotus, resplendent with a variegated crest,
and possessing the hue of a yellow lightning bolt as the color of her upper garment;
The Goddess with a face like the full moon, whose nature is that of the dark fortnight.
Oṃ oṃ, svāhā to the dark fortnight! Oṃ oṃ.
The illustrious Śiva said:

O Goddess! for that wise person who day after day performs the meditation on the lunar day (tithi) along with its mantra, as well as the meditation on the fortnight (pakṣa) and likewise the mantra of the fortnight,
success is not far off.
O Goddess! These lunar days (tithis), however, are situated within the solar disc.
O Beloved! First comes the meditation on the fortnight (pakṣa), and after that, the meditation on the lunar day (tithi).
Having then recited the mantra of the fortnight, one should thereafter recite the mantra of the lunar day.

(245) Thereafter, one attains success (*siddhi*) in whatever [practice] there may be, such as recitation (*japa*) and worship (*pūjā*). O Maheśānī! He who performs the daily duty day after day shall attain success after first performing the fortnightly worship (*pakṣapūjā*).
O Goddess, without the worship of the lunar day (tithi), all rites such as recitation (japa) and sacrifice (yajña) become fruitless,
like an unbaked clay vessel in water.
Day after day, O Goddess, having diligently reached the specific lunar day (tithi),
the wise one should then perform the meditation on that lunar day during the morning hours. Having beheld the Sun with effort, he should recite the mantra ten times.
Then, having obtained the fruit of the lunar day (tithi), one attains the entire fruit of worship.
Without knowing this truth, life passes away day by day.
The Great Goddess, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), who consists of the universe, is the very form of the lunar day.

O Goddess! Without the mantra of meditation, [the practice] destroys the spiritual attainments of all. O Beloved! He who performs japa and meditation every day obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā; of this there is no doubt.

O beloved! If Vyāsa were the Hotṛ priest at the great Aśvamedha sacrifice, that Aśvamedha would indeed be fruitless without the meditation on the lunar day (tithi). O Kṛṣṇe! By means of nectar, the deities are pleased in their proper order.
Fire drinks the first digit, the Sun drinks the second;
the Viśvedevas drink the third, and Prajāpati drinks the fourth. Varuṇa drinks the fifth, and Vāsava drinks the sixth.

The divine sages drink the seventh digit; likewise, the eight Vasus drink the eighth. Indra drinks even the ninth digit of the dark fortnight, and the Maruts drink the tenth, while Rudra drinks the eleventh digit.
Viṣṇu drinks the twelfth digit, and Dhanada the thirteenth;
Paśupati constantly drinks the fourteenth digit,
and thereafter the ancestors drink the fifteenth digit as well.
Now, the Armor of the Lunar Days (*Tithi-kavaca*).
Of this Armor of the Lunar Days, the seers (*ṛṣis*) are Aśvatthāman, Bali, Vyāsa, Hanumān, Vibhīṣaṇa, Kṛpa, and Paraśurāma;
the meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī; the deity (*devatā*) is the illustrious Śiva Mṛtyuñjaya; and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
May the eternal Krīṅkārī, the first lunar day (pratipad), protect me in the east forever;
may the eternal Klīṅkārī, worshipped by Brahmā, protect me on the second day;
may the eternal Aiṅkārī protect me on the third day; and may the supreme Vluṅkārī protect me on the fourth day in the west.
Worshipped by Viṣṇu,
may Vlūṅkārī protect my upper body day and night;
may Hrīṅkārī, the fifth [goddess], protect my face forever.
May Pārvatī in the form of the sixth [vowel], Śrīṅkārī, protect me eternally;
may Strīṅkārī, the seventh, eternally protect the region of my navel;
and may Huṃkārī, the eighth, always protect my throat.
May Śrīṅkārī, the ninth [tithi], always protect my Svādhiṣṭhāna;
may the tenth protect my pair of hands, both right and left, forever;
and may the eleventh always protect my pair of eyes day and night.
May Dvādaśī protect my two hands always, in whatever manner they may be; may Trayodaśī Mahālakṣmī, who dwells in sacred sites, protect me;
and may Trayodaśī, whose essence consists of the syllable "haṃsa," protect me always.
May the syllable *Haṃ* protect my pair of feet constantly, day and night; may the syllable *Saḥ* protect from the tips of my feet up to the circle of my hair;
may Mahāmāyā, who is the fourteenth [tithi], protect me everywhere.

The syllable *svā* is the fourteenth lunar day (*caturdaśī-nityā*), which constantly bestows upon me an abundance of wealth. The syllable *hā* is the full moon (*pūrṇimā-nityā*), O Goddess, which constantly increases my lifespan.
*Śrīṃ huṃ hrīṃ svāhā*—may the Goddess of all forms, who embodies the lunar days, protect me at all times.
Huṃ hrīṃ! May Amāvāsyā always protect my wife, sons, and attendants.
Hrīṃ huṃ hrīṃ svāhā! O Goddess, this armor (kavaca) has been declared; it is difficult to find even throughout the three worlds.
He who recites another armor without knowing this armor [is ignorant].
This lunar day (tithi) also robs the splendors of other armor-protective mantras;
therefore, O Goddess, one should recite the armor-mantra of the lunar days with great effort.
O Beloved! One should likewise recite the meditation, the mantra, the hymn, and the armor-mantra.
O Goddess! The doctrine of the Kali Age has emerged as the supreme reality. Thus, O Goddess, I have told you that which is the essence of essences, higher than the highest.
Thus ends the *Tithi-kavaca* (the Armor of the Lunar Days) within the *Śrī-Varṇavilāsa-tantra*, in the dialogue between Gaṇeśa and Jātūkarṇa concerning the auspicious [days].
The meditation on the months and so forth should be sought in the *Kāmadhenu-tantra* and other such works; it is not written here for fear of making this treatise too voluminous.
Now, the meditation and so forth of the phonemes are as taught in the *Varṇoddhāra-tantra*,
while the mantra of salutation is, in all cases, as taught in the *Kāmadhenu-tantra*.
It is as follows:
Having the luster of the interior of a *ketakī* flower, two-armed, with eyes like those of a swan,
wearing white silk garments, adorned with lotus garlands,
the supreme goddess who eternally bestows the four aims of life and consists of perpetual bliss.

Having thus meditated upon the Goddess, who displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness and is endowed with a serpent-noose, one should recite her mantra, beginning with the syllable *A*, ten times: *A*.
I shall now describe her meditation: she has six arms and red eyes;
her body is radiant with jewels, bracelets, armlets, and necklaces;
she is perfected, the bestower of perfection, gentle, and served by Siddhas and Gandharvas.
Having meditated thus upon the most excellent of goddesses, one should recite her mantra ten times. Āḥ.
Smoky-colored, most fierce, clad in yellow garments,
supreme, the granter of desires, the bestower of success, gentle, ever-increasing one's enthusiasm,
four-armed, granting boons, and adorned with yellow sandalwood paste.
Having meditated thus upon her in the form of Brahmā, one should recite her mantra ten times. ||i||
Four-armed, red in color, adorned with red flowers,
her limbs smeared with beautiful sandalwood paste, her eyes like red lotuses,
dressed in red garments, she is the bestower of dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
Having meditated thus upon the supreme goddess, one should recite her mantra ten times. ॐ.
Having thus meditated upon the supreme goddess— the yellow-colored one with three eyes, wearing yellow garments,
two-armed, with matted hair, formidable, and the bestower of all siddhis—
one should recite her mantra ten times. ||u||
She has two arms, is white in complexion, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair;
she wears white garlands and garments, is embellished with beautiful sandalwood paste,
is the eternal bestower of the four aims of life, and has eyes like red lotuses.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the recitation of that mantra ten times. || Ū ||

The supreme Goddess has six arms and is blue in color; she wears blue garments, is enriched with various ornaments, and her head is adorned with every decoration. She is the Blessed Lady who bestows devotion and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having meditated thus upon the most excellent of goddesses, one should recite her mantra ten times.
I bow to the syllable *Ṛ*, which consists of the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*), likewise consists of the four gnoses (*jñāna*), and has the form of a red streak of lightning. *Ṛ*.
I shall describe his meditation: [the goddess] with two arms and lotus-eyes,
possessing the luster of molten gold, adorned with all ornaments,
the goddess with eyes like red lotuses, and decorated with necklaces of jewels.
Having meditated thus upon the most excellent of goddesses, one should recite her mantra ten times.
"I always bow to the syllable consisting of the four gnoses, ever composed of the five vital breaths, and endowed with the three powers, O Dear One! (Ṛ)."

I perpetually bow to the Goddess, who has the hue of a golden campaka flower, whose form is adorned with golden ornaments, who possesses four arms and three eyes, who is anointed with red sandalwood paste, and who bestows virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation.
Having meditated thus upon her in the form of Brahman, one should recite her mantra ten times. Ḷī ||
I shall now describe her meditation: she is yellow in color, four-armed,
clothed in yellow garments, with various ornaments upon her head,
adorned with diverse garlands and jewelry, and served by gods and demons.
Having thus meditated upon her who bestows the fourfold aims of life, who is eternal, and who increases perpetual enthusiasm—one whose form is Brahman—one should recite her mantra ten times. Ḷḷ ||
Clad in red garments, six-armed, and with red eyes;
adorned with various ornaments, eternal, and the bestower of the four aims of life;
her face slightly smiling, gentle, and served by gods and gandharvas.
Having meditated thus upon her form as Brahmā, one should recite her mantra ten times. || e ||
The goddess of manifold forms, wearing variegated garments,
adorned with diverse garlands and ornaments, and endowed with four arms.
Adorned with various ornaments and bestowing the fruits of the four aims of life, she is served by gods, demons, and celestial musicians who long for liberation.
Having thus meditated upon her as the embodiment of Brahman, one should recite her mantra ten times. Ai.
Adorned with jewel ornaments, auspicious with the luster of rubies,
her face like the full autumn moon, clothed in variegated garments,
four-armed, three-eyed, with a smiling countenance and dark blue locks of hair.
I worship her whose limbs are like streaks of lightning and who wears a garland of pearl strings;
having thus meditated upon her as the embodiment of Brahman, one should recite her mantra ten times. ||o||
Four-armed, three-eyed, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
beautified by garlands of white, red, yellow, and other flowers,
always smiling, gentle, and the bestower of the four aims of human existence.
Having meditated thus upon her form as Brahmā, one should recite her mantra ten times. Auṃ.
She has the luster of a fresh pomegranate flower, possesses two arms, and has red eyes;
she is clothed in red garments and adorned with red ornaments.
She bestows the four aims of human life, is gentle, grants boons, and has a serpent as her crest-ornament.
Having meditated thus upon her in the form of Brahman, one should recite her mantra ten times: Aṃ.
She has the luster of molten gold, is adorned with every ornament,
wears a sacred thread of jewels, and is resplendent with jeweled bracelets;
her face is like the full moon, she is gentle, and her fourth hand is joined [in the gesture of granting boons].

Having thus meditated upon her who is of the nature of Brahmā, endowed with three eyes in the form of the moon, sun, and fire— the eternal one who grants the desires of the practitioner and bestows virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation— one should recite her mantra ten times: *Aḥ*.
The supreme beloved, resembling the Javā flower, liquid lac, and vermilion,
four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with creeper-like arms,
and graced by a pair of breasts shaped like Kadamba buds.
Having thus meditated upon the letter *Ka*, adorned with jeweled bracelets, armlets, necklaces, and anklets, one should recite its mantra ten times. *Ka*.

Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Goddess— who resembles the *bandhūka* flower, is adorned with jewel ornaments, holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, is eternal, and has a slightly smiling face— one should recite her mantra ten times while focusing on the syllable *kha*.
O Goddess! I bow to the syllable *kha*, which is always endowed with the three qualities (*guṇas*), consists of the five deities, and is joined with the three powers. *Kha*.
Having thus meditated upon the eternal [Goddess] who resembles the pomegranate flower, possesses four arms,
wears red garments, and is adorned with red ornaments,
one should recite her mantra ten times while focusing on the syllable *ga*.
O Dear One! I bow down to Kuṇḍalinī, who consists of the five vital breaths, whose nature is all powers, and who resembles the rising sun. (Ga)
She has the luster and color of a *mālatī* flower, possesses six arms, and has red eyes;
she is clothed in white garments and adorned with white garlands;
at that time, she is lovely, with a smiling face and graced by three eyes.
Having meditated thus, one should recite that mantra beginning with the letter *gha* ten times:
"I bow to the letter *gha*, which is devoid of qualities yet endowed with the three qualities, eternally joined with the triple sphere (*trigola*), all-pervading, and ever peaceful. *Gha*.
Having thus meditated upon her who is smoke-colored, most terrible, with a lolling tongue and four arms,
clad in yellow garments, and the bestower of the desired accomplishments of the practitioner—
one whose form is Brahman— one should recite her mantra ten times.
O lady of tremulous eyes, I bow to the syllable *ṅa*, which consists of all the gods, possesses the three qualities (*guṇas*), and is composed of the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*). Ṅa.
She has the luster of snow and the kunda flower, is adorned with various ornaments,
is eternally sixteen years of age, and is the supreme goddess who displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
her waist is draped in white garments, and she wears a white upper cloth.
Having thus meditated upon her as the bestower of boons, beautiful, delightful, and endowed with eight arms, one should recite her mantra ten times. || Ca ||
I shall describe her meditation: she has two arms and three eyes, wears yellow garments, is eternal, bestows boons, and is affectionate toward her devotees.
Having meditated thus, one should recite her mantra, beginning with the letter *cha*, ten times.
I bow to the syllable *cha*, which is endowed with three dots (*bindu*), eternally united with the Lord (*Īśvara*), and having the form of a streak of yellow lightning. *Cha*.
She is endowed with two arms adorned with various ornaments;
her limbs are smeared with red sandalwood paste, and she wears variegated garments.
She has three eyes, is the sustainer of the world, the bestower of boons, and is affectionate toward her devotees.
Having meditated thus, one should recite that mantra beginning with the letter *ja* ten times: *ja*.
The supreme goddess has the luster of molten gold, is adorned with red garments,
her limbs are smeared with red sandalwood paste, and she is decorated with red garlands;
she possesses fourteen arms and is radiant with necklaces of jewels.
Having meditated thus, one should recite that mantra beginning with the letter *jha* ten times. *Jha*.
Four-armed, smoke-colored, adorned with black garments,
endowed with various ornaments, and resplendent with a crown of matted hair;
her face bears a slight smile, she is eternal, the bestower of boons, and affectionate toward her devotees.
Having meditated thus, one should recite that mantra beginning with the letter *ña* ten times. *Ña*.
Resembling the *mālatī* and *kunda* flowers, with eyes like the full moon,
endowed with ten arms, adorned with all ornaments,
the eternal bestower of supreme liberation, whose face is always smiling— the Supreme Goddess.
Having meditated thus, one should recite that mantra ten times, beginning with the letter *ṭa*: *ṭaṃ*.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess— who resembles the full moon, whose eyes are like blooming lotuses,
who is beautiful, possesses sixteen arms, and bestows virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation—
one should recite her mantra, the syllable *Ṭha*, ten times. *Ṭha*.

Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Goddess— who resembles saffron and vermilion, who displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who is three-eyed, the eternal bestower of boons, and the giver of supreme liberation— one should recite her mantra, beginning with the letter *ḍa*, ten times.
I bow to the syllable *Ḍa*, which consists of the four gnoses, is endowed with the reality of the self and other principles, and has the form of a yellow flash of lightning. *Ḍa*.
Having thus meditated upon her— who resembles a red lotus, who is beautiful, whose eyes are like red lotuses,
who has eighteen arms, who is formidable, and who bestows great liberation—
one should recite that mantra beginning with the letter *ḍha* ten times.

I bow to the syllable *Ḍha*, which is eternally joined with the three qualities (*triguṇa*), eternally consisting of the primordial principle (*āditattva*), and having the form of a streak of red lightning. Ḍha.

Having thus meditated upon her— who has two arms, who bestows boons, who is worthy of worship, who grants the desires of her devotees, who has lotus-like eyes, who is eternal, and who bestows virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation— one should recite that mantra beginning with the letter *ṇa* ten times. *ṇa*.
Four-armed, supremely peaceful, and the bestower of great liberation;
eternally sixteen years of age, wearing red garments, the supreme goddess adorned with various ornaments, the giver of all accomplishments.
Having meditated thus, one should recite that mantra ten times, beginning with the syllable *ta*: *ta*.
Having thus meditated upon the supreme goddess— who is blue in color, three-eyed, six-armed, bestowing boons,
clad in yellow garments, and always granting spiritual accomplishments—
one should recite the mantra of the letter *Tha* ten times.
I bow to the syllable *tha*, which consists of the five deities, which always consists of the five vital breaths, and which resembles the rising sun. *Tha*.
Having thus meditated upon her who has four arms, is clad in yellow garments, is established in the bloom of youth,
and is adorned with necklaces and anklets fashioned from many jewels—
one should recite that mantra, beginning with the syllable *da*, ten times.

O Goddess! I bow to the letter *da*, which is always accompanied by the three powers (*triśakti*), endowed with the three points (*tribindu*), and joined with the principles beginning with the Self (*ātmatattva*). Da.

Having thus meditated upon the supreme goddess— who has six arms, the color of a cloud, wears red garments, bestows boons, grants auspiciousness, is beautiful, and bestows the four aims of human life— one should recite her mantra, beginning with the letter *Dha*, ten times. *Dha*.
Having the luster of crushed collyrium, with a protruding tongue and beautiful eyes,
four-armed, with eyes like those of the cakora bird, anointed with lovely sandalwood paste,
clad in black garments, and always possessing a slightly smiling face.
Having meditated thus, one should recite that mantra beginning with the syllable "Na" ten times: Na.
The goddess has diverse garments, two arms, and lotus-like eyes;
her limbs are smeared with red sandalwood paste, and she is adorned with garlands of lotuses. Her form is graced by armlets and necklaces made of jewels and gems.
Having thus meditated upon the syllable *pa*, which bestows the fourfold aims, is eternal, consists of perpetual bliss, and is supreme, one should recite its mantra ten times: *pa*.
Having thus meditated upon her— who has the hue of a cloud at the time of universal dissolution, whose tongue is lolling, who possesses four arms,
who eternally bestows fearlessness upon her devotees, and who is adorned with various ornaments—
one should mutter the mantra of the letter *pha* ten times: *pha*.
She is blue in color, has three eyes, wears blue garments, and is supreme.
Having thus meditated upon the goddess— who is radiant with a serpent-necklace, two-armed, and lotus-eyed—
one should recite her mantra ten times,
beginning with the syllable *ba*, which is conjoined with the three powers (*triśakti*) and anointed with various nectars.
I myself perpetually bow down to the goddess Kuṇḍalinī. || ba ||

Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess, who possesses the luster of lightning, who is adorned with serpent-bracelets, who bestows the four aims of life, and who grants the fulfillment of the practitioner's desires— one should recite her mantra, beginning with the letter *bha*, ten times.

O Dear One! I bow to the syllable *Bha*, which is endowed with the three powers (*triśakti*), accompanied by the three points (*tribindu*), and joined with the principles beginning with the Self (*ātmatattva*). *Bha*.

Having thus meditated upon the eternal Kṛṣṇā— who is ten-armed, formidable, with yellow and red eyes, clad in black garments, and the bestower of virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation— one should recite her mantra, beginning with the syllable *ma*, ten times.
I always bow to that syllable which is endowed with the three powers, accompanied by the three points, joined with the principles beginning with the Self (ātman), and residing in the heart. Ma.
She is smoke-colored, exceedingly fierce, six-armed, and red-eyed;
she is clothed in red garments and adorned with various ornaments;
she is the eternal bestower of great liberation and the granter of the eight supernatural powers.
Having meditated thus, one should recite that mantra beginning with the letter *ya* ten times.
One should always contemplate this syllable as being endowed with the three powers (*triśakti*) and accompanied by the three dots (*tribindu*).
I perpetually bow to this syllable, which possesses power, is liberation itself, and is imperishable. *Ya*.
With a lolling tongue, she is most fierce, with a red face and red eyes;
she is red in color, possesses eight arms, and is adorned with red flowers,
wearing red garlands and garments, and decorated with red ornaments.
Having thus meditated upon her who is of the nature of Brahman— the eternal bestower of great liberation and the granter of the eight supernatural powers— one should recite her mantra ten times,
O Goddess, together with the three Śaktis and conjoined with the principles (tattvas) beginning with the Self (ātman).
I perpetually bow down to that color which consists entirely of splendor. || Ra ||
Four-armed, clad in yellow garments, with eyes like red lotuses,
always bestowing boons, formidable, adorned with all ornaments,
served by the lords of yogis, eternal, a yoginī whose very form is yoga.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess, who bestows the fourfold aims and is adorned with a serpent necklace, one should recite her mantra, beginning with the letter *la*, ten times. *La*.
The supreme goddess, possessing the luster of a *kundapuṣpa* flower, two arms, and lotus-like eyes; wearing white garlands and garments, radiant with jeweled necklaces;
the perfected one who grants the desires of practitioners, bestows success, and is served by the *siddhas*.
Having meditated thus, one should recite that mantra ending in the letter *va* ten times: *va*.
Four-armed, with eyes like those of the cakora bird, anointed with beautiful sandalwood paste,
white in complexion, three-eyed, granting boons, and possessing a pure smile;
richly adorned with jewel ornaments and graced with white garlands.
Having thus meditated upon the letter Śa—which is worshipped by hosts of gods and served by those desiring liberation—one should recite its mantra ten times: Śa.
She is clad in white garments, white in complexion, two-armed, and red-eyed;
her limbs are smeared with white sandalwood paste, and she is adorned with pearl necklaces.
She is being sung of by Gandharvas and is the supreme goddess, eternally composed of bliss.
Having thus meditated upon the letter *ṣa*, which bestows the eight siddhis, is eternal, and increases the bliss of devotees— one should recite its mantra ten times,
together with the three śaktis and conjoined with the principles (tattvas) beginning with the Self (ātman).
O Goddess! O beautiful one! Bowing down constantly, meditate [on her] within your heart. (6)
Her limbs adorned with human skulls, laughing with a boisterous laugh, she is naked and wears a garland of bones;
she has eight arms, bestows boons, and has lotus-like eyes;
she is richly decorated with necklaces of lordly serpents and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
Having thus meditated upon the syllable *SA*, which bestows all accomplishments, is eternal, and grants the goals of Dharma, Kāma, Artha, and Mokṣa, one should recite its mantra ten times: *SA*.
Four-armed, red in color,
adorned with white garments and joined with red ornaments, granting boons, with lotus-like eyes,
her face slightly smiling, graceful, and anointed with red sandalwood paste.
One should meditate upon the primordial Sovereign of the Gods, who is the bestower of the four aims of life, gentle, captivating, and meditated upon by Gandharvas, Siddhas, gods, and others;
having thus meditated, one should recite the mantra of the letter *Ha* ten times: *Ha*.
Having encased it within that mantra, one should then recite the root mantra.
Thus it should be understood regarding all castes (*varṇas*).

Otherwise, the practice of recitation, worship, and other means should be known as fruitless; likewise, initiation (*dīkṣā*) should be known as fruitless. Therefore, one should perform [these rites] with great effort.
Having performed the recitation (*japa*), one should carry out [the ritual] so as to obtain the fruit as described. This procedure applies to all Tantras—whether Śaiva, Śākta, or Vaiṣṇava.
One should recite the mantra ten times, encased within that [specific] mantra.
At the beginning of initiation (dīkṣā) and other rites, the purification of the mantra must be performed together with the Guru;
otherwise, the initiation, as well as the recitation (japa), worship, and so forth, will be fruitless.
A true Guru, ever self-restrained, having meditated upon and worshipped [the deity], performs the recitation and other rites.

Then, by the mere consciousness of the Guru, he should generate consciousness [in the disciple]; specifically, through the Āgama, he should perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) and purification (*śodhana*). Having encased it with that mantra, he should recite it one hundred and eight times.

This sequence must always be performed first by the Guru at the beginning of initiation and other rites. O Dear One! Mantras that are encapsulated by the mantra of the fifty letters are peaceful, bestow the four aims of life, and always grant the fruits as described.
Otherwise, initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the means such as recitation (*japa*) and worship (*pūjā*) are fruitless.
That initiation which is devoid of this procedure shall become fruitless;
it brings incomparable poverty in this world and one shall go to hell at the end.

At the beginning of the initiation and other rites, the sequence of the guru’s duties must be performed with great care. At the start and at the end, the disciple should diligently recite the mantra encapsulated by the seed-syllable (*varṇa*), O Dear One! He should always perform this procedure with diligence.
Whether in worship or in recitation, otherwise it would be fruitless.
Thus ends the meditation on the phonemes.
The mantra for these should be understood as "Oṃ, obeisance to A-kāra," and so forth.

Because it is useful for all the worship rites beginning with the five deities and ending with the [worship of the] letters, the installation of the general *arghya* (general water offering), written first, must be performed immediately thereafter.
This is stated in the fourth chapter of the *Śāradā*.
Having sipped water according to the rule and having prepared the general offering (sāmānyārghya) there,
one should sprinkle the doorway with the waters of the door-mantras and perform the worship of the door.
As for the placement of the general offering, it should be right at the entrance of the pavilion.
The worship of the doors, however, should be followed in the section on the ritual objects (Arthakāṇḍa).
In the second chapter of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the Rudrajāmala.
The sage (ṛṣi) is declared to be Merupṛṣṭha; Sutala is said to be the meter (chanda);
and Kūrma is proclaimed as the deity for the application (viniyoga) in the yoga of the seat.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), one says: "Salutation to you, the Kūrma-seat."
One should ward off terrestrial obstacles with three strikes of the heels,
and likewise ward off celestial obstacles with three claps of the hands.
In the Picchilā Tantra, in the fifth chapter.
The passage beginning with "saure māsi" and so forth has been explained previously.
In the Viśvasāra:

Then one should offer perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings to the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrādhipa), the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla), and the Goddess of the House (Gṛhadevī). Having performed the worship of these, one should not then worship any other deity.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
One should sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion with the five products of the cow and with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*).
One should perform that purification up to the crossroads by means of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and other rites.
Inspection is held to be performed with the root-mantra, while sprinkling is performed with the arrow-mantra (*śara*).
Striking with those very [darbha blades] and sprinkling with the armor-mantra (varma) is prescribed.
The wise one should fumigate the interior with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
There, he should scatter the *vikira* offerings, consecrated seven times with the weapon-mantra (*śarāṇu*).
Roasted grain, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, and unbroken rice grains—
these are designated as the *vikira* offerings, all of which destroy the multitude of obstacles.
As for the specific procedure of Somaśambhu, it is maintained by Rāghavabhaṭṭa as follows:

These scattered offerings, consisting of pure parched rice grains (*lāja*) consecrated with the seven mantras, sprinkled with water from the *astra* mantra, and veiled by the *kavaca* mantra— appearing in the forms of various weapons and warding off the multitude of obstacles— [should be offered].
One should cleanse that [site] with a handful of *darbha* grass consecrated by the recitation of mantras (*astramantra*).
Then, having bound it in the direction of the Lord (the northeast), one should prepare a seat.
Having caused the Brahmins to recite the *puṇyāha* formula and having seated them, [one proceeds].
Among the mandalas described, one should draw a single one upon the altar.
The mantra-practitioner should enter and sit upon a soft seat, facing either east or north,
having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), remaining silent, composed, and with senses subdued.
The reading in the Merutantra is: "with an upright body and conquered senses."
The preceptor should place the auspicious seed-vessels in the cardinal directions;
the meaning is that he should place those vessels for the sprouts, which have been described as being of an auspicious nature according to the aforementioned method, in the various directions.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, he should [place them] on the left and right sides.
Having bowed to the Guru and Gaṇeśāna, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having accomplished the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi), one should then perform the three claps (tālatraya).
Thereafter, the preceptor should perform the binding of the directions (digbandha) with the *ūrdhvordhva* mantra.
With that [mudrā], he should perform protection from the palms joined together on all sides.
The knower of mantras should assign the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas), and the deity of the mantra to his own head,
face, and heart, respectively.
In the eighth chapter of the *Prapañcasāra*.

The Seer (ṛṣi) should be borne upon the head because of his gravity; the Metre (chandas), being composed of syllables, should reside on the tongue; and the Deity of Manu, who is always to be understood by the intellect, has entered the heart. Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to rule with the root mantra, [one should proceed].
One should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, and after that, the Mantra-nyāsa.

One should place [the mantras] upon the fingers beginning with the thumb along with their respective limbs (aṅgas). Having placed the Astra-mantra upon the two palms, one should perform the triple clapping (tālatraya) and so forth.
With a concentrated mind, one should bind the directions with finger-snaps using that very [mantra];
then, the wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the heart and other limbs with the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*).
First, "Salutation to the Heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*), and for the head, "The Beloved of Fire" (*vahnivallabhā*).
Having uttered "Vaṣaṭ" for the crest (śikhā), "Hum" is recited for the armor (kavaca);
"Vauṣaṭ" should be for the three eyes, and "Phaṭ" for the weapon (astra) in due order.
One should apply these six limb-mantras (ṣaḍaṅgamantra), as thus described, to the six limbs.
The wise preceptor, having performed the placement (nyāsa) of Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in a clockwise direction upon the two shoulders and the two thighs,
should then assign Adharma and the others to the face, the sides, and the sides of the navel in a counter-clockwise direction.
Dharma and the other [virtues] are remembered as the feet; others are the limbs of the pedestal.
One should place Ananta in the heart-lotus, and within this [lotus], the Sun, Moon, and Fire;
upon these, one should assign their respective digits (kalās), preceded by the first letter of each of their names.
The supreme guru should likewise place the three qualities, sattva and the others, right here; then,

having duly placed the Self (ātman), the Inner Self (antarātman), and the Supreme Self (paramātman)— and here indeed the Knowledge-Self (jñānātman)— he should thereafter place the mantra of the seat (pīṭha).
Thus, one should meditate upon the chosen deity within the seat consisting of the body;
having displayed the mudrā according to rule, one should perform the ritual placement of the arghya water.
Having sprinkled [the area] with water from the conch-mantra, one should place it to the left in the fire-maṇḍala.

The wise one should place the support (ādhāra) and worship it according to the prescribed rite with waters consisting of nectar dripping from the *bindu*, along with fragrant flowers and other offerings.
[One should contemplate] the support as fire (*pāvaka*), the conch as the sun (*sūrya*), and the water as the moon (*niśākara*).
One should meditate upon the digits (kalās) of Fire, Sun, and Moon within those [elements] in their proper sequence;

these digits have been described in the first section (kāṇḍa). Having performed the emanation, one who knows the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) should mutter the root-mantra during the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having filled [the vessel] with water while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra) and covering it with both hands,
the wise preceptor, perceiving the water as the deity, should recite the mantra according to the rule;
then, having protected it with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and veiled it with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Having formed the *dhenumudrā*, one should awaken [the vessel] with its respective mudrā.
Placing the *prokṣaṇī* vessel on the right, one should fill it with water.
Taking a small amount of the *arghya* water, one should join it with the water in the *prokṣaṇī*.
To the north of the *arghya* vessel, the *pādya* and *ācamanīya* vessels should be placed.
The Guru should sprinkle himself, the sacrificial materials,
and the mandala with water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, using the mantra, and likewise other items in due order.

Then, by means of the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should worship Dharma and the other [principles] within one's own body with flowers and other offerings, ending with the mantra of the pedestal (pīṭha). And upon that [pedestal], one should worship the Supreme Deity. With a mind focused on nothing else, one should again offer handfuls of flowers five times.

One should worship [the deity] in sequence at the head, heart, base (navel), feet, and all limbs with offerings such as scents and so forth, excluding the food offering (naivedya). One should complete the remainder according to the procedure taught by the Guru.
One should perform all this with the water contained in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel;
having poured out that water from the *prokṣaṇī*, one should refill it as before.
Then, the practitioner of mantra should properly worship that mandala with perfumes and other offerings.
Having filled the center of the pericarp with śāli rice and decorated it further with taṇḍula rice, the knower of mantras, having spread darbha grass upon them,
should then place a kūrca-bundle together with unbroken grains (akṣata) on top of those.
Also in the fourth chapter of the Merutantra:
One should first fill the pericarp with *śāli* rice, and then with *taṇḍula* rice;

upon these, one should place *darbha* grasses, followed by a *kūrca* bundle containing unbroken grains (*akṣata*). These *kuśa* blades should have their roots cut off, be long, and number twenty-seven.
The *kūrca* is said here to be that which is joined with the *brahmagranthi* at its upper end.
One should worship the mantra of the pedestal (*pīṭhamantra*), beginning from the *ādhāraśakti*.
[She is] mounted upon the *kūrca* stone below, possessing a luster like the autumnal moon.
One should worship Ādhāraśakti, who holds two lotuses;
upon her head, one should worship the dark-blue Kūrma seated there;
and [one should worship] Ananta, resembling a jasmine flower, seated upon the upper Brahma-stone.
One should worship the Earth-goddess, who holds a lotus blue as the Tamāla tree, who bears the Cakradhara [Viṣṇu] upon her head as he supports the earth,
and who is girdled by the shimmering oceans.

Upon that [lotus] is an island made of jewels, and upon it is a pavilion of gems. Therein one should worship the Kalpavṛkṣa (wish-fulfilling tree), which grants the desired accomplishments of the practitioner.
Below that, one should worship the altar-platform, radiant with its mandala.

Afterwards, one should again worship the pedestal (pīṭha) upon that [seat] with Dharma and the other [principles]. One should worship Dharma and the others, who have the forms of a bull, Keśava, Viśvabhū, and Indra, and whose feet possess the luster of red, dark-blue, yellow, and sapphire.
One should worship those deities on the limbs with their names preceded by the negative particle (nañ), as described by their characteristics.
One should worship the lotus in the intermediate directions beginning with the southeast, in the cardinal directions, and in the center.
First, one should worship the Root of Bliss (Ānandakanda), and immediately after, the Stem of Consciousness (Saṃvinnāla).
Immediately after worshipping the lotus that consists of the essence of all principles (tattva),

the mantra-practitioner should then worship the petals consisting of the primal nature (prakṛti), the filaments consisting of the transformations (vikāra), and the pericarp enriched with the seed-syllables of the fifty letters.
On that [day], one should worship the Sun, Moon, and Fire together with their constituent parts (kalās);
then, by means of the three divisions of the Praṇava, one should worship the qualities beginning with Sattva,
as well as the Ātman, Antarātman, and Paramātman.

And [one should worship] the Self of Knowledge according to the rule, ending with the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra). One should place the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśakti) upon the filaments and in the center, [accompanied by the gestures of] boon and fearlessness. A jar fashioned from gold or other materials, its interior washed with water consecrated by mantras, [should be prepared].
It is perfumed with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, possessing a beautiful form,
its body wrapped tightly with a triple-stranded thread,
worshipped with scents, flowers, and the like, and accompanied by kūrca-grass and unbroken rice grains (akṣata).

The mantra-practitioner, an expert in ritual procedure, should place [the vessel] within the interior of the nine gems while reciting the *tāra* (Om); having conceived the oneness of the pitcher and the pedestal,
he should [rinse it] with a decoction of milky trees or with that derived from the bark of the *palāśa*.
Or, with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha) well-scented with camphor, fragrance, and flowers,
one should duly recite the Mātṛkā in reverse order according to the division of the self; likewise, one should worship [the deity] with the thought that it is the Deity itself.
Having stirred the eight fragrances (gandhāṣṭaka), which grant all desires, in a conch filled with water boiled with [the same ingredients], one should fill it; then, having invoked all the *kalās*:
first the ten *kalās* of Fire, and then the twelve of the Twelve-fold Self (*dvādaśātman*).
Having recited the root mantra in reverse order one hundred and fifty-six times after the *soma* syllable, the knower of mantras,
with a concentrated mind, should meditate upon the deity of the mantra.
The wise practitioner should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (installation of the vital breath) in each respective place.
He should pour the decoction, which consists of the [sixteen] digits (*kalā*) and is contained within a conch shell, into the ritual jar (*kumbha*).
At the end of the three-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa*, the word *amuṣya* (of such-and-such) should follow.

In sequence, one should utter "the vital breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*), "here the vital breaths," and likewise "the individual soul" (*jīva*) is situated here; then "all the senses of this one," and again "the station of this one.
Then follow the words for speech, mind, eye, ear, nose, and vital breath.
"Having returned hereafter, may they remain here happily for a long time—thus, the two *ṭha*s [are uttered].
This is declared to be the life-mantra (*prāṇamanu*), which bestows life upon all living beings.
Afterwards, with tender sprouts of the *aśvattha*, *panasa*, and *cūta* trees..."
The Guru, perceiving the *indravallī* plants as the celestial trees (*suradruma*) bound together,
should cover the mouth of the jar with the consecrated cup; then,
regarding it as the fruit of the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpaśākhin*), he should duly establish it there.

Then, having recited the root mantra, the wise one should wrap the jar with a pair of stainless linen cloths; thereafter, he should perform the installation (saṃsthāpana), the presence (sannidhāna), and the invocation (sannirodha) by way of the suṣumṇā path.
Thereafter, one should perform the sakalīkaraṇa and the avaguṇṭhana;
having performed the amṛtīkaraṇa, one should effect the paramīkṛti.
Composed in mind, one should perform these in sequence with their respective mudrās.
Then, the knower of mantras should perform the ritual services beginning with the welcome. The Guru should first utter the words of welcome and inquiries regarding well-being.
He should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to the lotus-feet of the Deity while contemplating Him as the essence of the Heart-mantra.
With the mantra "Namaḥ" [addressed] to the heart-self,
the preceptor should then offer the *arghya* water upon the head with the *śiras* mantra;
he should offer the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*) into the mouth with the *svadhā* mantra.
Then, with his own essence, he should offer the madhuparka into the lotus of the [guest's] mouth;
with that same mantra, he should give the water for sipping (ācamanīya).
He should perform the bath with scented water and cause [the guest] to put on two garments.
One should offer the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) along with necklaces and other ornaments,
using the syllables of the *mātṛkā* encased by the mantra according to the sequence of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Having worshipped the deity with perfumes and other offerings, one should then worship the limbs and so forth.

In each respective place, one should offer water at intervals between the ritual services. One should worship the limbs up to the world-protectors (lokapālas), as well as the surrounding deities (āvaraṇas).
One should worship the heart-mantra and the others in the filaments, beginning from the southeast corner (agnikoṇa).
The sequence for the six-limbed worship and so forth is found in the fourth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*.

O Pārvatī! Having subsequently worshipped the young maidens of the six limbs according to the prescribed rite in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center, as well as in the cardinal points—one should first meditate upon the deities of the limbs: the Eye in front and the Garment in the directions.
The principal excellent women, possessing rays that are white as frost, crystal, dark, blue, black, and reddish-brown, and holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
should first be worshipped; thereafter, the sages mentioned in the ritual manual (kalpa) should be worshipped in due order.
First, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with their primary retinues,
accompanied by their weapons and the lords of their respective classes, in the directions starting from the east in due order.
Having thus worshipped them according to the rules up to the offering of food (naivedya), the preceptor then—
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the south and having placed the fire there,
the learned one, having consecrated it according to the rules, should perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice;
therein, he should worship the deity whose form has been described with perfumes and other offerings.
Having performed the *vyāhṛti* oblation for Tāra, the knower of mantras,
having offered twenty-five oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee using the root mantra,
and having again offered with the *vyāhṛtis*, should worship once more with perfumes and other offerings.
Having united [the fire] with the image situated on the pedestal, one should dismiss the fire; with the remaining oblation, one should scatter a bali offering all around,
provided with scents, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), for the attendants of the deity.
Then, having removed the offering and purified the ground once more,
one should worship with the five services (pañcopacāra) and display the parasol and the fly-whisk.
One should also present betel-leaf mixed with pieces of camphor.
Having recited the root mantra one thousand times with undistracted mind,

he should offer that which has been consecrated by recitation to the deity for the sake of all prosperity. Then, in the direction of Śambhu, the preceptor should scatter the materials previously collected.

Having placed a *ghargharī* (water-jar) filled with water and adorned with golden cloth and other ornaments, one should worship the weapon-deity within it— standing upon a lion, bearing a sword and a shield,
of terrible form, and facing west.
Having worshipped with the moving seat (calāsana) and taken it up again, the Guru,

while pronouncing the command of the gods, should circumambulate the interior clockwise, sprinkling water from the mouths of the [vessels] of the world-protectors (lokapālas) while saying, "Protect! (rakṣa).
Having recited the weapon-mantra (astramantra), the Guru should, as before,

cause that consciousness to enter [the disciple] by looking at him with divine vision; then, having united it with his own self from the heart-lotus, he should perform the purification of the paths (adhvaviśodhana).
To that disciple [he said]:
"The triad consisting of the path of the arts (kalādhvā), the path of the principles (tattvādhvā), and the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvā);
and the other triad consisting of the path of phonemes (varṇādhvā), the path of words (padādhvā), and the path of mantras (mantrādhvā)."
The five *kalās*, beginning with *nivṛtti* and the rest, are proclaimed as the *kalā-adhvan*.
The *tattva-adhvan* is divided in many ways according to the differences between the Śaiva and other Āgamas:
there are thirty-six *tattvas* in the Śaiva system, whereas there are thirty-two in the Vaiṣṇava.
Furthermore, twenty-four principles (tattvas) are said to belong to Prakṛti through Maitra; ten principles are spoken of as belonging to the three-footed Self (Tripadātman),
and the Śaiva principles are said to be Śiva, Śakti, and Sadāśiva.
Īśvara, together with Vidyā, constitutes these five pure [principles]. Furthermore, Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, Kāla-vidyā, Rāga, and Puruṣa— these seven are both pure and impure.
Nature (prakṛti), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), mind (manas),
the organs of perception, the organs of action, the five subtle elements (tanmātras), and the five gross elements— these twenty-four, O Teacher, are declared in the scriptures to be impure.
Thus, the classification of the principles (tattvas) according to the Śaivas is presented here:
the individual soul (jīva), vital breath (prāṇa), intellect (dhī), mind (citta), the organs of knowledge and action,
the five subtle elements (tanmātras), the five gross elements (bhūtas), the heart-lotus, and the triad of fires.
Vāsudeva and the others— these are the principles (tattvas) of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
The five elements, the subtle elements (tanmātras), the sense organs, as well as the mind,
ego (garva), intellect (buddhi), and primordial matter (pradhāna)— the wise know these to be the Maitreya-principles.

The five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, then the Bindu, and further the kalās; then the Nāda, Śakti preceded by Sadāśiva, and Śiva; they know [the sequence] as Prakṛti, Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva; and finally Śiva again through Vidyā and Ātman.
All principles (tattvas) have been declared as belonging to the threefold nature;
thus has the path of principles (tattvādhvan) been described by those who know the various Āgamas. And the worlds (bhuvanāni) have been proclaimed as the "path of worlds" (bhuvanādhvan) by the wise.
The wise declare that the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) consists of the letters from *a* to the end of the *anādīkṣā*.

A collection of phonemes constitutes the path of words (*padādhvan*), and the multitudes of mantras constitute the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*). The most excellent of gurus should purify these six paths in their proper sequence.
One should meditate on the infant’s feet, shanks, heart, forehead, and head.
The anus is the location of the rectum.
There, touching it according to the rules with effort,
the Guru should offer oblations in the preceptor’s fire-pit (ācāryakuṇḍa) with purified sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter,
using the mantra "I purify this path, svāhā" for each of the paths separately.
One should cause those eight oblations, beginning with Tārā, to dissolve in sequence;
having dissolved them into Śiva, one should generate them from Śiva by way of emanation,
beholding them with divine vision.

The preceptor, having offered a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the *sruva* ladle using the root mantra, should again apply that established consciousness to the disciple. He should then bind the eyes of the disciple with a cloth while reciting the eye-mantra (*netramantra*).
Taking that disciple by the hand, he should lead him from the *kuṇḍa* to the mandala. Then, having filled the disciple’s joined palms with flowers according to the ritual procedure,
he should cause them to be cast into the jar while reciting the root mantra for the pleasure of the deity.
Having removed that eye-bandage from the disciple seated upon the darbha grass mat,
the Guru, having again withdrawn and then re-emanated [the self] according to the sequence of the *ātma-yāga*,
should then perform the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) on the body of the disciple as prescribed by their respective mantras.
Having worshipped the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) residing in the water-pot with the five offerings (pañcopacāra),
one should perform the ritual of sakalīkṛti upon it according to the path taught in the Tantra.
Then, once the mandala has been adorned, one should seat the disciple upon another [seat] within it.
While the five musical instruments resound, the Guru, together with the blessings of the Brahmins,
having duly lifted the pitcher and placed the celestial trees situated at its mouth upon the head of the child, should mentally recite the Mātṛkā.
One should quickly sprinkle with water consecrated by the root mantra for the sake of protection.
Now follows the procedure for consecration.
In the Vāmakeśvaratantra, in the fiftieth chapter.

Consecration (abhiṣeka), moreover, is of two kinds: the Śākta and the Pūrṇa. The Guru who has transcended duality (avadhūta) should perform the Śākta consecration; he should pour a small amount of water from the ritual jars into the Brahmakumbha.
The wise practitioner, having brought the Brahma-pitcher, should place it in front;
[as stated] in the seventh chapter of the Niruttara-tantra.
The illustrious Śiva said:
Consecration (abhiṣeka) is of two kinds: that for kings and that for the wise.
O Goddess of the Gods! In the consecration of a king, one should perform the Vedic rites;
however, the consecration of the wise is concealed in all the Tantras.
It bestows all peace, is meritorious, and wards off all diseases;
it grants wealth and fame, increases the lifespan of men,
generates all forms of good fortune, and destroys even the most heinous sins.

O Goddess! It fulfills all desires, wards off all defects of mantras, accomplishes all aims, and bestows the fruits of all sacred fords (tīrthas). It removes malevolent spells and destroys the evils caused by all planetary influences.
O Goddess! It pacifies possession by spirits and the like, removes the fear of ḍākinīs, increases one's splendor, and is supreme for increasing strength;
it destroys the agony of poison even for one bitten by Takṣaka.
In cases of loss of luster, loss of strength, loss of intellect, or loss of wealth; likewise, when faults arise from women, or in disorders of body and mind—
the wise preceptor should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka).

O Goddess, Kuleśvarī! For women who lack good fortune, this consecration (abhiṣeka) is performed; and through the path of ritual consecration, one attains the status of a Guru. O Kuleśvarī, [such a one becomes] a Vaiṣṇava endowed with knowledge and likewise a Śaiva.
One who is devoted to Śakti and is an ornament of the Kula should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka).
Through consecration, the mantra and tantra of all are perfected;
through consecration, the entitlement of all becomes certain.
A Brahmin who has performed the consecration certainly attains the status of a Brahmā;
a Kṣatriya who has performed the consecration attains the duty of a Brahmin;
a Vaiśya attains the state of a Kṣatriya, and a Śūdra attains the state of a Vaiśya.
Through initiation, one abandons the status of all four castes. For a Brāhmaṇa, the drinking of liquor causes him to lose his Brāhmaṇahood in an instant.
When initiation has been performed, the drinking of liquor is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa.
The Āgama is the fifth Veda, and the Kaula is the fifth stage of life (āśrama).
Śiva is also the fifth caste, because by chanting the Mahāvidyā,
one abandons one's own respective caste and attains the state of Śiva.
Without initiation (*abhiṣeka*), a Brahmin must never drink liquor;
however, having mastered the secret lore (*siddhavidyā*), he then becomes one who knows the conventions (*saṅketajña*).
One who knows the conventions should perform the initiation within the conduct of the *kula*.
The mantra-practitioner who has received consecration should perform the worship of the family (kulapūjā).

The mantra-practitioner who has performed the worship of the family should then proceed to the ancestral ground (pitṛbhūmi). Having reached that place on the ancestral ground, he should then dwell there alone.
The hero should dwell alone in a remote forest during the latter part of the night;
there, O Goddess, he shall attain a perfection difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Without the practice of the Kula way, O Goddess, neither mantra nor tantra is successful.
In the Kulācāra, the accomplished vidyā brings about the attainment of the ritual substance with certainty.
One should offer the wine of consecration for the kula-rite in age after age.
Having drunk the wine, one should recite the vidyā, especially at the time of the Lord of Time (Kālādhipa).
In the absence of *surā*, one should offer *vijayā* as a substitute;
for without bliss (*ānanda*), there is a downfall, and the deities are not satisfied.
One should worship Kālī with the fifth [substance], especially at the site of Kāmākhyā.
In Kāmākhyā especially, Kālikā shall be the bestower of perfection;
yet the mantra of Kālī is not perfected without the practice of the Kula way.
O Goddess, he who performs the Kula rite without having received initiation [shall fail].

Rites such as worship for that [mantra] are prescribed for malevolent purposes (abhicāra). O Goddess! he who bestows a perfected vidyā without [the recipient having received] initiation shall dwell in a terrible state for as long as the moon and sun endure.

O Kuleśvarī! Through this consecration, the state of Brahmā, the state of Hari, the state of Śiva, and the sovereignty over all siddhis arise. O Deveśī! He becomes divine and a hero, devoted solely to devotion for the Kula.
O Goddess! One should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka), preceded by the preliminary rite of propitiation (adhivāsa).
Then, having performed the Vṛddhi-śrāddha, one should worship Śiva and Śakti. Having worshipped the Guru according to the rules with ornaments of gold and other finery, [one should proceed].
Then, having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) according to the rules, he should perform the selection of the gurus.

Thereafter, the lord of practitioners (sādhakeśvara), having prostrated before the true guru, the god, and the goddess, should perform the worship of the Goddess individually with the five [offerings].
Having performed the worship of the Guru, the practitioner, intent on the meditation of the Goddess,
should then perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) in a pure place—
whether in an empty house, on a riverbank, at the root of a bilva tree, or within a sacred tri-junction (tri-pāntara).
One should contemplate a location either within a great forest, or in a secluded cremation ground,
or in a village, or on a mountain, or on the bank of a river,
or even in a temple of the deities.
In the eighth chapter.

Having worshipped Śiva-Śakti, one should place an excellent vessel that is neither too short nor too long, fashioned from gold or silver. One should then set down the special *arghya* offering either in its own yantra or within a triangle.
All rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, as well as oceans and lakes;
all oceans, rivers, lakes, clouds, and streams;
and sacred pools and springs located in heaven, the netherworld, and upon the earth.
All meritorious holy places (tīrthas) bring their presence into the water-pot.
One should offer a sprout while reciting the Śrī-bīja;
with the Kūrca-mantra there shall be the granting of fruits, and with the Strī-bīja, stability of form.
One should apply vermilion with the seed-syllable of fire (Raṃ), and flowers with the word "preta.
Then, one should apply dūrvā grass with the root-mantra and perform the sprinkling with the Praṇavas.
Thereafter, one should perform the striking with the blade of kuśa grass using the mantra "Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā."

Having reflected thus, O Goddess! one should invoke and worship the Pīṭha there according to this very procedure in all rites, O beautiful one! One should establish the water-pot (ghaṭa), O Goddess! especially in the six types of ritual acts (ṣaṭkarmma).
O Goddess! One should perform the great worship with the sixteen types of offerings.
After that, one should perform the great worship of the gurus and the Śākta practitioners;
following that, the worship of the sādhakas and the young maidens (kumāris).
Having offered the bali-oblation to virgins, especially those of noble birth,
one should then perform the consecration (abhiṣeka), O Goddess, according to the path of one's own guru and by means of the recitation of mantras according to the procedure taught in the Svatantra.
The preceptor, the master of mantras, should move that jar with this mantra:
Oṃ! Arise, O Brahma-jar, bestower of the desired accomplishments of the deities!
Fulfill this person's heart’s desire with water filled from all sacred fords (tīrthas)!
Īśāna, Indu, Smara, Kṣauṇī, and Bhuvaneśvarī at its end—
by means of this mantra and the sounding of musical instruments, one should move the jar.
The Guru should consecrate the disciple, and the Purohita the patron.
One should sprinkle [the site] with sprouts from the Aśvattha tree during an assembly of spirits;
one should sprinkle with those from the Udumbara tree in the case of defects in the mantra, and with those from the Karavīra tree for the same.
One desiring fame, wealth, long life, and splendor should sprinkle with sprouts from the Cūta tree.
For those seeking the destruction of all sins, the consecration is performed with *tulasī* flower-clusters;
for the attainment of the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*), it is performed with *bilva* leaves for the devotees of Śakti;
and for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), the consecration proceeds with *nārasiṃha* mantras.
It is famous by the name Nārasiṃha-cuṇiyā-hāgaḍā.
One should perform an ablution with *darbha* grass that has no internal nodes even when faults have been accepted;
for the misfortune of women, an ablution with *dūrvā* grass;
and for the sake of accomplishing mantras in all undertakings, [an ablution] with mango sprouts.

For this consecration mantra, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), Śakti is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of the perfection of one's resolve.
Oṃ! The Goddess Rājarājeśvarī, Bhairavī, Kālabhairavī;
the Goddess Śmaśānabhairavī, Tripurānandabhairavī;
the Goddess Trikūṭātripurā, as well as Tripurasundarī.
May Tripureśī, the Great Goddess, as well as Tripurakārikā,
the Goddess Tripurānandinī, and likewise Tripurātanī—
may these [deities] consecrate you with water purified by mantra. (1)
The Great Goddess Chinnamastā, as well as Ekajaṭeśvarī,
Tārā, Jayadurgā, Śūlinī, Bhuvaneśvarī,
the Great Goddess named Tvaritā, and likewise Trikhaṇḍikā.
May Nityā, Nityarūpā, and likewise Vajraprastariṇī—may these consecrate you with water purified by mantra. (2)
The Great Sovereign mounted upon a horse, likewise the Slayer of Mahiṣa,
Durgā, Vanadurgā, Śrīdurgā, Bhagamālinī,
as well as the goddess Bhagandarī and another, Bhagaklinnā.
The goddess who is the sovereign of all wheels, as well as Nīlasarasvatī;
the goddess who bestows all accomplishments, served by all the gandharvas;
the great goddess Ugratārā, and likewise Dakṣiṇakālikā.
"These [goddesses] to you," and so forth. || 3 ||
Kṣemaṅkarī, Mahākālī, Aniruddhasarasvatī,
Mātaṅginī, Annaparṇā, and likewise Rājarājeśvarī.
(265) "These [goddesses] to you," and so forth. || 4 ||
Ugracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā,
Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Caṇḍarūpā, and Aticaṇḍikā—
these [goddesses] protect you, and so forth. || 5 ||
Ugradaṃṣṭrā, Mahādaṃṣṭrā, Śubhadaṃṣṭrā,
Kapālinī, Bhīmanetrā, Viśālākṣī, Maṅgalā, Vijayā, and Jayā.
"May these [goddesses] protect you," and so forth. || 6 ||
Maṅgalā, Nandinī, Bhadrā, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Yaśasvinī, Puṣṭi, Medhā, Śivā, Sādhvī, Yaśaḥ, Śobhā, Jayā, Dhṛti, Śrīnandā,
Sunandā, and Nandinī, who is worshipped with joy.
"These [goddesses], however, [protect] you," and so forth. || 7 ||
Vijayā, Nandinī, Bhadrā, Smṛti, Śānti, Dhṛti, Kṣamā, Siddhi, Tuṣṭi, Ramā, Puṣṭi, Śrī, Vṛddhi,
Ratī, Dīpti, Kānti, Yaśas, Lakṣmī, Īśvarī, and Buddhi.
Śākrī, Māyāvatī, Brāhmī, Jayantī, Aparājitā, Ajitā, Mānavī, Śvetā, Diti, and Aditi;
as well as Māyā, Mahāmāyā, Mohinī, and Kṣobhiṇī.
Kamalā, Vimalā, Gaurī, Śaraṇyā, Ambudhisundarī,
Durgā, Kriyā, Arundhatī, Ghaṇṭākarṇā, Kapālinī,
Raudrī, Kālī, Māyūrī, Trinetrā, and Aparājitā.
Svarūpā, Bahurūpā, and likewise Vigrahātmikā; Carcikā, another, Jyeṣṭhā, and likewise she who is worshipped by the gods;
Vaivasvatī, Kaumārī, Tārā, and the supreme Māheśvarī.
Vaiṣṇavī, Mahālakṣmī, Kārttikī, Kauṣikī,
Śivadūtī, and Cāmuṇḍā, who is adorned with a garland of severed heads.
"These [goddesses] to you," and so forth. || 8 ||
Indra, Vahni, Yama, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Pavana, Dhanada, Īśāna, Brahmā, and Ananta are the lords of the directions. "These [gods] address you," and so forth. 9.
May the year, the two solstices, the seasons, the fortnights, the days,
and the lunar dates consecrate [you] with water purified by mantras.
May the planets—the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu—constantly consecrate you. (11)
The lunar mansion, the Karaṇa, the Yoga, the Amṛta, and indeed the Siddhi; the burnt (Dagdha), the Pāpa, as well as the Bhadrā, the Yogas, the days of the week, and the Kṣaṇas;
likewise the Vāravelā, the Kālavelā, the Daṇḍas, and those such as the Vṛddhas.
May they constantly consecrate [me] with water purified by mantras. || 12 ||
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, the one known as Unmatta,
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra— may these eight Bhairavas consecrate [me], and so forth. || 13 ||
And likewise the sons of Ḍākinīs and the sons of Rākiṇīs.
There are others who are the sons of Lākinī, and still others who are the sons of Kākinī;
furthermore, there are the sons of Śākinī and likewise the sons of Hākinī;
thereafter are the sons of Yakṣiṇī, and after that, the sons of Devī.
Likewise, the sons of the Mothers— those who are the upward-facing sons,
those who are the downward-facing sons, and the other sons who are facing outward.
"These [elements], however, you... and so forth. || 14 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—these [address you], and so forth. || 15 ||
The Puruṣa, Prakṛti, and the sixteen transformations are proclaimed as the Self (Ātman), the Inner Self (Antarātman), the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and the Knowledge-Self (Jñānātman). Furthermore,
those qualities of the Self which are gross, subtle, and likewise beyond [the senses] are also enumerated.
"These [elements], however, you... and so forth. || 16 ||
The seed-syllable of the Vedas and others, the *huṃ*-seed, the female seed, the fish-bannered one (*mīnaketana*),
the seed of power (*śakti*), the seed of Lakṣmī (*ramā*), the seed of illusion (*māyā*), the moon of nectar,
the great jewel of thought (*cintāratna*), the great seed, and that which belongs to Narasiṃha and Śaṅkara.
The Mārttaṇḍabhairava mantra, the Durga mantra, the seed-mantra of Śrī Puruṣottama, the Gāṇapatya mantra, the Vārāha mantra, and the seed-mantra of Kālī which removes fear— these [mantras],
beginning with "etāstvām," [protect you]. || 17 ||
The Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Revā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī;
the Ātreyī, Bhāratī, Sarayū, and likewise the Gaṇḍakī;
the Karatoyā, Candrabhāgā, Śvetagaṅgā, and Kauśikī.
And Bhogavatī is in Pātāla, and likewise Mandākinī is in Svarga.
"May these [goddesses] protect you," and so forth. || 18 ||
May Bhairava, Bhīmarūpa, Śoṇa, and Gharghara,
as well as the lakes of Sindhu waters and those originating in the netherworld (pātāla), protect us; and may whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) and holy shrines there are likewise protect us.
"May they consecrate you," and so forth. || 19 ||
The continents such as Jambūdvīpa, the oceans such as the salt ocean, the infinite Nāgas, and the serpents such as Takṣaka—these [all] you... and so forth. (20)
Rati is the beloved of Agni; thereafter are vaṣaṭ and kūrcam;
may vauṣaṭ and phaṭ always consecrate [me]. (21)
May the pretas, kuṣmāṇḍas, rākṣasas, and dānavas perish;
may the piśācas, guhyakas, and bhūtas be struck down by this consecration.
May misfortune, Kālakarṇī, and very great sins be destroyed, struck down by the consecrated seed-syllable of Tārā. (23)
May diseases, sorrows, weakness, poverty, and mental disturbances perish,
struck down by the very seed-syllable of speech during this consecration.
May their attachment to the world, their renunciation, and even their ill fortune—which is difficult to control—perish, struck down by the very God of Love during the consecration. (25)
May the loss of splendor, the loss of strength, and likewise the loss of intelligence perish through this consecration, struck by the seed-syllable of Śakti.
Poison, untimely death, disease, and likewise the fear of ḍākinīs and others;
terrible spells, cruel planets, and other nāgas—may these all perish through this consecration, struck by the seed-syllable of Kālī. (27)
May all calamities perish, and may all prosperities remain firmly established;
through this empowerment of Śakti, may all desires be fulfilled. (28)
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
With the remaining water, the Guru should cause the disciple to perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana).
Then, the knower of the Self, identifying himself with the deity, should effect the sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of making the disciple manifest as the deity).
Having performed the rinsing and becoming restrained in speech, the disciple should sit in the presence of the Guru.
The supreme teacher, contemplating the identity of those two, should worship the deity who has been transferred into the disciple with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
In the *Niruttaratantra*:
Having thus sprinkled the disciple, one should again perform worship; as it is stated in the third chapter of the Merutantra:
Then, for the sake of swiftly attaining perfection, the preceptor should consecrate the disciple;
the preceptor places the divine tree (kalpavṛkṣa) situated upon the mouth of the pitcher upon the head of the child,
accompanied by the five sounds and the benedictory words of the Brahmins.
Having first taken up the consecrated water-pot (karaka) which has the form of a weapon,
the best of preceptors should sprinkle him with its waters for protection.
The disciple, having likewise worshipped there, should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru.
O Pārvatī! Cows, land, disciples, and sentient beings, as well as silver and jewels—these constitute the entire property, or half of it, or even a quarter of it, as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
This is the fee (dakṣiṇā): it should be performed if the consecration (abhiṣeka) is carried out immediately after receiving the mantra;

however, if the reception of the mantra occurs after the consecration, then the fee for that [consecration]—or rather, the fee for the consecration and so forth which have become its constituent parts—is thereby established as the fee for this [mantra].
In the fifty-third chapter of the Vāmakeśvaratantra.
O Dear One! The best of practitioners, once consecrated, should become proficient in ritual action;
O Goddess! the purification of the body cannot be accomplished without ritual action.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].

One should bestow another vidyā upon that disciplined disciple preceded by the offering of water. Having received the vidyā from the guru again, the wise one should recite it eight times while contemplating with his intellect the identity of the guru, the vidyā, and the deity.

One should prostrate like a staff upon the ground before that Guru, who is the very essence of the deity; one should place his pair of lotus-feet upon one's own head and offer to him one’s body, wealth, and honor— everything.
From that time forward, with undivided mind, one should do what is pleasing to the guru;
with a joyful heart, one should give the full sacrificial fee to the officiating priests;
and afterwards, one should gratify the Brahmins with various kinds of food and sacrificial fees.
This initiation, which bestows all prosperity, has been described as consisting of ritual action.
In the third chapter of the Vṛhannīlatantra.
One should follow his shadow and dwell near him for three days;
otherwise, there is no doubt that the mobile power (śakti) will not reach the Guru.
Thus concludes the initiation involving ritual action.
The individual initiation (āṇavī dīkṣā), however, is of ten kinds; namely:
The wise, learned in the scriptures, recite that initiation is manifold as the Āṇavī, the Nādeyī, and furthermore the Śāmbhavī, which is indeed single-fold.
A statement cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
The *āṇavī* [initiation] has been described as being of many kinds; its divisions are now stated:
the *smārtī*, the *mānasikī*, the *yaugī*, the *cākṣuṣī*, the *spārśikī*, the *vācikī*, the *māntrikī*, the *hautrī*, the *śāstrī*, and the *abhiṣecikā*.

Having remembered the Guru residing in a foreign land, the disciple— by means of the ritual procedure for dissolution (*laya*) and absorption (*layabhāga*) into the supreme Śiva, which consists of the sequential separation from the three types of sin and their perfect union— is said to undergo what is called the "mental initiation" (*smārī dīkṣā*).
Having perceived with a pure mind one seated in his own presence, that [purity] which is to be understood as arising from the means for removing the three impurities is indeed mental.
Having entered the body of the disciple according to the sequence taught in Yoga, the yogi takes hold of that disciple’s self and unites it with his own body;
this is declared to be the yoga-initiation (yogadīkṣā), which destroys the three impurities.
Having ascertained, "I am Śiva," she gazes with a vision moistened by compassion;
that is the ocular initiation (cākṣuṣī dīkṣā), which destroys all sins.
Having himself become Paraśiva with a mind free from doubt,
the Guru should touch the head of the disciple with his own mantra using the hand of the disciple.
This is declared to be the "Initiation by Touch" (sparśadīkṣā), which effects the manifestation of Śiva.
The characteristics of Śiva’s hand are as described in the Somaśambhu [Tantra].
One should prepare a mandala with one's own perfumes on the right hand;
according to the prescribed rite, one should worship the deity in this manner, for it is called the "Hand of Śiva.
"With one's own perfumes" means with the eight specific perfumes belonging to each [deity].

The preceptor, having visualized his own mouth as the mouth of the Guru, should with reverence bestow upon the disciple the divine mantra and so forth through the application of the Guru’s mouth, together with the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra and other rites; this is the oral initiation (vācikī). || 6 ||
Just as a lamp’s flame [is transmitted], when the body is joined with the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa),
one becomes the very embodiment of the mantra oneself; by respectfully transmitting the mantra to the disciple, that initiation is the "Mantric Initiation" (māntrī dīkṣā) which destroys impurities.
Having deposited the fire according to the prescribed rite either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
one should proceed through each path in due order according to the sequence of the stages of dissolution (layabhāga):
therein [are] the mantra, phoneme, and kalā, as well as the pada and viṣṭapa.
