Having purified [the disciple] through forms of oblation, that which is proclaimed as the *hautrī* initiation is completed.

When the words of the scripture, along with their essential meaning and the ritual substances, are imparted to a worthy disciple who is devoted and intent upon service and worship, that is called scriptural initiation (śāstrī-dīkṣā). || 9 ||
Having respectfully worshipped both Śiva and the consort of Śiva in the water-pot (kumbha),
the initiation consisting of the consecration from the Śiva-pot is known as the Abhiṣecikā.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
Now I shall describe the initiation consisting of phonemes (varṇa), as enjoined by the Āgamas. Phonemes consist of the Puruṣa and Prakṛti, and the body is likewise of that nature;
therefore, the preceptor should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the phonemes upon the body of the disciple.
The best of teachers, through the command of the deity-nature, should dissolve those letters joined with their respective locations in reverse order; then,
having purified that water, the disciple shall become possessed of a divine body.
Having united that consciousness with the Supreme Self, the supreme guru should then project the phonemes produced from it onto the body of the disciple;
he should duly apply the consciousness according to the sequence of emanation.
The state of divinity, consisting of supreme bliss, arises in the child;
this is declared to be the initiation consisting of the phonemes (varṇa-dīkṣā), which bestows knowledge.
The *kalāvatī-dīkṣā* has been written by Kṛṣṇānandāgamavāgīśa— the most eminent member of our community— in his own work, the *Tantrasāra*;
since the *saṃkṣepadīkṣā* is also [described there], there is no need for these two here.
The initiation consisting of piercing (vedhadīkṣā) has also not been written down here, as its form is no longer in practice.
It is stated by the investigators in the fifth chapter of the *Śāradā*: "having investigated."
Now, the initiation by stages.
In the thirty-second chapter of the Kāmākhyātantra.
The Goddess said:
O Lord! If you have compassion for me, please explain the sequential initiation (kramadīkṣā). O Sovereign of the Universe, how does one perform initiation in its proper sequence?
Śiva said:
Various types of initiations that grant pleasure to the gods have been heard by you.
Now I shall speak [further], provided you do not tell this to anyone;
many faults arise from disclosure, and I have kept [this] hidden everywhere.
In the Kali age, characterized by sinful conduct, success (siddhi) shall never occur. There shall be no success, there shall be no success in the Kali age through any other method.
For one devoid of the Krama initiation, there shall be no success whatsoever in the Kali age.
Knowing this, O Maheśānī, one should perform the Krama initiation.
Just as iron, when pierced by mercury and mantras, attains the state of gold,
so too the self attains the state of Śiva through the power of the Krama initiation.

The rite of mantra-repetition and the method of deity-worship must indeed be performed according to the sequence of initiation (dīkṣā). O Goddess, they never accept [this worship] endowed with thousands of ritual services and joined with devotion, if it is devoid of the sequential initiation (kramadīkṣā).
First Kālī, then Tārā, and after that Sundarī;
this is known as the "Successive Initiation" (Kramadīkṣā), always intended for those desiring spiritual perfection.
One may give away a kingdom or even one's head, but the [teaching] of the Krama-yoga must never be given away.
O Pārvatī! Success comes from the ritual procedure performed in due order and from initiation.

A teacher who is pure by birth from both parents, has conquered his senses, is learned in all the scriptures, is compassionate toward the suffering of others, is peaceful, and is of noble lineage—such a one is indeed the Guru. For the disciple of noble family, the ritual procedure is to be performed in due order.
In this matter, there is no requirement for purity and the like, nor is there any consideration of the *siddha* and other classes;
nor is there any deliberation regarding eligibility (*adhikāra*) in the sequential practice of receiving [initiation].
Whether on a single day, or after a year, or even at the end of a year, O Pārvatī!
Therefore, a disciple should diligently grasp [the teachings] through the sequential method;
having grasped them from the mouth of the Guru, he should worship them in sequence.
And he should worship them in sequence, O Goddess, according to the procedure for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).

On the first day, the disciple, with self-restrained mind and conquered senses, shall observe a fast on the second day; on the third day, the Guru should initiate him. Having caused him to accept his noble lineage (*kulīnatva*), the Guru should recite the mantras.

The single syllable, the three syllables, and likewise the twenty-two syllables are proclaimed for the second [day]; for the third, they are from the three peaks (trikūṭa). This occurs either in sequence by day or in sequence over the course of a year.
At the end of the year, O Goddess, the Guru should likewise initiate them in due order.
He should give villages, male servants, female servants, and gold to the Guru as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to their respective sequence and in accordance with his means.

O Goddess! if, by the power of fortune, the Krama initiation is obtained, then success shall come to him; there is no need for deliberation on this point. How could there be success in the Kali age for one who is devoid of the Krama initiation?

O Goddess of Excellent Vows, O Maheśānī! Among all stages of life, among all beings, and among all gods, everything becomes futile for them without the proper sequence. Therefore, with every effort, one should be initiated by a Guru.

The entire world has its root in Krama; the supreme austerity has its root in Krama. If one who is uninitiated should know [this] and, having taken something, cause it to be eaten, his gift becomes fruitless; therefore, one should avoid all such things.
Initiation conferred by a true guru shall effect all ritual actions.
Thus concludes the initiation by stages.
In the *Guptadīkṣātantra*, as cited in the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*.
Even after death, one follows knowledge and especially mantras;
it is the mind alone that proclaims a person's past actions. O Maheśānī! If this mind did not exist, how could a person even come to be?
And how does his mind become [prepared] during initiation, O Pārvatī?
Therefore, O Goddess, one should diligently extract the prior mantra (pūrvavidyā).
Listen, O beloved, to the jewel among leaves: that of the Vakula, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees.
O Maheśānī! O beloved! One should write the Śakti-mantra on a banyan leaf;
the Viṣṇu-mantra on an aśvattha leaf, and the Śiva-mantra on a vakula leaf.
O Deveśī! O Maheśvarī! [One should write them] with red sandalwood or with saffron.
O Goddess! One should write the Śakti-mantra on sandalwood; O Supreme Sovereign! one should write the Viṣṇu-mantra [on sandalwood] and the Śiva-mantra with ashes.
The meaning is that one should write the respective mantra of each deity upon seven sets of seven leaves.
The wise practitioner should diligently perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) with that mantra;
he should effect the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* of each respective deity.
O Supreme Goddess! having worshipped [the deity] with offerings according to one's capacity, [he should proceed].
Then, O Maheśvarī, the disciple, holding the arghya vessel in his hand,
should offer it to the Sun-god while reciting this mantra.
He states the substances for the *arghya* offering:
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, ghee, curd, as well as honey,
red karavīra flowers, and likewise red sandalwood—
this is proclaimed as the eightfold arghya offering for the Sun.

Oṃ! O Lord! O Protector of the Earth! Endowed with all powers, please accept this water offering (arghya) from me and reveal the ancient knowledge. Having offered the arghya and prostrated with palms joined in reverence, one should then recite:
In the case of the Gāndharva [marriage].
O Maheśvarī, one should not offer the *arghya* to the Sun with water from a conch shell.
*Oṃ! Sūrya, Soma, Yama, Kāla, and the five great elements—these nine are indeed the witnesses here in this world of both auspicious and inauspicious actions.*
"All the gods residing within my body are witnesses to my mantra.
Grant the knowledge acquired in my previous births into my hand!
Having recited this, O Great Goddess, one should quickly extract the leaf.
Having extracted one leaf, one should cause it to be placed in the hand of the Guru.
O Parameśvarī! The Guru, having extracted the series of syllables and established the *setu* (the bridge), O Maheśānī! should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the eight hundred [verses] there.
Placing his hand upon the head of the disciple, the Guru, facing eastward, should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while the disciple stands facing westward.
Otherwise:
the Guru sits facing east while the disciple stands facing west;
[the mantra is whispered] three times into the right ear and likewise once into the left ear.
Regarding women and Śūdras, one should perform contemplation in the reverse manner;
having sipped water (ācamana), become self-restrained, and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma),
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, accompanied by the [recollection of] the seers and other [limbs].
O Goddess of the Gods! One should mutter the mantra eight times into the left ear;
this initiation is proclaimed in all tantras as that of Śakti.
Having received the Great Vidyā from the Guru, one should mutter it one hundred and eight times.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru; one must not practice stinginess regarding one's wealth.
One should cause it to be given to the guru, to the guru’s son, or to the guru’s wife.
In the Kulārṇava:
When the Guru is pleased, the deity attains pleasure;
when the deity is pleased, the accomplishment of the mantra becomes certain.
In the Kali age, one should perform initiation primarily with the "jewel-leaf" (patraratna).

Then the practitioner of mantra becomes a perfected one; there is no need for deliberation on this point. O Goddess, that man who performs initiation without this knowledge—his initiation is fruitless, and at the end he shall go to hell.
Then, O Maheśānī, the disciple should prostrate himself on the ground like a staff.
Then the guru should say:
Arise, my child! You are liberated; be one who perfectly observes right conduct.
May fame, prosperity, beauty, intelligence, longevity, strength, and health ever be yours.
In the Yoginīhṛdaya.
Having bestowed the mantra, the Guru himself should observe a fast;
otherwise, he becomes a worm in the hell of great darkness—there is no other way.
In the Rudrajāmala:
O Bhairava! The wise perform the five-limbed placement (pañcāṅganyāsa) upon Śyāmā, Abhayā, Bhairavī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, Mañjughoṣa, and likewise Raudrī.
In that regard, concerning Guhyakālī, the initiation into the five abodes has already been explained previously.
(p. 273) In the Kali age, it is taught that there are Tantric purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) by means of leaves or gems (*patraratna*).
Now, having reached the stage of the syllable, that which is characterized by powerful delusion is described.
As it is stated in the fourth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra:
But when the Vedic initiation as well as the Paurāṇika initiation no longer remains, O lady of beautiful hips! then indeed Kali becomes powerful;
and when the examination of merits and demerits based on the Vedas [ceases].
O Śivā! O Peaceful One! Only then will the powerful Kali prevail. O Mistress of the Kula! Only when the celestial river is cut here and broken there will the powerful Kali prevail.

O highly wise one! when women become exceedingly difficult to restrain, harsh, and addicted to quarreling; and when kings are of barbarian descent and greedy for wealth—then indeed will the Kali age prevail with great force.
But when men on earth are conquered by women, enslaved by desire, and act with hostility toward their teachers, friends, and others— then indeed Kali is powerful.
When the earth yields little fruit and the clouds do not rain water.
When trees bear fruit out of season, then the Kali age is powerful;
when brothers, kinsmen, and ministers strike one another for the sake of wealth and its fruits, then the Kali age is powerful.

When meat from the middle part of the body and other such things are openly consumed while avoiding censure and the commencement of such acts, they practice secret drinking; at that very time, the Kali age becomes powerful. Just as there was the consumption of liquor and so forth during the Satya, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages.
Even in the Kali age, one should act in the same way, following the path of the Kula.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of intense delusion.
The manner in which even the *upaśama* (subsidence) of the *kali*-age occurs is also described in that very same place.
Kali does not afflict those who follow the traditional conduct of their lineage, who are purified by truth, have conquered their senses, and possess manifest discipline and a nature of compassion.
Devoted to service of their gurus and devoted to the lotus feet of their mothers,
and being deeply attached to their own wives, Kali does not afflict them;
they are observers of truthful vows, steadfast in truth, and dedicated to the dharma of truth.
For indeed, Kali oppresses those by whom the truths of the Kula practice are violated;
but Kali does not oppress those who give the purified principles according to the Kula path to the yogi who speaks the truth.
Those who are free from violence and envy, devoid of hypocrisy and malice,
and who remain steadfast in the duties of their lineage— Kali does not afflict them.
They maintain association with worldly people while dwelling among the virtuous of their family.
Kali does not indeed afflict those who perform the service of the Kaula;
the Kaulas, assuming various guises and remaining steadfast in the Kula practices,
worship you through those Kula observances— Kali does not indeed afflict them.
The Kali age does not obstruct those who perform the purificatory rites such as the sprinkling of seed, as well as rituals such as the ancestral *śrāddha*, according to their family traditions.
[This applies to] the *kula*-principle, the *kula*-substances, and the *kula*-yogi alone.

Kali does not afflict those who pay homage with devotion; for Kali is a servant to the virtuous— those who are free from crookedness and falsehood, who are pure, who follow the path of their lineage, and who are committed to the welfare of others.
Now, the virtue of the Kali age: O beloved, there is one great virtue in the multitude of faults of the Kali age:
the Kaulas are true to their promise, and [their] welfare is achieved by mere intention.

But in another age, O Goddess, merit and demerit for men were mental; in the Kali age, however, merit is mental, but not so evil-doing. Those who, though devoid of family customs, are always speakers of truth—
Those men who are intent on harming others are servants of the Kali age;
those who are unattached to the duties of their lineage and lustful toward the wives of others,
and those who hate the pillars of their family, should be known as servants of the Kali age.
O Goddess, in this manifest Kali age, all dharmas are weak;
only truth alone shall remain. Therefore, one should become composed of truth. Whatever action a person performs by taking refuge in the dharma of truth, [that alone endures].
Know that very action to be fruitful and true, O lady of noble vows!
Indeed, there is no dharma higher than truth, nor is there any sin greater than falsehood.
Therefore, a mortal should with all his soul take refuge in truth alone.
Worship devoid of truth is in vain; recitation devoid of truth is in vain.
All ritual actions have truth as their root, for there is nothing higher than truth.
Therefore, I have declared this regarding the powerful Kali age of evil deeds.
Even the conduct of the Kula must be performed with truthfulness and manifest intent;
for truth is lost through concealment, and concealment is impossible without falsehood. Therefore, the Kaulika should perform the Kula-sādhana openly.
For the sake of protecting the family tradition (*kuladharma*), dancing should not be considered loathsome;
as it is stated in the *Kulatantres*, [such acts] are not recommended during the powerful Kali age.
In the Kṛta age, Dharma has four feet; in the Tretā age, it is diminished by one foot.
O Goddess! In the Dvāpara age, it was two-footed; in the Kali age, it remains as a mere foot.
Even then, truth, austerity, a portion of charity, and compassion remain.
When the foot of truth is lost, the destruction of Dharma arises.

Therefore, relying upon truth, one should accomplish all ritual actions. O Mistress of the Kula! Where there is no means other than the conduct of the Kula, there would be the entry of falsehood; how then could there be the supreme good?
In every way, a person whose soul is purified by truth should perform all actions prescribed for their respective caste and stage of life according to the path uttered from my mouth—
namely, initiation, worship, recitation, fire-offerings, preparatory rites, and libations.
The vow-taking, marriage, the *puṃsavana*, the *sīmantonnayana*, as well as the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), the naming ceremony, the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*), the journey,
the entry into a new house, and the wearing of new garments and the like.

A person should accomplish all these— the restoration of ponds, wells, and tanks, as well as rites on auspicious lunar days (tithi), the commencement of building a house, consecration, and the installation of deities— according to the procedure prescribed by me.
O Great Goddess! if, in this powerful Kali age, one abandons my teaching, then whatever action is performed will lead to the opposite result.
In the eighth chapter (ullāsa).
Therefore, O Goddess, this has been declared here for the twice-born in this powerful Kali age.

The entitlement to the Gāyatrī belongs [only] to the twice-born, never to others, nor to other mantras, O Supreme Goddess, for the purpose of distinguishing the classes of the twice-born from the Śūdras. This Vedic Sandhyā has been declared prior to the daily ritual (āhnika).
In this world, the most excellent man of virtuous fame and merit, named Rāmahari, was Viśvāsa; he was Dharma incarnate, a great soul who begat two sons, Śrīla and Nārāyaṇa.
These two were peaceful, self-controlled, and possessed of pure hearts; they were the lords of speech, Śrī and Vāṇī, who had become the very life-breath that enchants the world.
He who has consumed the forest of the great enemy's lineage with the fire of his majesty.
Śrī Prāṇakṛṣṇa Viśvāsa begot seven highly prosperous sons who were devoted to the gods and Brahmins and endowed with various virtues.
The elder brother of Śrī Lāṇḍamaya, the virtuous Sadānandamaya;
thereafter Śrī Rāmacandra, possessing the majesty of compassion and righteousness;
and thereafter Śrī Viśvanātha, the soul of the universe, the bestower of knowledge.
After him was Śrī Śambhunātha, whose form was gentle and who was composed of compassion;
then Śrī Kāśīnātha Viśvāsa, the purifier of the Viśvāsa lineage;
and after him, Śrī Candranātha, whose eyes were like the moon and whose nature was one of virtue.
Since these [scholars] are also always striving for the purpose of composing treatises,
I therefore record their names here with great care.
The wise and illustrious Kṛṣṇānanda, renowned throughout the world as the author of the *Tantrasāra*, was born on earth as a lamp for the land of Navadvīpa.
His son here was Kāśīnātha, the author of the *Sārāvalī*; his younger brother was a learned and honored man.
Therefore, he is named Viśvanātha.
Gopāla, renowned for his definitive compositions, had two sons from Madhusudanā: the famous Madhusuta and Kālidāsa.
Kālidāsa’s son was Nātha, who was devoted to Raghuvara and possessed single-minded intellect; and his son here was the wise Maṅgala.
Preceded by Kṛṣṇa.

Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa, the son of Śrī Kṛṣṇamaṅgala and Navavallikā, has composed this second book, titled *Dharma*, endowed with refinement and adorned with flowers and fruits, for the attainment of all desired goals by those possessed of creative genius— thus [ends] the work approved by the venerable Prāṇakṛṣṇa Viśvāsa.
The Dharma-kāṇḍa, comprising the sixth chapter on the description of the fruits of initiation, in the Śrī-Prāṇatoṣiṇī composed by Bhaṭṭācārya Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṅkāra, is completed.
